2021-1-HR01-KA220-HED-000023012.title: Zero food waste education of "Z" generation of European citizens
2021-1-HR01-KA220-HED-000023012.summary:
<< Background >>

The project partners applied for this project to tackle the important issue of waste management, because according to the latest Eurostat data, the EU produces around 2.2 billion tonnes of waste every year. This means that 224.8 million tonnes of municipal waste is generated, which corresponds to an average of 513 kg per person per year. Each year, the EU produces around 86 million tonnes of biowaste, a significant proportion of which is food waste. It is estimated that around 59 million tonnes of food is wasted in the EU each year, which is around 127 kg per person per year, to which young people make a significant contribution. The EU has made separate waste collection one of its key objectives for the coming period, emphasising that effective waste management is priority. The EU is actively working to reduce waste, especially food waste, through various initiatives and strategies. Therefore, the project aims to address the challenges related to food systems, which play a crucial role in economic growth and sustainability in the EU. By focussing on the entire food production cycle, from processing to consumption and recycling of food waste, the project is in line with the EU's objectives to promote environmental sustainability.

<< Objectives >>

The main objective of the ZeeWaste4EU project is to provide a specific age group between 18 and 24 years old, the so-called Generation Z, with additional knowledge and skills on an innovative approach to waste management focussing on food waste (FW). A further aim was to increase young people's understanding and awareness of their responsibilities in relation to FW management and the use of natural resources. To achieve this, it is necessary to strengthen young people's sense of responsibility and enable them to develop and implement effective FW prevention on a personal level and within their families and friends.
Furthermore, through the project we aim to reshape Generation Z's relationship with food resources so that they adopt smarter lifestyles, sustainable consumption patterns and place more emphasis on the prevention of FW. To prepare young people to think critically about FW, the project developed benchmarks on FW in each partner country (PR 1), a data analysis on FW among young people (PR 2), educational materials on FW tailored to young people (PR 3), a self-assessment of FW prevention skills in digital form (PR 4) and the development and maintenance of the online education hub (PR 5) responsible for FW management.

<< Implementation >>

The ZeeWaste4EU project carried out various activities aimed at addressing the generation of food waste and promoting sustainable practises among young people, especially Generation Z. Firstly, the project partners developed standardised methods for conducting research on food waste generation and prevention in the partner countries to ensure the consistency of research in the partner countries. This included the definition of key terms, the creation of data collection protocols and the definition of analytical techniques to be used consistently in all participating countries. 
At the beginning of the project, a Project Steering Committee (PSC) is formed to monitor the progress of the project, consisting of one representative from each partner appointed to the project. A project work plan is developed at the beginning of the project to guide the execution of the work throughout the implementation period to ensure that the roles, responsibilities, rights and obligations of the partners are clearly defined and to ensure consensus and clarity within the consortium on reporting processes, technical and financial management, means of communication, decision-making processes, conflicts and other issues. The roles and responsibilities of each partner are formalised and confirmed in comprehensive partnership agreements signed between the lead applicant and each partner. 
Project management was fully implemented in each partner institution. A work plan with Gannt chart for the project was developed and agreed by the partners. All partners worked closely together to develop the administrative documents of the project, such as the work plan, the dissemination plan and the quality assurance plan. To facilitate the communication of the consortium, the partners jointly decided to share all documents related to the activities and all relevant parts of the project on Google Drive. The lead partner opened the project's Google Drive and was responsible for regularly uploading material to the Drive so that it was visible and accessible to all partners. This method greatly facilitated the availability, visibility and transparency of all documents, activities, budgets and the like for the partners. All these documents were uploaded to a shared folder in Google Drive.
The consortium organised the project planning, implementation and evaluation functions by applying a logic model throughout the project. The basic logic model used in project development defines the following five key areas: (1) Activities, (2) Results, (3) Resources/Inputs, (4) Outcomes and (5) Impact. These five key areas of the logic model are applied to each project activity: (1) Activities: The planned project activity and the tasks to be completed are described in detail. (2) Results: The desired/expected results to be achieved as a result of the planned activity are specified. (3) Resources/Inputs: Data and resources required to complete the activity. (4) Outcomes: Identification of the short and long-term outcomes expected/desired for the activity. (5) Impacts: Description of the long-term impact that the project is expected to have on young people and how each activity will contribute to achieving this impact.
The project results (PR) leaders were selected on the basis of their expertise, capacity and relevant experience. The PR leader was responsible for the coordination of activities and the allocation of resources as well as the quality assurance of results and reports to the project coordinator. A number of specific tools were developed and used throughout the project, including a project contact list and a project folder on Google Drive. The project team reviewed the expected implementation process within the project and defined several activities to achieve it. Specifically, as part of the project, we collected data about food waste generation and practices in the partner countries and the EU. We actively involved the students in monitoring the food waste they generated on a weekly basis by creating food waste diaries that the students who were actively involved in the project kept over a 7-day period. During the seven-day period, in addition to the diary, the students documented their meals with images photos in order to develop mathematical model using Python programing language software that allowed us to calculate food waste after each meal. We also created materials, including manuals and interactive PowerPoint presentations, as well as video content and infographics, with the primary aim of improving students' existing knowledge and skills about food waste. In addition, as part of the project activities, we developed an online self-assessment tool that allowed students to assess their level of knowledge about food waste before and after consulting the e-learning material.
In addition, the partners have carried out many dissemination activities within the project management and implementation budget line, such as the design of the project logo, the creation of the social media pages (Facebook, LinkedIn page), the active preparation of posts on social networks, the project's e-learning platform and organization of multiplier event.

<< Results >>

The following results were achieved: (1) Benchmarking of food waste management, (2) data collection and analysis of food waste generation and behaviour of young people, (3) development of an e-learning toolkit, (4) self-assessment of trainees to improve food waste prevention skills and (5) a food waste e-learning platform. The concrete outputs and results of the project include several key deliverables aimed at addressing food waste generation and prevention. 
(1) Benchmarking: The purpose of benchmarking in the first phase of the project was to create a clear understanding of the current state of food waste production and management practises in the participating countries. Benchmarking enabled the project partners to assess the existing food waste management systems and practises in their countries. By comparing these practises, the project was able to identify the strengths and weaknesses of current approaches to preventing and minimising food waste. In addition, the benchmarking process encouraged knowledge exchange between the project partners and enabled us to exchange best practises and innovative solutions for food waste management. This collaborative approach improved the overall effectiveness of the project and contributed to the development of a trans-European network focussed on food waste prevention. Benchmarking served as a fundamental step in the project, allowing partners to assess the current situation, identify gaps and develop sound strategies for effective food waste management and education. In the end, all the data and results of this benchmarking were included in the handbook jointly produced by the project partners entitled “Food waste generation and prevention: Benchmarking the National Situation”. This handbook was printed and served as promotional and educational material for this project and is available on Erasmus+ project results platform.
(2) Data collection and analysis: The project used both qualitative and quantitative methods, including diaries and images of food waste, surveys, in-depth interviews and questionnaires, to collect data on the generation of food waste among young people. This comprehensive data collection provided a solid foundation for understanding the specific challenges and needs of young people in each country. The most important part of the project from a scientific perspective was the collection of data on the generation of food waste among young people. This was done by using a self-assessment method where participants tracked their food waste over a period of time and recorded the type and amount of food discarded. Namely, participants were asked to keep a food waste diary for one week in which they recorded the types and quantities of food thrown away. A standardised definition of a portion was provided to ensure consistency in the data. As the participants took images before and after the meal, one of the activities was to develop a convolutional neural network (CNN) model to accurately recognise different foods from the participants' images. It aims to assess food waste by comparing images of plates before and after meals to quantify the percentage of waste and integrates advanced machine learning techniques with practical applications in food recognition and waste management. This data of collected images was then compiled for analysis and the results were later published in a scientific journal dealing with waste management (Lubura, J.; Pezo, L.; Sandu, M.A.; Voronova, V.; Donsi, F.; Šic Žlabur, J.; Ribić, B.; Peter, A.; Šurić, J.; Brandić, I.; Kloga, M.; Ostojić, S.; Pataro, G.; Virsta, A.; Oros, A.E.; Micić, D.; Đurović, S.; De Feo, G.; Procentese, A.; Voća, N. (2022): Food Recognition and Food Waste Estimation Using Convolutional Neural Network; Electronics, 11; Article number 3746; https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics11223746). In addition, the partners have developed a unique questionnaire to assess young people's attitudes and behaviour towards food waste, including self-reported data on food waste generation. The questionnaire was distributed to young people in each partner country to assess their food consumption habits, their awareness of the issue of food waste and their personal experiences of food waste. As a final addition to the data, a paper was submitted to the journal Waste Management (IF 7,9). (Voća, N.; Donsi, F.; Sandu, M.A.; Voronova, V.; Šic Žlabur, J.; De Feo, G.; Virsta, A.; Klõga, M.; Lubura, J.; Peter, A.; Scăețeanu, G.V.; Ostojić, S.; Brandić, I.; Pataro, G.; Balaban, D.; Micić, D.; Šurić, J.; Đurović, S.; Procentese, A.; Pezo, L. An Analysis of Food Waste Production and Behavioural Patterns Among Generation Z in Five European Countries). The paper investigates the food waste behaviour of Generation Z in five European countries (Estonia, Italy, Romania, Croatia and Serbia) by analysing food waste diaries and newly developed image recognition techniques. The research aims to understand the types of food most commonly wasted by young people, assess the impact of daily behaviour on waste generation and identify areas for behaviour change. Using the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) model, the study examines the factors that influence the extent of food waste in participants aged 18-24 years. The results show that there are differences in the generation of food waste between the different nationalities analysed. The study also examines constructs such as food waste knowledge, attitudes, financial concerns and health risks associated with food waste behaviour. Structural equation modelling (SEM) is used to assess the consistency of the study expressions with the constructs and to ensure measurement accuracy. The results highlight the complex interplay of sociological, psychological and economic factors that influence food waste behaviour. Recommendations include targeted interventions and policies to close knowledge gaps around waste and promote sustainable food handling practises among young people. By understanding these factors, effective strategies can be developed to reduce food waste and lessen the financial burden on the younger generation. 
(3) Development of educational materials: As part of the project, the partners developed educational materials, including handbooks, interactive PowerPoint presentations, video materials and infographics that emphasise the importance of reducing food waste and provide tips on how to avoid waste in everyday life. These packages were tailored to the interests and needs of young people, with the aim of raising awareness and providing practical guidance on how to reduce food waste. In addition, the partners designed and implemented a training course focussing on food waste prevention and tailored to the needs of young people to equip them with knowledge and skills to prevent food waste. To achieve these outcomes, the authors designed interactive training sessions that included presentations, group activities and discussions on food waste management strategies. This course has been published on an online platform to encourage the active participation and engagement of young people. The e-course consists of 4 modules with the following topics: Module 1 - “Food waste and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)”; Module 2 - “Strategic plan to reduce waste”; Module 3 - “Food waste in urban areas” and Module 4 - “Smart solutions and innovative technologies for sustainable food waste management”. 
(4) Self-assessment tools: The project included the development of an educational self-test that young people can use to assess their own skills and understanding of food waste management. This self-assessment tool can help students recognise opportunities for improvement and encourage them to take proactive steps to reduce their food waste. Self-assessment tools are essential for measuring the project's impact on participants' knowledge and behaviours regarding food waste. By providing a personalised feedback, they contribute to motivate the participants and facilitate continuous improvement and adaptation of educational strategies, ensuring that the project remains effective and responsive to the needs of its participants. This ultimately contributes to the project's goal of promoting sustainable food waste management practices.
(5) Development of an online platform: It is created not only provide information about the project and project results and online courses, but also resources, training materials, videos, interactive tools and information about food waste management that are accessible to young people and the general public. The hub has been designed to be user-friendly, accessible to young people and the general public and to promote continuous learning.
In addition to the results, the partners also delivered: (1) A concrete overall work plan and activity-specific work plans describing all necessary steps and procedures for a smooth implementation of the project (structure, tasks per partner and responsibilities, project milestones, communication arrangements and reporting); (2) Minutes after each partner meeting, written and submitted by the project leader in co-operation with the project partners; (3) A quality assurance plan covering the entire project process to ensure that all activities are carried out effectively and lead to the desired results based on the quality standards agreed in the partnership; (4) A dissemination strategy with a detailed description of the dissemination tools and activities needed to reach the target groups and a final report on dissemination activities at the end of the project; (5) Participant lists of all local national events; (6) Project logo; (7) Production of informative printed material (brochures, posters); (8) Multiplier event and (9) Social media posts on Facebook and LinkedIn.

2021-1-HR01-KA220-HED-000027562.title: Collaborative and transparent use of Learning Analytics in online university courses, valuing the learner role and exploiting advanced monitoring equipment
2021-1-HR01-KA220-HED-000027562.summary:
<< Background >>

The Project with its purpose supports the priority of implementing innovative practices in the digital age. Priority is given to activities promoting innovative methods and tools for learning and teaching as drivers of improving digital transformation. By introducing learning analytics as well as neuromarketing tools and methods, the Project contributed to innovativeness in higher education. All involved partners, as well as other stakeholders, have the opportunity to learn about these tools through the project results publicly available at the project website and Erasmus+ Project Results platform presenting a system of support for upgrading social values and encourage inclusion and internationalization. With the aim of bridging the gap of insufficient student engagement in online learning, Project activities and defined results are derived from focusing on: selecting and exchanging different learning materials, use of sophisticated analysis as learning analytics, eye tracking and neurophysiological responses, and, based on previous analysis, best practices guidelines providing.

<< Objectives >>

The Project objectives included: 
1. Understanding an individual – relating to the problem which occurs in the online environment of students’ low engagement in online teaching and need to find the way how to include them more actively and reach their higher engagement.
2. Exploring environment and engagement – behavioral data analysis and neurophysiological data analysis was used to gather findings that enhance students’ engagement. 
3. Analyzing background processes – use of Learning Analytics  in order to upgrade learning approaches in online learning environment.

<< Implementation >>

The Project included following important activities with the purpose of strengthening consortium and providing contribution to the society: transnational meetings, learning, teaching and training activities, and multiplier events. Within transnational activities, knowledge and experience were exchanged among partners. Learning, teaching and training activity provided practical participation in innovative approach and research, based on which training scheme was assured contributing to sustainability of the Project. Partners learned new skills which they are able to use in their practice now. Multiplier events ensured dissemination of the gathered findings and spreading them much broader from the target groups (students and teachers), as well as establishing contacts with parties having interest in project’s topics assuring further collaborations.

<< Results >>

Project results are divided into 6 results, although separated, they are connected in a way of supporting each other, ensuring a strengthening consortium and delivering value. Results include the following. Firstly, an e-learning platform and learning analytics infrastructure was be provided. This represented the bases for continuing with the following project results. Project then continue with the second result which is focused on collaboration, networking and peer-learning activities. Different online learning materials and approaches were collected and exchanged, and all included partners were able to use them for further analysis and use, as well as target groups (students and teachers) and stakeholders. As the Project is focused on innovative approaches, third result learning/teaching/training material refers to learning analytics and learning how to use it appropriately to provide benefits for students and teachers. The fourth one is focused on forming a training scheme with the purpose of sharing knowledge and ensuring sustainability. Those results revealed findings about  applying bio-metric and neuro-metric data in the process of planning and improving online learning material and gathering insights about students' reactions to different learning materials and approaches. To gather even more precise insights, approach was upgraded with even deeper analysis providing insights about individuals’ neurophysiological data to find out what kind of learning materials and approaches are more engaging to the students. Final, the sixth result implies best practice guidelines/report uniting findings from all previous results and providing concrete examples of upgrading online learning materials and approaches.
topics: New learning and teaching methods and approaches

2021-1-HR01-KA220-HED-000029742.title: Artificial Intelligence for People, Planet, and Profit
2021-1-HR01-KA220-HED-000029742.summary:
<< Background >>

The AI4PPP project was born out of a clear need to equip future leaders with the knowledge and skills to navigate the rapidly evolving world of AI. Universities and MBA programs, as incubators of tomorrow’s decision-makers, have a critical role to play in preparing students for the challenges and opportunities AI presents. Our target audience, MBA students and executives, are poised to lead organizations across both public and private sectors. Yet, research conducted by Algebra University’s MBA program and EY in 2020 revealed a significant gap: while C-level executives recognized the importance of AI, they lacked the understanding to assess its benefits, take the first steps toward integration, or manage the human and organizational changes required for successful AI adoption.

This project aimed to address that gap head-on. By demystifying AI, we sought to provide the education and tools needed to not only understand AI but also to harness its potential effectively. We created a learning environment that bridges the gap between theory and practice. In doing so, we aimed to empower leaders who can drive innovation responsibly and ethically in an AI-driven future.

<< Objectives >>

The AI4PPP project aimed to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into business education, equipping future leaders with AI-driven decision-making skills that align with the People, Planet, Profit (PPP) sustainability framework. By collaborating with universities and MBA programs, the project sought to develop AI-based teaching methodologies, digital tools, and real-world case studies that enhance the understanding of AI’s role in sustainable business. AI4PPP focused on bridging the gap between AI innovation and business education, ensuring that graduates are prepared to apply AI ethically and effectively in tackling economic, social, and environmental challenges. Additionally, the project aimed to increase AI literacy among educators, enabling them to integrate AI-driven insights into curricula and foster a new generation of responsible business leaders.

<< Implementation >>

The AI4PPP was implemented through a series of carefully planned and executed activities, divided into horizontal and theme related tasks, each contributing to the project’s overall success.
Horizontal tasks focused on the overall project management and coordination. This involved keeping activities on track, both in terms of timelines and budgets, organizing regular meetings, preparing detailed reports, and maintaining clear communication with the National Agency. Transnational Meetings played a crucial role in ensuring quality control, financial oversight, and the evaluation of progress. Additionally, Multiplier Events were held to share the project’s achievements and insights with a broader audience, fostering engagement and collaboration beyond the immediate team.

The theme-related tasks formed the heart of the project. It all started with a Gap Analysis, which assessed the potential of AI across industries and identified the specific training needs of our target audience. This was followed by a DACUM Analysis, which delved into the roles and responsibilities of AI experts, ensuring the educational content was both relevant and aligned with industry demands. These insights directly informed the development of a tailored syllabus, designed to be practical, adaptable, and impactful for diverse learner groups.
Next, we developed educational materials grounded in real-world industry examples, making the content relatable and actionable. These materials were rigorously tested in pilot programs, allowing us to evaluate their effectiveness and refine the learning experience. To further enhance the program’s relevance, we conducted in-depth interviews with industry representatives, gathering up-to-date AI implementation scenarios that brought the theoretical concepts to life.

Finally, we prepared the necessary documentation for micro-credential certification, ensuring the program’s credibility and long-term value. This step offered partners the opportunity to integrate the program into their broader educational offerings.

These activities collectively aimed to build a sustainable, high-quality AI education program that would benefit the partners, target groups, and industry long after the project's completion.

<< Results >>

The AI4PPP project produced a range of tangible outputs and impactful results that significantly contribute to the integration of AI into business education and practice.

The GAP analysis report was the starting point, providing meaningful insights about the modern MBA program landscape. It touched upon the inclusion of AI and digital transformation in business education and projected the growing necessity of AI-driven knowledge among business leaders (beyond IT). The report acted as a basis for creating further project deliverables, including syllabus development, learning materials, and applied case studies.

DACUM analysis report was to determine industries that were ready for AI adoption. The report was created through interviewing non-technical, C-level executives, which set the stage for AI issues faced in various industries. Analysis was crucial in setting up the design of educational materials because it provided direct needs of the industry and understanding of AI issues, thus making the project tailored to real demands.

One of the main deliverables of the project was the syllabus, to enhance MBA and MA business courses with a focus on the application of AI in business. Written in English to be globally usable, the syllabus provided a blueprint for the production of learning materials in the next phases and was to be universally transferable across higher education settings.
The educational material that was created was at the centre of the AI4PPP initiative. Nine industry-based modules were created, with each one focusing on an actual business case that illustrates AI applications in sectors like tourism, logistics, healthcare, and smart cities. These ready-to-use, open-source resources are designed to introduce AI to business education naturally, offering universities and training institutions flexible resources easily customizable to varied environments.

The piloting report documented the experiment and evaluation of these learning modules in real-life settings, ranging from university teaching, workshops, and industrial practices to web training. This report highlights implementation methodology, participant recruiting (both the AI professionals as well as other non-technical professionals), and customization to align with diverse needs for learning. Feedback gathered from 124 participants across Croatia, Spain, and Slovenia was invaluable, providing insights into the effectiveness of the materials, their impact on participants, and areas for improvement.

The AI implementation scenarios report explored the real-world applications of AI across various industries, sharing success stories, challenges, and best practices. By conducting interviews with AI implementation companies and industry specialists, this report bridged the gap between AI theory and practice and offered actionable recommendations for companies considering AI adoption.

In addition to these core outputs, each of the project partners created the documentation to support the application for micro-credentials for the piloted programs. Such documentation facilitates compliance with national legislation and micro-credentialing standards, allowing the easy recognition of such programs across partnering countries.
The AI4PPP project achieved several other important outcomes. The integration of AI in higher education was substantially facilitated, particularly in the case of MBA, imparting business students with strategic insights into AI-driven decision-making and paving the way for future leadership roles in an AI-empowered business environment.
The initiative also contributed to improving data literacy, enabling individuals, regardless of technical skills, to process and analyse data efficiently. This core ability is relevant to the successful integration of AI so that more professionals can engage with AI technologies and apply them in practice.
Moreover, the project acted as an important driver to accelerate AI adoption in non-tech industries, with the aim to equip businesses with the technology and expertise needed to harness AI towards enhanced efficiency, innovation, and competitiveness. In providing actionable insights on AI application, AI4PPP facilitated businesses to make conscious decisions on the manner in which they ought to apply AI within their business.

Lastly, AI4PPP fostered greater collaboration between higher education institutions (HEIs) and businesses, consolidating relationships that foster innovation and regional economic growth. By bridging the gap between industry and academia, the project facilitated successful transfer of AI skills and knowledge to real-world application, enabling both academic success and business development.
topics: Creating new, innovative or joint curricula or courses
Cooperation between educational institutions and business

2021-1-HR01-KA220-HED-000031177.title: Introduction of joint short-cycle ICT courses for better employability of students and graduates
2021-1-HR01-KA220-HED-000031177.summary:
<< Background >>

The primary objective of this project was to effectively respond to the continuously increasing demand for additional data science and artificial intelligence (AI) competencies in professional fields that have not been traditionally or directly associated with these disciplines. In today's rapidly evolving technological landscape, data science and AI are being increasingly integrated into a wide range of industries, including but not limited to medicine, healthcare, traditional engineering, and economics. As a result, there exists a growing knowledge gap among both recent graduates and current professionals in these and other domains, where foundational and applied knowledge in data science and AI is becoming an essential asset rather than an optional skill.  

With this in mind, the project aimed to bridge this knowledge gap by providing opportunities for individuals working in these fields to acquire a fundamental understanding of key concepts, methodologies, and applications of data science and artificial intelligence. The intention was not only to help professionals and graduates develop a clearer comprehension of the digital and data-driven environment in which they operate but also to facilitate their professional growth.

<< Objectives >>

The first objective of the project was to determine the knowledge gap of current or recent graduates of the fields that are not traditionally connected to the data science and artificial intelligence - such as medicine, economics or engineering, in regards to that area. Then, the second objective was to create a set of classes, to be integrated into a short-cycle course that will serve to directly address the determined knowledge gaps. The course was designed as a short-cycle course split into mandatory and elective parts. Allowing the participants to cover what were determined as basic, fundamental knowledge points, in the field of data science and artificial intelligence and then select additional courses to address their specific upskilling needs - whether it is additional knowledge in fundamental structures of data science and artificial intelligence (such as mathematics, big data), or domain specific knowledge that may be helpful for them personally.

<< Implementation >>

Three main activities were implemented in the project. 

First activity was the design of a survey for determining the relevant knowledge gaps, targeted at the potential participants of the project. After the potential participants filled the survey, the provided information was analyzed. This was done to fulfill three separate goals - first it was to identify the potential participants and disseminate the possibility of participating in the course. Second was to determine the knowledge gaps that the potential participants are interested in addressing. The third was determining the access to computers and types of tools the participants may have and be comfortable using, to lower possible barriers to entry.

The second activity was the development of the classes that covered the needs identified in the first activity, This was achieved through the detailed analysis, combined with the existing knowledge-base of the participating organizations. The determination was to organize the course in two parts - mandatory and elective. The mandatory part consisted of four classes that were designed to cover the basics necessary for other classes, and the knowledge which is generally beneficial in the data science and artificial intelligence landscape, such as mathematics and computer programming (with focus on the tools and concepts used in the data science and artificial intelligence). Each of the partners was then tasked with the design of the courses, according to their specialized knowledge and expertise, resulting in a planned curriculum and course materials.

The third activity was the organization of the pilot course. The pilot course lasted for four weeks and accepted over 100 participants. The realized classes and materials were used in this course. Before and after the completion of the course, the participants filled out a self-assessment survey, which was analyzed as the final part of the final activity.

<< Results >>

The main results of the project were:

1. The Report on in-depth analysis of the state-of-the-art in the area of DS and AI. This report consists of the analyzed results of the survey, as well as the disseminated survey itself. This report was internally used for the process of curriculum and class design, in order to determine the topics of interest and preliminary abilities of potential applicants, it can also serve as an outward report towards wider education area as to an informative document on current interests and knowledge gap in data science and artificial intelligence, for those students and recent graduates who study areas not traditionally associated with data science and artificial intelligence.

2. The curriculum of the course. This document lists the classes and described them in the context of aims, objectives, expected learning outcomes and subject content. The document in question can be used as a blueprint for application of similar courses in different countries and institutions, as it was designed in mind with accreditation requirements for non-ECTS courses organized by higher education institutions.

3. The course materials - the full course materials for the fourteen classes that were the part of the designed curriculum are available publicly as the course result. These documents allow for two important elements. First is the ability for interested parties, and past participants, who were unable to asses the courses and learn using the provided materials. The second is a simpler application of this or similar course methodology to different organizations who may be interested.

4. Course lectures in video form - at request of participants all of the lectures were filmed and made publicly available to them and other interested parties, in order to facilitate simpler learning in tandem with the course materials.

5. Course evaluation - the final result is the analysis of participants self-assessment in data science and artificial intelligence knowledge performed prior and after the course, as well as their overall satisfaction with the course.

2021-1-HR01-KA220-HED-000032220.title:
QUEST- promoting Quality intErnships in Sustainable Tourism and cultural heritage
management
2021-1-HR01-KA220-HED-000032220.summary:
<< Background >>

According to the WTTC, in 2019, travel and tourism contributed 10.3% to global GDP, encompassing both direct and indirect impacts. The sector accounted for 4.4% of total global investments and 6.8% of global exports of goods and services, making it the third-largest export sector globally. Before the pandemic, tourism supported 333 million jobs worldwide, representing 10.3% of global employment. Moreover, each job within the tourism sector was estimated to generate approximately 1.5 additional jobs in related industries.
The Mediterranean region remains one of the world’s most popular tourist destinations. However, it faces critical vulnerabilities. Post-COVID, the region’s tourism sector is grappling with several pressing challenges, particularly:
*Workforce vulnerabilities: Many tourism jobs are precarious, with low wages and a lack of skill development. Vulnerable groups—including young people, women, migrants, and individuals over 50.
Tourism remains a key economic driver for rural economies in Europe, offering employment opportunities that can help reduce global youth unemployment. In today’s VUCA world, ensuring that tourism graduates are adequately prepared has become essential for the sector’s resilience and sustainability

<< Objectives >>

The primary objective of QUEST is to enhance the employability of higher education (HE) students in the tourism sector—an industry characterized by rapid innovation and significantly impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic. Addressing the ongoing challenge of equipping students with relevant knowledge and employability skills involved two key approaches:
1.	Integrating employability skills into curricula: This is achieved by embedding supervised work experience directly within academic programs.
2.	Providing stand-alone skills-based training: This approach focuses on offering dedicated training modules to build essential job-related skills.
By adopting these strategies, QUEST aimed to prepare students for the dynamic and evolving demands of the tourism sector.

<< Implementation >>

To achieve its objectives, the QUEST partnership addressed student employability by analyzing skill gaps, developing a flexible long-distance training program supported by innovative tools (the QUEST project results) created during the project, and organizing five blended mobility sessions for students (involving a total of 30 participants). Additionally, specific training sessions were conducted for HEI staff and company internship tutors to better support students.
In parallel, QUEST developed and implemented new policies and a cooperative methodology to foster collaboration between the education and business sectors, aiming to enhance the effectiveness of the designed methodology in improving student employability.

<< Results >>

The QUEST project achieved the following key outcomes:
•	PR1 QUEST Flexible Learning Programme: An innovative, skill-based program designed for higher education (HE) students entering the tourism sector labor market.
•	PR2 QUEST E-Learning Platform: A unique digital platform developed to support HE students, HEI trainers, and organizational tutors throughout the learning program and work experience phases.
•	PR3 QUEST Policy and Cooperation Methodology: A formalized cooperation agreement established between HEIs and tourism organizations in the Mediterranean region, supported by a Cultural Route of the Council of Europe.
•	PR4 QUEST Manual: A comprehensive publication documenting the QUEST methodology, learning program, activities, and results, created to facilitate future implementation and further exploitation of the project’s outcomes.
topics: Cooperation between educational institutions and business

2021-1-HU01-KA220-HED-000027542.title:
LEAN in Medical Education: Reaching for Quality Management Tools to Teach
Human Anatomy Effectively in a Multicultural and Multilingual Learning Space
2021-1-HU01-KA220-HED-000027542.summary:
<< Background >>

University of Pécs applied for this project because we recognized the growing need for medical educators in Central Europe to align with global standards in medical education. As the World Federation of Medical Education (WFME) introduces new accreditation requirements in 2024, there is a significant gap in knowledge and teaching practices among anatomy educators in the region. This project offers an opportunity to address these gaps and enhance the quality of education in multicultural and multilingual contexts.
The key needs we aimed to address include improving awareness of international quality standards, promoting student-centered pedagogy, and enhancing assessment methods for evaluating students' professional attitudes. Additionally, we planed to focus on mental health management in the academic environment, an area where many educators in Central Europe lack training despite their medical backgrounds. By providing modern teaching tools and methodologies, such as online training modules and cross-cultural collaboration, this project will help anatomists globally adapt to evolving educational standards, ensuring that anatomy teaching remains relevant and of high quality, meeting the needs of future medical professionals.   

<< Objectives >>

By implementing this project, the beneficiaries achieved several key outcomes. Participants gained a comprehensive understanding of legal requirements and international standards, helping them identify gaps and misconceptions in their knowledge. They explored the history and evolution of anatomy teaching, recognizing strengths and weaknesses in their own methods. The project enhanced their understanding of the psychological and cognitive processes involved in studying anatomy, fostering professional attitude development in medical students. Participants learned about student-centered learning and relevant pedagogical tools, identifying areas for improvement in their practices. The project also highlighted the relationship between mental health, student attitudes, and teaching methods. By addressing these issues, the project supports Central European universities in aligning their teaching traditions with international standards. It fosters collaboration with renowned institutions, revealing gaps in existing traditions and exploring their sources. Ultimately, the project aims to improve dropout rates, mental health, and professional attitudes among anatomists and students, contributing to global improvements in medical education.

<< Implementation >>

The most essential activities of the project were connected to the development of the project results. In the first period of the project, partners conducted research to map the anatomy teaching practices and traditions of each participating medical schools.
Each partner coordinator researched national requirements for quality teaching and intended learning outcomes (ILOs) in medical education based on their country’s legislation.
We also conducted questionnaire surveys to assess the quality of anatomy education and to identify the satisfaction of students and teachers.
At the Kick-off meeting in Brno, Czechia, international standards were presented, and key definitions for relevant assessments and documentation were clarified. Over the first half of the project participants conducted a literature review on the epistemic, psychological, sociocultural, and economic values of studying human anatomy.
Throughout the research work and professional discussions, as the first phase of the project was implemented, we were able to identify 5 TOPICs around which the results of the project were organised.
1. TOPIC 1 - Quality Standars of Medical Education
2. TOPIC 2 - Development of Professional Values and attitudes Through Teaching Anatomy
3. TOPIC 3 - Traditions in Anatomy
4. TOPIC 4 - Pedagogy in Medical Education
5. TOPIC 5 - Mental Health Management of Students and Teachers
In summer 2022 experts led a brainstorming workshop (LTTA 1) at Magdalene College, Cambridge, exploring the influence of culture and society on doctors' attitudes, both historically and in modern anatomy education. The workshop also focused on student-centered pedagogy, with educational developers from Karolinska Institute guiding participants. An important seminar on mental health management in academic settings was conducted, discussing how medical performance indicators can impact mental health and strategies for managing these risks.

In the second project period (2023), participants developed assessment tools with guidance from Karolinska Institute experts. These tools focused on measuring anatomists attitudes toward professional values while teaching anatomy. A training workshop at the University of Pécs in Summer 2023 (LTTA 2) helped to understand sustainable development goals, and how it can be integrated into anatomy teaching.

During the final period, new tools were tested within anatomy courses (as pilot acions), and feedback was gathered from other anatomists, from national anatomical societies and other participants of multiplier events, including medical students. The findings were shared at multiplier events in Pécs, Telc and Zagreb, including national conferences, and incorporated into an online teacher training module.

To ensure the collaboration and knowledge exchange among partner institutions 5 Transnational Project Meetings were organised during the project implementation period. These meetings allowed participants to align project goals, share best practices, and it ensured that the project's objectives were being met consistently. Additionally, they promoted a sense of shared responsibility and strengthened partnerships, enhancing the overall impact and sustainability of the project outcomes. These meetings were also important from a project management point of view, as participants coulf discuss milestones and stages of project implementation, and could discuss technical, financial issues as well.

<< Results >>

We have developed training materials for the exploration of attitudes, skills and knowledge of any anatomists about teaching in medical education institutions globally. 
First we organized and recorded academic lectures from experts of leading European universities about teaching anatomy in the contexts of existing traditions and best practices, of fostering professionalism, of global standards in inclusive medical education, of student centered pedagogy, and of mental health management. These were published on the internet. 
Next, we developed self-reflective tools for the exploration of attitudes, skills and knowledge of any anatomists in the contexts of the same topics: teaching traditions, professionalism, global standards in medical education, management of student centered pedagogy: constructive alignment and mental health management. These were also published on the internet. 
After validation of these tools, explorations among partner anatomists were conducted, analysed, and prepared for publication in peer-reviewed international educational journals. Based on our findings, recommendations for effective teacher development strategies were formulated for any anatomists globally. These were published on the internet in short summaries and in a downloadable Guidebook. Lecture materials, self-assessment tools, and recommendations were disseminated by organizing workshop events in 2023 and in 2024 at national anatomical societies’ conferences of partner countries (Hungary, Czechia, Croatia). A teacher training MOOC has also been developed and is now available globally for free enrolment through the ‘EDUC’ digital alliance of European universities.
All of these results were initially pursued and finally achieved. There was no result which was initially pursued but finally not achieved.

Other achievements of this project which were not planned, include:

1.	a Central European partner (Zagreb) of this project has performed a substantial curricular reform. A full report of this pilot achievement is published on the project website.  Smaller scale pilot actions have also been implemented, in Brno and in Pécs. The pilot measurements, their analysis, and experiences from the project events have been compiled into a key intellectual outcome: an online training course for anatomists worldwide.
2.	another Central European partner (Masaryk) is coordinating a new Collaborative Online Interactive Learning (COIL) course for medical students to foster the development of professionalism through learning anatomy. This course is called ‘COIL Clinical Anatomy Lecture Series’ and has been successfully launched during this project through four academic semesters at four partner universities.
3.	the project coordinator institution  (Pécs) of this project has been invited and successfully applied for joining an international student research collaboration in anatomy fostering the development of professionalism through joint research projects (https://www.internationalcollaborationexchange.org/). Joining this partnership is a direct result of the successful collaboration between partners of this project (Cambridge and Pécs). 
Pilot actions have also been implemented in Zagreb, in Brno and in Pécs. The pilot measurements, their analysis, and experiences from the project events have been compiled into a key intellectual outcome: an online training course for anatomists worldwide.
topics: Initial and continuous training for teachers, trainers and other education staff

2021-1-IE02-KA220-HED-000027590.title: Undergraduate Physiotherapy Pain Science Curriculum Augmentation Project
2021-1-IE02-KA220-HED-000027590.summary:
<< Background >>

The UPPScAle strategic partnership is a transnational collaboration aiming to innovate, improve and standardise Bachelor Physiotherapy pain science curricula across Europe. Pain science is a core field in a physiotherapy curriculum and physiotherapists are essential members of healthcare teams managing people with pain. Chronic pain affects millions of people worldwide across the lifespan and is a global cause of disability in the developed and developing world. Pain management is the primary reason people attend physiotherapy for treatment. 

However, there is currently no standardised curriculum or common training framework for physiotherapists, with professional education about pain management repeatedly documented as inadequate worldwide. Hence the inequities in pain science knowledge across Europe results in inequitable health service delivery and costs and most importantly to significant differences in patients quality of life. 
Greater connectivity between higher education systems with standardised curricula will also reduce obstacles that face physiotherapists applying to practise their profession across geographical borders in EU member states.

<< Objectives >>

The UPPScAle project objectives focused on harmonising pain science education in Physiotherapy programmes across Europe by offering a roadmap for academics 

UPPScAle had three main objectives:
Objective 1: Curriculum benchmarking of Bachelor Physiotherapy pain science curricula against international best practice (European Pain Federation EFIC Pain Physiotherapy curriculum) to identify gaps in learning;

Objective 2: Augmenting knowledge and skills through evidence-based professional practices

Objective 3: Enhancing and standardising teaching and learning by developing an Open Education Resource that addresses identified limitations to support academics with student learning across Europe and beyond.

<< Implementation >>

(i)PA1: Needs Analysis: A curriculum mapping matrix was developed and undertaken to identify limitations in current teaching and learning in pain science and management. This included partners (i) mapping the content of their pain science curricula against the European Pain Federation EFIC Physiotherapy core curriculum, (ii) identifying the stage where pain science was taught (iii) the number of teaching hours and (iv) how pain science was taught (clinical education, lecture, practical session etc). Partners circulated the mapping matrix to their relevant colleagues in their department to complete
 A 3 day curriculum planning session was then undertaken with partners.  The results of the mapping matrix were reviewed and common content taught as well as and limitations identified. Stakeholder feedback was also sought as to curriculum content requirements. This involved a one day workshop with partners and stakeholders [current physiotherapy students  / recent graduates from all Partner organisations, along with people living with pain  (recruited from Ireland) to inform the curriculum content]. This one day stakeholder session was facilitated by experts in curriculum design in NUID UCD Teaching and Learning Centre. The 3 day meeting was held 03/2022 (Dublin, UCD). (WP1). This took place at the end of the pandemic but to be cautious the stakeholder session took place virtually. A positive of this is that it allowed students from the five partner sites to meet and discuss their physiotherapy programmes, as well as hearing the 'patient's' voice. The partners met in person.

 (ii) PA2: Capacity Building: Based on the identified common limitations in the partners curricula (PA1) two week long in-person Train-the Trainer Pain Schools were developed and run in order to standardise and up-skill academic partners with both theoretical and hands-on skills development sessions.The first School was held in September 2022 (Utrecht, HU) (TtT1) the second in January 2023 (Ljubljana) Advanced TtT. Comprehensive School manuals were developed to support participants' learning that included key learning objectives, references, self-assessment section for each lecture / practical session. A reflective journal (not part of the original grant) was also developed to allow participants to reflect after each lecture, at the end of each day and at the end of the School on what they had learnt and how it could be integrated into their own Physiotherapy programme. Bringing together academic and clinical education staff facilitated intercultrual learning throughout the duration of the Schools

(iii) PA3: The UPPScAle team planned and developed an Open Education Resource (OER) that housed the materials developed during PA2 Train-the-Trainer Pain Schools and was widely disseminated through national and international conferences and via the projects social media platforms (twitter, facebook). Feedback about the OER content was sought and where appropriate implemented into the individual lectures to enhance the content.


<< Results >>

1. Open educational Resource

We developed the UPPScAe OER to house all educational outputs from the UPPScAle project. 
This included
 (i) the content developed for the two Train-the Trainer Pain Schools that had been identified during the curriculum review process (PA1) which will support key competences development and new pain science and management teaching and learning
(ii) Pain School manuals- developed to comprehensively support the knowledge and skills content of the Pain Schools  They includes learning objectives, key references and a self assessment quiz for each lecture. 
(iii) Reflective Journals - allow those reviewing the platform to consider their new learning and plan for new teaching (translated into partners language)
This will augment and promote excellence on pain science learning, teaching and skills development that healthcare professionals, patients and health services will ultimately benefit from. 
(iv) New EFIC core curriculum for pain science education in Bachelor / pre-registration physiotherapy programmes (not in original grant)

The OER is hosted by UCV and is fully accessible. https://uppscale.eu/

2. Open source files accessibility

All resources from the UPPScAle Project (submitted academic paper, content from the Train-the Trainer Pain Schools including a comprehensive supporting manual and a reflective journal, and the EFIC core curriculum for Undergraduate / pre-registration physiotherapy programmes are all freely available for institutions removing the barrier of funding issues that arise in institutions across Europe

3. Special interest group

A  New network of Physiotherapists in pain science education has been approved within the European Network of Physiotherapists in Higher Education (ENPHE).  This was  established and is being led by the HU Partner lead Harriet Wittink. The first meeting is in April 2024 (annex, dissemination). This is a significant sustainable development as it will help academics and clinical education staff to engage with each other, sharing knowledge on the topic within a large European organisation (156 member institutions and representing 31 countries). It will promote the UPPScAle OER and the new EFIC BSc Pain Science Physiotherapy curriculum. Going forward it will also allow for discussion around the development of a common training framework for physiotherapy education. This would ultimately enhance patient care, reduce healthcare costs and limit obstacles faced by physiotherapists seeking to have their qualifications recognised when they wish to practice professionally across geographical borders of European Union member states. 

4. Interconnectivity

Greater interconnectivity was achieved through (i) academics and clinical education staff meeting and networking during the Pain Schools (ii) The ENPHE pain education  network group will ensure that thoose teaching pain science can formally meet to network, learn and lead on the development of pain education in physiotherapy programmes across Europe. ENPHE holds two meetings annually. (iii) Through the promotion of the UPPScAle project and dissemination of results through multiple outlets: international conferences, social media, the Erasmus+ results platform and posting on https://use.edusources.nl/instellingen/hu-nl which is a national Dutch platform for sharing higher education resources, this project will further enhance inter-connectively and teaching excellence between universities in Europe, increasing their capacity to operate jointly at transnational level, boosting internationalisation of their educational and research activities, and through exchanging or developing new practices and methods as well as sharing and confronting ideas. 

Interconnectivity between the UPPScAle partners has led to future projects. The UPPScAle Partners have agreed to continue to work together to enhance pain science education. Led by the University of Applied Science, Zagred, Croatia we have submitted an application for Erasmus Blended Intensive Programme in Higher Education (BIP) for a BSc Physiotherapy students pain science summer School (August 2024, see annex). This will bring students together from the five Partner sites to learn together. The Partners have also joined the University College Dublin Centre for Translational Pain Research to continue to collaborate in the future on research studies (www.ucd.ie/CTPR)

2021-1-IE02-KA220-HED-000035812.title: Developing Information and Research Skills for Business, Innovation and Entrepreneurship
2021-1-IE02-KA220-HED-000035812.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project with the aim of reinforcing and enhancing knowledge transfer between academia and business in European Union (EU) countries and to enable HEI's to provide increased and specialist information support to Research, Business and Innovation in the EU and in the regions that they serve. This was achieved by improving and increasing the level of competencies & skills of Information Specialist staff in the EU partner institutions in the project. INRS enhanced and built on the skills of staff in these universities, so as to strengthen their abilities to provide quality, relevant supports to business, researchers and local enterprise in the Regions. The project has addressed the need to improve the relevance of higher-level skills provision to Society and to the economy in the Regions. INRS has addressed
the most critical training needs of 21st century Information Specialist staff in the Information Age to enhance their library skills in the area of business, research and innovation. This has been achieved through the creation of the INRS Modular Curriculum featuring a complete range of modern Information Specialist, Information Literacy and other key transferable skills need for enterprise.

<< Objectives >>

The main objectives of the INRS project were to reinforce and enhance knowledge transfer between academia and business in European Union (EU) countries and to enable HEIs to provide increased and specialist information support to Research, Business and Innovation in the EU and in the regions that they serve. The project aimed to develop an Information Specialist (IS) staff development strategy focused on improving the standards, range and quality of library performance in providing support to business, entrepreneurship, innovation and research in the EU with particular focus on improving key transferable, lifelong learning skills. The project aimed to improve the relevance of higher-level skills provision to Society and to the economy in the Regions and expand Information Specialist engagement with employers and business for the development of key transferable skills in the Regions that are critical for business, research and innovation. The project aimed for an enhancement in quality of teaching and learning in the EU, hence it was vital that the project was carried out transnationally. INRS increased participation in education, training and the labour market to significantly expand skills supply to our stakeholders. 

<< Implementation >>

The following activities were implemented:

- Developed and implemented the Blended INRS Curriculum including associated training events for staff
- Developed the Guide for Best Practices and Case Studies
- Held various Transnational Project Meetings including the Kick off, Interim and Final Meetings
- Created a Handbook for Information Specialists
- Develop with Partners the INRS Trainers Toolkit
- Held three INRS Short-term joint staff training events and three Multiplier events during the project lifetime
- Effectively developed and maintained the INRS Online Platform.
- Disseminated effectively about the project results on the institutional, national and international levels.

<< Results >>

The project has produced the INRS Training curriculum (PR1) for Librarians, developed jointly by the project partners based on international recommendations, covering 6 modules. INRS has also produced the Handbook for Information Specialists (PR2)  containing recommendations and examples of good training practice for librarians and information specialists in providing enhanced support and services to research, business, innovation and entrepreneurship. The project also delivered the INRS Trainers Toolkit (PR3), consisting of support materials such as lesson plans, PowerPoint presentations, and example assignments for use by the staff involved in the teaching and mentoring process of the new INRS Training curriculum to library users to provide them with a set of materials to support them in rolling out the INRS curriculum. The project has delivered the INRS Online Platform (PR4) providing up-to-date information on Knowledge Transfer and Entrepreneurial education as well as functioning as an online repository dedicated to Information Specialists, offered in open access, as an E Learning Platform addressed to the project target group, that includes the online version of modules developed within O1. Finally, another key concrete result of the project is the Guide for Best Practices and Case Studies (PR5), this a resource that Librarians have available to them when teaching the INRS Curriculum to library users. It helps them be more proficient in implementing the new INRS training curriculum and fostering the professional development of all stakeholders.

2021-1-IT02-KA220-HED-000027572.title: Beyond the Emergency. Telecare for Non-Communicable Diseases through Simulation Techniques
2021-1-IT02-KA220-HED-000027572.summary:
<< Background >>

The Beyond the Emergency. Telecare for Non-Communicable Diseases through Simulation Techniques- BeEmTel project was created as a response to the pandemic. Covid-19 revealed weaknesses in the health-care system, especially in connection with the care of fragile patients, and in the training system, which remains unable to tackle the important challenge of reforming the ways that patients are treated and monitored. By 2050 in Europe the proportion of older adults will be increased. Most Non-Communicable Diseases (NCD) are deeply connected with aging. Given the main gaps highlighted in the G20 digital health report of December 2020, it was time to strengthen specialist training courses for additional skills so that NCD patients can be taken care of with telemedicine support at the European level. In such a challenging context, the BeEmTel Partnership is still convinced that there is an urgent need to promote strategies for improving teaching methods in the clinical practice, both face-to-face and remote.This is essential in order to meet the needs and continuous attention required by the most fragile subjects with NCDs as well as address the need for support by family members and caregivers.

<< Objectives >>

Doctors, nurses, psychologists, and psychiatrists will increasingly require multidisciplinary training that includes digital skills and more specific practical and clinical competencies. However, there is no widespread availability of specific courses and exams on the characteristics of telecare at the European level, which, in practice, is not taught during the ordinary academic degree course in medicine or nursing. Specialised training, when possible, is filled in later in a phase of working life that is already professionalized. This approach not only provides valuable training but also has the potential to significantly reduce healthcare costs and improve patient access to care. The BeEmTel Partnership strongly believes that by integrating telemedicine into degree curricula, medical schools can enhance learners' education by equipping them with essential competencies for patient care. This approach not only provides valuable training but also has the potential to significantly reduce healthcare costs and improve patient access to care. The pilot e-course proposed by the BeEmTel project seeks to fill this serious and educational gap.

<< Implementation >>

The main specific objectives of the BeEmTel project are two: 
1.	The creation of the course (divided into 2 parts, each of 80 hours). 
2.	Creation of the freely downloadable Digital Toolkit. 
The general objective of the BeEmTel partnership was to create an innovative European curriculum dedicated to Telecare for chronic diseases through educational tools based on remote simulation techniques. BeEmTel believes that remote simulation techniques - such as Telesimulation - should be implemented by university students as early as undergraduate courses. Telesimulation refers to a new teaching methodology in which telecommunication and healthcare simulation are combined to provide effective educational support. One of the aims of the advanced training project is precisely to disseminate theoretical and applied knowledge through high-fidelity simulations. This knowledge will be useful for developing a new clinical and decision-making approach as future professionals. The Partnership is convinced that there is an urgent need to promote strategies to improve teaching methods in clinical practice, both face-to-face and remotely. This is essential in order to meet the needs and ongoing attention required by the most vulnerable subjects with NCDs, and at the same time address the need for support from family members and caregivers. The pandemic crisis has accelerated the adoption of remote simulation (i.e., live simulation of clinical observation scenarios), enabling inclusive and high-quality multidisciplinary training aimed at a variety of recipients with social and economic difficulties, educational differences, and physical impairments. The implemented activities were focused on the creation of e-course, its delivery including two immersive weeks of learning and teaching experiences, the creation of the Digital Toolkit, and therefore the general dissemination of the Telemedicine-teaching method created by the BeEmTel Group, starting from the Universities involved in the Partnership.

<< Results >>

The concrete outputs of BeEmTel are 5 and coincide with the Project Results.
PR 1. Outline the curriculum for the management of chronic conditions through Telemedicine. Thanks to the literary review and a Delphi study, the BeEmTel Partnership was able to identify the skills needed for chronic care management through the use of telemedicine. The Partnership, then, defined the main topic areas and learning outcomes to be translated into the planning of the e-Course and training modules. 
PR 2. Design the training and create the content for the modules of the “European course on management of chronic conditions through Telemedicine.” The final organisation of the modules’ contents entailed the allocation of teachers, preparation of didactic materials (including video lessons and learning tools), and the recruitment of participants from degree courses. 
PR 3. Create the digital platform for the e-Course. The digital platform ensures that all participants can access materials in English, Italian, Croatian, Greek, Romanian, and German. The BeEmTel digital platform hostes material in several languages and be a virtual hub under constant monitoring: from online lessons, to handouts in the various European languages, to participant enrolment, to forums for peer discussion and questions for teachers and tutors. 
PR 4. Deliver the training course through e-Learning modules and contents. To ensure equal and high-quality learning, participants carried out an evaluation at the end of the e-Course. The LTTA workshops at UPO and LMU (C1 and C2) represented an educational challenge for teachers and an intense training experience for participants. Here the participants had the chance to enjoy being at the heart of pedagogical medical simulation. PR 4
involves an evaluation of the curriculum and skills acquired during the e-Course and LTTAs. 
PR 5. Creation of the Transferability Digital Toolkit (TDT), including educational resources and good practices. The Transferability Digital Toolkit (TDT) aims to support public and private institutions that wish or need to design, develop, implement, and promote teaching-learning strategies on Teleassistance, applied to chronic diseases and emergencies, through both traditional and innovative Medical Simulation methodologies.
The current TDT, in particular, provides tools, models, best practices, and specific case studies derived from the pilot educational experience delivered by the BeEmTel project, focusing on chronic disease management through the use of proven technologies in the educational field. The TDT contains numerous qualitative and quantitative resources from the BeEmTel project e-Course, representing a valuable educational and content-rich repository of the latest evidence on telemedicine practices and telesimulation in the management of chronic diseases.
The educational measures presented offer academic institutions and Life Sciences associations guidance, suggestions, and a successful and positive model for both online courses and in-person teaching-learning experiences, leveraging the advanced and cutting-edge equipment of leading European Simulation Centres.
The TDT can serve as inspiration for exploring a wide range of educational approaches aimed at individuals with no prior experience (such as undergraduate university students) in a Medical Simulation Centre, or for delivering impactful distance education practices in collaboration with Simulation Centres by adopting Telesimulation educational strategies. This online resource is available free of charge, as recommended by Erasmus project policies.

2021-1-IT02-KA220-HED-000032085.title: T.E.S.T.: Technologies for STEAM Teaching
2021-1-IT02-KA220-HED-000032085.summary:
<< Background >>

The T.E.S.T. project emerged from the need to address key challenges in the field of education, particularly the urgency to modernize learning and teaching in STEAM disciplines (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art, and Mathematics) through the integration of innovative methodologies and digital technologies. With the advancement of Artificial Intelligence and the growing need for digital skills in the job market, it has become essential for educational institutions to offer an education that not only conveys traditional knowledge but also promotes digital competencies, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills. The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the need for flexible teaching methods and distance learning, highlighting the importance of adaptive educational approaches capable of meeting diverse student needs. This context motivated the application for the TEST project, aiming to develop and implement open educational resources (OER), toolkits for adaptive teaching, and to promote the effective use of digital technologies in higher education, addressing existing gaps and contributing to the training of more prepared and versatile future professionals.

<< Objectives >>

The main goal of the TEST project was to revolutionize the approach to teaching and learning in STEAM disciplines, integrating advanced digital technologies and promoting innovative teaching methodologies. We aimed to develop and implement a training program that would equip teachers with the necessary skills to become "Adaptive Teachers," capable of customizing learning according to the individual needs of students, using open educational resources (OER) and digital experiential learning techniques. Another crucial objective was to increase student engagement and digital competencies, effectively preparing them for the challenges of the modern world. Furthermore, we intended to create a network of collaboration among educational institutions for the exchange of best practices and resources, and to support continuous innovation in the field of STEAM education. In summary, TEST aimed to create a lasting impact on higher education, improving the quality and relevance of STEAM teaching to meet the needs of the 21st century.

<< Implementation >>

Within the TEST project, we implemented a series of key activities to achieve our set goals. First, we developed and disseminated open educational resources (OER), including video-pills and branch scenarios realized with IA technology, tutorials, and educational materials, to support digital learning and adaptive teaching. We organized training sessions for teachers, focused on improving digital skills and adopting innovative teaching methodologies, with the goal of transforming them into "Adaptive Teachers." The project also involved creating a comprehensive toolkit to facilitate the implementation of virtual labs and inquiry-based learning. We conducted testing and evaluation activities to ensure the effectiveness and usefulness of the materials and teaching strategies developed. Finally, we promoted dissemination and networking events to share results and best practices with a wider audience, engaging other educational institutions and stakeholders in the dialogue on educational innovation. We also published several papers and publications about the project results, helping the dissemination 

<< Results >>

The project yielded tangible and wide-reaching results in the field of STEAM education. It includes the creation and dissemination of a comprehensive set of Open Educational Resources (OER), featuring interactive video-pills and branch scenarios realized with IA, educational materials, and learning scenarios based on real-life cases, accessible through the ERUDIRE platform in multiple languages to facilitate inclusive and flexible learning. We developed an Adaptive Teacher Toolkit, providing teachers with a practical guide for integrating innovative methodologies and digital technologies into their teaching practices. This toolkit contains tools for designing virtual labs and implementing inquiry-based learning strategies. The project directly involved 536 teachers and 600 students in testing activities, ensuring the feedback necessary for further refining the tools and resources developed. Additionally, it promoted multiplier events and training sessions that reached over 22,000 participants, significantly contributing to disseminating educational innovations to a broader audience. We published several papers and publications about the project results, disseminating them to national and international scientific communities.
