2021-1-RO01-KA220-YOU-000028774.title: GenZ4GreenDeal – Generation Z for community development and sustainability
2021-1-RO01-KA220-YOU-000028774.summary:
<< Background >>

The partners wanted to seed a learning/teaching community which is able to interwove a variety of interests, competences and capacities. The overall goal of the project is to increase the competencies of young people for positive action aimed at the development and sustainability of communities through the support of civil society organizations, local communities and peers from other cultural backgrounds. GenZ4GD project aims to develop a training and capacity building program for young people to actively participate in the development of their (local) community and environment and encourage young people to think more actively about sustainable development, environmental protection and other "green" topics.  Based on the project results and gathered experience, young people has to learn how they can advocate for the positive changes they see a need for.

<< Objectives >>

The partners wanted to seed a learning/teaching community which is able to interwove a variety of interests, competences and capacities.  The overall goal of the project is to increase the competencies of young people for positive action aimed at the development and sustainability of communities through the support of civil society organizations, local communities and peers from other cultural backgrounds. GenZ4GD project aims to develop a training and capacity building program for young people to actively participate in the development of their  local community and environment and encourage young people to think more actively about sustainable development, environmental protection and other "green" topics.  Based on the project results and gathered experience, young people has to learn how they can advocate for the positive changes they see a need for.
The activities and the course for the youth workers and youth aimed at long-term changes of the beliefs and behaviors, to trigger transformation from knowledge -takers in agents of change. The in-house learning was experience sharing between partners on the influence of the local culture on the capacity to instrumentalize the sustainable development concepts.

<< Implementation >>

The partners elaborated training material and shared experience and expertise, The IOs were proved in LTTA/Ambassador Training and disseminated by using  them  on Youth Workers, in multiplication events.
Production of the IO 1 - Visualization of the Status-quo first step was to develop the methodology for the mapping, recoding and presenting in a visual and interactive form
the good practices, policies, initiatives etc. taken in each partner country in relation to following: o the strategies/policies/good practices/initiatives at the regional/national level that works with young people on „green topics “– sustainable development, SDGs, recycling, ecology, energy efficiency and alternative energy, healthy food, ... o any useful EU and National programs that support youth and youth organizations in practices, activities, education on the mentioned topics • to present the findings in a
multi-media way using visual representations for ease of reading. The partners generated this IOs under direct supervision of ADEMED, using an innovative approach to georeferenced information gathering and data labelling to facilitate GIS and SQL recording, elaborated by ADEMED (see innovation section of the report). The classification/labelling exercise, lexicon and basic taxonomy was developed by ADEMED following extensive documentation.
This tool filled in the gap that exists at the EU level especially for partner countries which is the first time that a mapping of national policies, initiatives and practices will be made through a custom-made tool using Google maps. 

The elaboration of GenZ Course started by investigation of themes to be treated, in order to ensure comprehensive approach to  designing  and piloting a course.  The course was planned in a joint effort of the partners to include  design and implementation of local actions in the community where participants will have the opportunity to immediately apply what they have learned and gather others from their environment to do the same. Local actions selection was planned to directly affect the goals of sustainable development and thus involve young people from local communities to act and improve the quality of their lives, but also the lives of their families and peers. 

The partners discussed under the guidance of ADEMED in the first TNM and further on by email and by ADMIN how to tackle the themes, in a way that corresponds to the expectations of the GenZ and to balance the theoretical background with pragmatic training, focused on immediate t angible results. The coordinator warned the partners to observe the intellectual property rights, The coordinator insisted on having graphics in the Course, visual representations of the content and together with PiM stressed the editing requirements. Each partner was in charge to elaborate one module. The course were elaborated gradually, under continuous improvement strategy.

Elaboration of the GenZ4GD podcast, IO of the project, started by a discussion between partners about what type of podcast shall be produced, format, duration, technical features. A variety of formats were discussed, at the end each partner got the permission to select the format that suits best its experience, expertise and available resources. The Coordinator stressed the main requirements for the podcasts: to be correlated/complementary with the course IO2, to have a very clear education value and to be based on something else than delivering information. Then each partner produced its 3 episodes, All other partners commented the first version, under the supervision of SbS and ADEMED. 

GenZ4GD ambassadors training gathered 14 youth workers, professionals. The Partners trained to use the GenZ4GD youth course in their future work with youth. The objectives of this were  • to capacitate youth workers to implement the GenZ4GD course • to clearly explain and identify ways to conduct this course  • to empower youth workers to become true ambassadors of the GenZ4GD program in their local community • to encourage and explain to ambassadors how they will attract new users (young people) to their activities and program activities. The LTTA youth workers were trained in the Gen4GD course and they empowered and capacitated to use this tool in their future work with young people. A specific target was to show the Youth workers how to adapt the course to their individual circumstances, by asking them about case studies they encountered in their professional experience, both from personal history and from other sources. Another target in the training was to foster innovative approaches, identify novel solution and thinking-outside-the box, in order to stimulate local sustainable development and turn to life the Green Deal at small scale.  

The partners delivering training encouraged communication, dialogue and pragmatic approaches. The training took place in Malta, at the premises made available by PiM partner, Each partner was in charge in delivering its own module and to pay attention to the delivery of the other modules. Each task Coordinator took notes about how the Ambassador training made use of the IOs. Following the training, partners contacted the participants by phone to identify use and adaptation. 
====
Project in Motion (PIM), the leading organization, set up the organizational details. The ambassador training took place in  Valletta Volunteer Centre, Valletta Hall, Melita Street, Valletta, between 19-21 of April  2023. There were 22 participants from the seven partner's counties.  Each day the training started at 9.15hrs and finalized at 16.00hrs. 
The partners  conducted a meticulous selection process, focusing on identifying youth workers from institutions with which they maintain close collaboration. The partners were guided by the principle of including participants who are active in the field of youth work, regardless of non formal education. 
Indicatively, the identification and selection of a GENZ4GD Ambassador were based on the following principles. 
•	The candidate should show an interest in the project topics (Sustainability and Green Topics); 
•	The candidate should demonstrate willingness to disseminate the project results in their country with their peers; 
•	The candidate should already be working with young people/youth organizations;
o	The candidate should possess as a minimum a basic English Level to communicate effectively (at least a B2 LEVEL is requested). 
The candidates sent to the project partners a motivation letter regarding the willingness to be part of the trainers’ activity and a  CV.
The trainers are representatives of each partner’s organization  with teaching skills, mostly of them being Youth Workers, Training Companies or NGOs and who actually participated at elaboration of the Handbook modules.

The participants were given a CERTIFICATE OF COMPLETION  to certify that each participant has successfully attended the “Ambassadors Training Programme” which was held in Malta between 19th and 21st April 2023 organised by the GenZ4GD project, funded by the Erasmus+ Programme of the European Union.

After the Handbook modules were completed,  each partner carried out an internal evaluation of the quality of its module, relevance and comprehensiveness. So they were able to present in the training activity in Malta an updated version to their fellow youth workers.

Each modules was presented in power point by each trainer and after each presentation trainers introduced an interactive exercise for testing the skills provided in the course and podcasts. The exercise consists in a guided role-playing game, in which groups of 3-4 participants assumed for instance  a role in a sustainable development event of a local community. The game can be  designed to practice for instance negotiation techniques in a setting that mimics the real world or in main topic of the module.
a)	The game was guided by Stakeholder Fiches and by theory and orientation rules explained by the trainer.
b)	The participants had 10-20 minutes to discuss and prepare their negotiation positions, interests list and compromise strategy.
c)	Then, the participants presented their strategy in front of the other groups.
d)	All other groups have their saying in debating the position of the group that presented the strategy
e)	All groups are guided to reach a common position that is also in line with Sustainable Development Goals
f)	Along the exercise, the Trainer highlighted the European Union programs and Directives that apply to the case in hand.
g)	At the end of each presentation, the Trainer highlights the particular points in the debate slot, insisting on positive developments and avoiding criticism. Black board notes were used to focus on main aspects.
In a final section of the event, the Trainer recap knowledge gathered, necessary skills for local sustainable development and the relevance of negotiation, compromise and advocacy.

They were aware about what to do and what to follow in pilot presentation: impact, attention caption, connection to the audience, interest response, questions about Youth empowerment and collect ad-hoc suggestions.
The LTTA was also broadcasted online, allowing interventions of Youth Workers from the participants countries.
The LTTA was both a training opportunity, carried out in supervised groups of 3-5 youth workers, each group drawing a scheme of their approach of the assignments derived from the Handbook. Then they shared and discussed their fiches. This was also an opportunity to evaluate the handbook, and the podcasts, in order to improve them.  
The ambassador training session was finalized by applying a questionnaire to evaluate the quality of the Handbook/course.
Most of the trainees made use of the approach in the course, to gain and keep the interest of GenZ and younger citizens in local sustainable development in the multiplication events that followed. Following LTTA and piloting, the course was subsequently improved and adapted to online chained modules on the project website, then to LMS on Udemy, also discussed with Youth Workers and Workers in the participants organizations and with Youth Workers they are in connection with. There was set a question list, to check and improve: gaps, practical aspects, assignments, full learning path presented. capacity to connect to local community.

Multiplication events took place according to the proposal and planning.

<< Results >>

The partners elaborated a methodology of data classification about the education projects in the proposals domain, a status-que database, an course structured to serve for self-directed learning, and a sed of podcasts to enhance the learning experience. The methodology to classify data about the education projects make use of labelling of the classes, that is to facilitate both human inquiry and machine reading. The data structure approach is similar to other EU-level digital storage of data, such as in Nature 2000 network. This approach facilitates further development of education projects to match the Common European Data Spaces, as it is  of a  clear and practical structure for accessing and using data, facilitates application of fair, transparent, proportionate and non-discriminatory access rules. 
The Course has a double-side structure- one one side it appeals to theory of the sustainable development in the framework of European Union values and aims, and on the other side it describes practical, down to earth mechanisms at the hands of GenZ to get involved in local sustainable development, in a result-oriented, non-conflictual way.
The course is structured in a hierarchical way, from modules to units and lessons, to be flexible in a way that facilitates navigation in line with individual needs and learning style. The course depicts grassroots and individuals based opportunities to get involved in the local sustainable development, including development of individual capacity to work effectively and negotiation techniques. Translating the information into slides makes the content even more accessible. Evaluation grids are placed at the end of the modules, in order to facilitate self-evaluation and to offer topics to debate while learning the techniques. The information presented is extensive, covering most of the sustainable development subjects. From both the content and the learning methodology, the Course offers an unique insight into the world of sustainable development. While elaborating the course, partners also learn how to foster application of the sustainable development interventions, based on local actions and using a multi-dimensional approach, which is critical for obtaining timely results in small-scale applications of the Climate Change, Green Deal, sustainable development and inclusion principles, at the base of the European Union construction , in a way that brings more stakeholders into action and grounds scaling up the endeavors. The partners learning from each other: negotiation techniques, cross-sectorial approach, personal development, strengthening social webs, use of simulation and case-studies, and elaborating learning materials in a way that matches the expectation of the GenZ. Besides the IOs produced according to the proposals, this collegial learning is a valuable result of the project, to which partners devoted all efforts. In reaching this, ADEMED  made full use of its educational and teaching experience and guided the partners in the journey to elaborate a course which was farther on completed by  a series of 21 podcasts  of various lengths - the third IO of the project. The series of podcasts accounts for practical experiences of environmental activists at local level , which further enhances the applicability of the Course as a whole. The podcasts offer a living face of the sustainable development, Climate change and Green Deal, as they reflect personal experiences, feelings and opinions of more than 30 activists, that are useful to understand that such interventions are not merely science based, but they have to rely on personal feelings and skills, that are both acquired by learning from handbooks and from down-to-earth experience in more than 2o projects, Making the podcasts in itself was also useful for the partners, the result being a deeper knowledge and skills on how to use the visuals in building up learning environments.

2021-1-RO01-KA220-YOU-000029016.title: Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors Network
2021-1-RO01-KA220-YOU-000029016.summary:
<< Background >>

The CyberBullying Peer Ambassadors Networks was a strategic partnership in the youth field among organizations from four EU countries: Romania, Italy, North Macedonia, and Croatia. The goal was the reducing of cyberbullying and social exclusion among vulnerable youth. This was achieved through the establishment of a peer program dedicated to cyberbullying prevention and intervention.
At the levels of partner countries, organizations, and communities, several challenges have been identified based on desk research and target group analysis: Lack of Legal Clarity - Cyberbullying is not explicitly defined by law, and there are no specific legal instruments at the EU level to tackle it, Data Collection and Awareness - Statistics on cyberbullying are not systematically collected by public authorities, leading to a lack of structured prevention and response programs,  Educational System Gap - While the school environment is conducive to prevention actions, there is a lack of coherent policies and programs at the national level among partner countries. In response to these challenges, we proposed three key recommandations: integration of online safety in youth programs, integrated resources and community involvemnt & peer learning. 


<< Objectives >>

The specific objectives of the project were as follows:
Obiective 1: The project aimed to develop the knowledge and skills of 20 youngsters from the partner countries to act as cyberbullying peer ambassadors. This was through the development and implementation of an international training program organised in Romania. 

Obiective 2: To foster the engagement and cooperation between youth and various educational actors. This was accomplished through the development of an online network, https://ambassadors-network.eu/, of Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors, serving as a means to facilitate networking, peer learning, and the perpetuation of anti-cyberbullying discourse. 

Obiective 3: The project aimed to develop skills and mechanisms to address situations of social exclusion and cyberbullying among 400 vulnerable young people. This was  realized through their participation in local activities conducted by the newly created Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors Network, spanning over a period of 2 months. 

<< Implementation >>

During the lifetime of the project we have implemented the following activities: 

1. Elaboration of Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors Training program -  With this activity our goal was to boost youth empowerment, connection, and engagement. Our team, along with our experts developed a practical training program. This program includes a set of skills to learn through hands-on activities and peer learning, with clear guidelines and materials. 
2. Piloting activity through an international learning mobility for young people for the testing of this program and put the basis of the international network - with participation of 20 young people from the partner countries.
3. 
Local activities which included:
a) The involvment of relevant stakeholers in delivering the final training program through the organization of local workshops. These workshops aimed to present the training program and collect feedback, allowing an assessment of the efficiency and relevance of the product for various participant profiles. This process facilitated adaptations to the material, ensuring its pertinence and utility across diverse education sectors and contexts.
b) An enrollment campaign targeting other young people for knowledge transfer. This campaign was designed and implemented with the proactive support of national youth groups. They replicated the international training under the guidance of partner experts, with the intention of establishing a foundational engagement. This approach aimed to diffuse learning on a large scale and promote the creation of the Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors Network. 
4. The Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors Network aimed at establishing an online network of cyberbullying peer ambassadors to address the cyberbullying phenomenon. This initiative facilitated the formation of a European peer learning community, initially comprising empowered youngsters from the partner countries and later expanding to include participants from other EU Member states. The network served as a digital platform, https://ambassadors-network.eu/, creating interconnections among young people to collectively respond to cyberbullying through peer learning, functioning as an educational and empowering tool.
After the formation of national youth groups, they were first involved in virtual meetings for shaping the format and content of the digital platform. This step aimed to ensure ownership by the youngsters. Subsequently, the youth groups participated in planning network activities. Our organization's youth workers orchestrated virtual meetings and discussions centered around pertinent topics, fostering the creation of various activities. To ensure our ambassadors were well-prepared, collaborative training sessions were conducted by each partner in conjunction with the national groups. These sessions honed in on efficiently navigating the website and utilizing its functions. As the youth groups gained proficiency, they spearheaded local initiatives for preventing and intervening in cyberbullying. This undertaking received support from partner organizations, leading to the gradual rise in popularity and promotion of the digital platform across local, regional, national, and international spheres.







<< Results >>

Quantitative results:
Development of one Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors Training Program, comprising theory and experiential learning, created by partner organizations and available in digital format.
Establishment of a digital platform, https://ambassadors-network.eu/, serving as an online resource to facilitate peer learning processes and international youth engagement. Twenty young individuals from four European countries underwent training to become Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors by participating in an international mobility program in Romania.
Informing and training 40 young people, young leaders, and volunteers during the local work phase conducted by participants in the international mobility (with 10 external beneficiaries per partner country). This phase included two training events in each country to transfer knowledge, expand the Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors Network, and recruit additional ambassadors within local youth communities.
Providing information and training to 400 vulnerable young people over a two-month testing phase of the Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors Network (100 young people  from each partner country). The testing phase involved developing activities for all actors in cyberbullying situations (victims, aggressors, witnesses), as well as awareness-raising and counseling activities. 
Conducting three workshops per partner for the quality assurance of the training program. These workshops involved 50 representatives from NGOs, schools, youth centers, school education, and public institutions to enhance the training program and maximize its transferability potential.
Involving  over 20 stakeholders per partner country in local activities developed by trained participants within the Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors initiative. Trained participants, under the supervision and support of youth workers from each partner, created and implemented events and concrete actions for each covered topic as practical activities, with the collaboration of identified stakeholders and partner organizations.
Attracting a number of  124 Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors who joined the online platform. 
Organizing four multiplier events with a total of 349 participants attending these events.

Qualitative results:

Youth who participated in the pilot of the training program gained knowledge, competences, and methodologies to combat and prevent cyberbullying.
A community of ambassadors was established through the Cyberbullying Peer Ambassadors Network during the pilot phase. This community sustained peer learning and engagement in cyberbullying prevention and intervention at the European level. It positioned youngsters at the forefront, empowering them as leaders of the anti-cyberbullying discourse and Upstanders in their communities.
EU citizenship was developed among the youngsters.
Cooperation between the youth sector and other educational actors, including schools, public authorities, was fostered. This collaboration enhanced capacity development through joint activities, promotion, and providing access to the digital platform.
Partners' capacity to create and develop new learning opportunities for youth was increased.
The quality of education and training was enhanced through the development of new resources in the youth field and cyberbullying.
Awareness about the cyberbullying phenomenon increased at the partners' level, EU, and international levels.
Contributions were made to perpetuate the anti-cyberbullying discourse, support existing initiatives, and diversify youth activities. This included thematic activities offered by civil society outside the school environment to youngsters who no longer participated in formal education.

2021-1-RO01-KA220-YOU-000029192.title: Rural Business Innovation Hub
2021-1-RO01-KA220-YOU-000029192.summary:
<< Background >>

The evolving economic and social changes in Europe demand constant innovation and adaptation from villages, businesses, and public institutions.Rural areas face challenges in maintaining attractiveness, competitiveness, and sustainable economic growth, exacerbated by the migration of youth and individuals with potential to urban areas.
Young people in rural settings encounter difficulties acquiring entrepreneurial skills and accessing opportunities comparable to their urban counterparts. Limited options hinder exposure to diverse opportunities, emphasizing the need for alternatives to explore their interests. Moreover, a lack of encouragement and motivation inhibits their active contribution to rural community development.
As a result, we aimed to analyse and understand young people’s needs in this context and come up with a solution. To tackle these challenges, our project developed a new curriculum for entrepreneurship skills, incorporating EU best practices to promote growth and sustainability in rural areas. Business Hubs, including a Digital Business Hub for young entrepreneurs, were introduced to enhance their skills and competencies, enabling them to initiate businesses in their local communities. 

<< Objectives >>

The vision of the project “Rural Business Innovation Hub” was to help solve the lack of entrepreneurship education in rural areas. The aim of our project was to build and foster entrepreneurship competences among young people from rural areas, starting from an entrepreneurial attitude, and apply it to solutions to today's society challenges.
There were 4 objectives that the consortium aimed to achieve:				
Increasing the level of entrepreneurial competencies among youth (18-30 years) in 6 rural areas
Encouraging the development of 6 rural communities and the creation of opportunities for better living
Creating awareness about the importance of entrepreneurial literacy among youth aged 18-30
Document/prove the utility of a Business Innovation HUB in expanding opportunities for youth aged 18-30 from rural areas
Through our project we wanted to motivate young people from rural areas to overcome their barriers , to empower them and enhance their self esteem, to highlight the massive role of the youth workers in supporting young people from rural areas and to create a supportive ecosystem that not only addresses immediate challenges but also fosters a long-term positive impact on youth from rural backgrounds.

<< Implementation >>

We implemented all the activities we aimed to do since the start of the project application and start date. 
We  had 2  international TPMs face to face  (1 in Romania and 1 in Portugal) and 1 online TPM during the project lifetime.
-  Developed IO1: Booklet-Gathering of good practices/analysis-entrepreneurship in rural areas
-  Developed IO2: Educational content for youth entrepreneurship in rural areas
-  Developed IO3:Digital HUB 
-  Developed IO4:Guide to setting up and running a business hub
-Carried out an LTTA (Learning, Teaching and Training Activity) in Romania, Targu-Jiu, where youth workers and practitioners around Europe, from the 6 partner countries, expanded their knowledge about entreprenurship and developed their skills of transferring and promoting entrepreneurship to the target groups in rural areas
-Online final conference-multiplier event
-One face to face multiplier event

<< Results >>

The results of our project are:
-a new booklet that includes practical information and 34 success stories of entrepreneurial startups from Slovenia, Romania, Croatia, Slovakia and Portugal, designed to assist rural youth in launching their own business ideas and fostering an entrepreneurial spirit among them. The primary objective is to offer an inspiring solution to unemployment by instilling a sense of entrepreneurship in young individuals.
-a new enhanced methodology addressed to the youth workers was developed to cultivate entrepreneurship skills among young people. The updated approach guided practitioners in refining their knowledge and approach to entrepreneurship, providing a framework for introducing and applying entrepreneurial instruments in their daily work with young individuals.
-one online platform (https://rbih.scoutsociety.ro/digital-hub/)-Digital Hub focused to offer young people from rural areas the basic tools and knowledge to start discovering entrepreneurship with information and resources from different fields such as:marketing, accountability, finance, networking, services and products, events and trainings, legal, business ethics, innovation, green practices in business, leadership
- a new guide on how to conceive, establish and maintain a Rural Business Center (RBH), aimed at rural municipalities; With this comprehensive guide, city governments and local leaders will find a systematic way to harness the rich resources and talent in their rural communities.
- 21 trained youth workers equipped with the necessary skills, knowledge and tools to work closely with the young people in rural areas that developed their entrepreneurial skills.
-235 participants with fewer opportunities involved during the project lifetime
-almost 80.000 persons reached with the dissemination activities 
-5 youth centers involved in the project as stakeholders 
-90 participants in the online conference and 30 in the face to face multiplier event
-1 project website -https://rbih.scoutsociety.ro/

2021-1-SE02-KA220-YOU-000029050.title: Open Minds - synchronising creative minds for social cohesion and radical inclusion
2021-1-SE02-KA220-YOU-000029050.summary:
<< Background >>

Radical Inclusion transcends traditional accessibility compliance. It advocates for integrating a wide array of perspectives and experiences at the initial stages of design, fostering a mindset where accessibility and inclusion are embedded within all design endeavours. Radical Inclusion challenges the notion that it is an ‘impairment’ that restricts someone’s full and effective engagement in society. It highlights how historically constructed disabling environments are the true barriers to participation. We can actively involve affected individuals in the solution design process, in collaboration with a diverse group of innovators, entrepreneurs and policymakers. The method includes those from marginalised communities to mitigate the hidden barriers and biases leading to their exclusion. It stresses the critical need to identify and confront these invisible impediments, which result in the oversight of invaluable talent, expertise, and experience. Through this project, we aimed to address these needs by cultivating environments where every individual has the opportunity to contribute fully and effectively, enriching society as a whole with their diverse capabilities and insights.

<< Objectives >>

To empower all young individuals to become architects of their own futures, cultivating resilience and life skills needed to navigate a rapidly changing world. We aspired for them to emerge as active citizens, agents of solidarity, and catalysts for positive transformation within communities throughout Europe while also striving to mitigate the social exclusion of any young person. Open Minds leveraged technology and the arts as mediums to inspire and introduce young people to the concept of radical inclusion through social innovations. Participants were taught to co-create solutions for societal issues, drawing upon interdisciplinary knowledge alongside cutting-edge technologies. They engaged in collaborative innovation and co-design at the confluence of science, humanities, and arts, laying the groundwork for the development of inclusive and accessible communities. The project successfully established a network comprising 253 young individuals, 30 youth workers, and 31 organisations from civil society organisations, formal and higher education, research, the business sector, and policy-making spheres, all committed to the mission of fostering a truly inclusive Europe.

<< Implementation >>

Open Minds shifted the narrative from viewing individuals with disabilities as problems needing solutions to address the structural barriers of a disabling society as the primary concern. This initiative championed equal participation in a range of events, initiatives, and both formal and non-formal education settings, enabling young people with disabilities to engage alongside their peers. This exposure to diversity is crucial for normalising such interactions and fostering a natural acceptance of differences. Open Minds not only focused on individuals but also targeted local ecosystems—the interplay of communities, infrastructures, and resources that collectively define a locale's unique socio-political and economic landscape. Engaging with these ecosystems rather than merely with individuals facilitated a ripple effect of positive change, enhancing community-wide benefits and promoting local social and educational advancement.

To disseminate radical inclusion principles within local communities where partner organisations operate and to young people, we developed an encompassing Open Minds approach. This comprised a Curriculum featuring an Open Minds card game, a Facilitator’s Guide complete with a physical computing Toolkit, and a Handbook.

The design of the curriculum involved a series of activities to elucidate radical inclusion and explore the various disabling environments encountered by people with diverse conditions. This process challenged the notion that an environment that is enabling for one individual might be disabling for another, leading to a paradigm shift among young participants. To aid this attitudinal change, we introduced Open Minds cards to deepen the understanding of radical inclusion and the array of conditions and disabling environments people face. Following this, a facilitator's guide was developed to enhance young people's knowledge and experience in creating inclusive designs that transform disabling environments into enabling ones. This included generating a series of activities for young participants and creating introductory videos to expound on key concepts of the methodology, including radical inclusion, research fundamentals, practice-based research methodologies, hypothesis generation, digital assets management, and design principles. These videos served as a foundation for further discussion and learning. Additionally, a physical toolkit was devised to facilitate Creative Innovation Labs (CILs), offering a tangible platform for idea generation and hands-on prototyping, thereby empowering youth workers with varying technological proficiency to guide young individuals in devising technological solutions to counter disabling environments.

After developing these documents, tools and methodologies, we trialled the Open Minds approach with 253 young individuals, 30 youth workers, and 31 local organisations through sessions and CILs. Each partner conducted two sessions (face-to-face or blended) with 50 young participants, including at least 10% young disabled artists, and participated in a blended Learning, Teaching, and Training Activities (LTTA) for young people. Local CILs were organised in Albania, Croatia, Finland, and Portugal, alongside an international CIL in Sweden, all operating concurrently to facilitate shared presentations and international cooperation. These CILs resulted in the development of eight international and 28 local projects, each addressing disabling environments and crafting solutions to overcome related challenges.

The culmination of this process was the creation of a Handbook, enabling other youth workers and educators to foster and support local ecosystems using the Open Minds methodologies. Designed for adaptable application across various contexts—from educational settings to workplaces—the Handbook allows for flexible adoption of the methodology to suit specific needs, ranging from brief sessions to comprehensive programmes within organisations. Additional efforts were made to elucidate the methodology's transferability across different educational environments, ensuring broad applicability and impact.

<< Results >>

Our project's approach, centred on Radical Inclusion, produced tangible outputs and impactful results, reshaping perspectives on disability and inclusion. The curriculum we developed outlines the Open Minds methodology's objectives, learning goals, prerequisites, and corequisites for implementation, detailing the process from registration and selection of young participants to course delivery, evaluation, and teaching resources, alongside highlighting valuable Open Access Educational Resources (OERs) on the topic.

A significant innovation was the Open Minds card game, designed to shift young people's attitudes towards disability—from seeing disability as a problem to be tackled to addressing the structural, psychological, and physical barriers of a disabling society. The game facilitates the exploration of diverse disabilities and conditions, prompting participants to consider how design impacts lives. It comprises three types of cards: Person cards, introducing specific characters rather than stereotypical 'types'; Condition cards, emphasising disability as a result of person-environment interaction rather than an inherent attribute; and Disabling Environment cards, highlighting the role of physical and virtual spaces in creating exclusion.

The Facilitator's Guide and a physical computing Toolkit were also developed to support the learning objectives and promote radically inclusive local ecosystems. The Guide outlines how to conduct activities, from face-to-face or blended sessions to Creative Innovation Labs, focusing on building inclusive designs and reconfiguring disabling environments. The Toolkit, centred around the Raspberry Pi Pico board, enables the creation of prototypes addressing these environments, designed for ease of use even without a technical background. These resources were piloted by 30 youth workers with 253 young participants, including 28 with disabilities and 44 facing other challenges, enhancing their skills in innovating for radical inclusion within their ecosystems. Through five simultaneous Creative Innovation Labs in Umeå, Tampere, Porto, Zagreb, and Tirana, young people developed innovative solutions, demonstrating the methodology's effectiveness.

The culmination of our efforts was the Handbook, a practical guide for CSOs, educational institutions, and businesses to implement the Open Minds approach. It provides a comprehensive toolkit and methodologies for adopting Radical Inclusion principles, with flexible content to suit diverse educational settings. Featuring detailed steps, case studies, and strategies, the Handbook aims to make Radical Inclusion an actionable concept, equipping educators to foster environments where every perspective is integrated and valued.

2021-1-SI02-KA220-YOU-000028912.title: Mladi zEKO
2021-1-SI02-KA220-YOU-000028912.summary:
<< Background >>

In our needs analysis, the partners of the project have found that young people are relatively well aware of environmental issues at a declarative level, but there is a more problematic gap with their actual environmental actions and behavior. In addition to the environmental challenges that coincided with the consequences of the COVID-19 crisis, our project partners found a decline in creativity, motivation, self-initiative, and self-confidence among our youth during the global pandemic. In the case of youth  from minority groups, there were also individual and systemic barriers to participation in educational activities.The project's main aim was to show that creativity through the arts provides young people with the opportunity and inspiration to create and promote different forms of education and networking. The project focused on improving the social inclusion of young (minority) people and youth workers from Slovenia, Croatia, and Serbia.The project pursued the priority areas of INCLUSION AND DIVERSITY, ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION, AND THE FIGHT AGAINST CLIMATE CHANGE, while promoting ACTIVE CITIZENSHIP, SELF-INITIATIVE, AND YOUTH ENTREPRENEURSHIP. We addressed green skills, creativity and the arts, and the minortiy challenges.

<< Objectives >>

The project aimed to improve the social inclusion of young people and youth workers with fewer opportunities, especially immigrants, while facilitating an effective two-way process of integration into the majority environment. The project activities involved young people, youth workers, various stakeholders, and decision-makers.

Creativity, non-formal learning, and youth work enhance young people's creative and innovative capacities in ways that are crucial for their activation. Our young people are the future creators and professionals who will contribute to Europe's rich natural and cultural heritage, while also acting as agents of social change.

Regarding ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION, we implemented an educational and creative process for youth workers and young people, resulting in three key project deliverables. This effort aimed to strengthen YOUTH LEARNING AND CAREER OPPORTUNITIES, FOCUSING ON SELF-INITIATIVE AND ENTREPRENEURSHIP, and fostering creative learning and social entrepreneurship.

In doing so, our goal was to address identified skills and knowledge gaps, promote creative learning, recognize the richness of diversity, facilitate networking with other cross-sectoral organizations and encourage self-initiative.

<< Implementation >>

To achieve our goal, we carried out various artistic-creative activities. Among the key training activities of the project are two international LTT activities for youth workers. In addition, we also carried out a youth LTT activity, Inclusive Arts Erasmus Istria 2023. For these trainings we developed professional and didactic materials. In addition, we also carried out four international partner meetings, three final multiplier activities and a wide promotional and targeted dissemination campaign involving renowned artists, experts and stakeholders. Through artistic creation, young people and youth workers learnt about the importance of waste, its recycling and transformation into works of art, and developed a sense and concern for the environment. Through creativity, non-formal learning and youth work, we have increased young people's creative and innovative skills in many ways, thus activating them. We have produced three core project outputs that have had or will have a significant impact on changing the patterns. The Green Compass publication, the online classroom with the documentary zEKOteka and Green 3D Art. We have also produced a large number of promotional materials to spread awareness about the topic adddressed.

<< Results >>

The project yielded three significant outcomes: the Green Compass publication, an online classroom featuring the educational documentary zEKOteka, and the Green 3D Art Showroom along with an accompanying 3D application. Additionally, we collaborated with differemt partners and stakholders to integrate green practices and methodologies into our youth programmess, enhancing international cooperation and leading to new projects and improvements in youth work. We're proud of increased participation in training activities, the development of innovative digital tools, expanded youth programmess and activities, and various partner achievements such as a new creative gallery and renovated youth spaces. Notably, we've increased involvement of disadvantaged youth, incorporated sustainability into operations of a newly opened Croatian home, and engaged stakeholders including the Permanent Representation of Slovenia to the EU and local media for extensive coverage. Our project's presentation at institutions like the Andragogical Centre of Slovenia further facilitated networking and dissemination of project updates.

2021-1-SI02-KA220-YOU-000029092.title: Dive IN - Participativna znanost v mladinskem delu
2021-1-SI02-KA220-YOU-000029092.summary:
<< Background >>

The DIVE IN project took as its starting point the concept of participatory science, in which the partners saw an opportunity and a useful tool to encourage young people to get involved in monitoring the state of a phenomenon or challenge in the environment in a simple way for the benefit of society. Through active participation in science we wanted to empower youth workers to take a key role in their own development as well as in the development of their communities. With the concept of participatory science, we offered the sector a new field that qualitatively complemented and built upon the sector's existing work on strengthening democratic participation and autonomy (Youth Goal 9 in the EU Strategy 2019-2027). The project provided youth workers, youth trainers and the youth sector with a tool that will help them in future programming and enable the qualitative introduction of participatory science in their organisations. We found that the project particularly built on the desire for more knowledge in the field of science and opened up opportunities for designing new programmes in the future.

<< Objectives >>

The aim of the project was to integrate the concept of participatory science into the field of youth work and to raise active
participation of young people in addressing societal challenges and to empower the youth sector for active involvement
young people in public affairs. 
The project pursued the following objectives: 
1. To introduce the concept of participatory science into the programmes of youth organisations. 
2. To train trainers in the youth sector in participatory science. 
3. to empower the youth sector and give it the tools to further develop and multiply the participatory science methodology within the youth sector.
sector and beyond. 
4. to enable young people to actively participate in addressing societal challenges.

<< Implementation >>

To achieve the project's objectives, the partners carried out the following activities: 
- We organised three transnational project meetings in Slovenia, Italy and Croatia, 
- We organised a 3-day study visit to Croatia for 16 representatives of the partner organisations (originally planned for 12), 
- the organisation of a 5-day international training course on participatory science in Italy for 20 trainers in participatory science - we had more people, which we co-financed from our own resources 
- Organisation of a 5-day international training course on participatory science in Belgium for 20 representatives of youth organisations - we had more people, which we co-financed from our own resources 
- we produced a workbook on the concept of participatory science with practical exercises, 
- we prepared a curriculum for the training of trainers, 
- we developed and delivered online training on the use of participatory science in youth work, 
- organised an international conference in Slovenia on Participatory Science as a Fuel for Youth Activation, 
- organised four national multiplier events, training trainers in youth work to deliver participatory science workshops with young people
- attended the Academy of Youth Work 

<< Results >>

The project partners have produced three key project deliverables:
A workbook on the concept of participatory science with practical exercises - This workbook was a key tool of the project for the implementation and introduction of the concept of participatory science in youth work practice. It contained all the key elements, from the theoretical concept to practical exercises and tips on how to apply participatory science in practice in a planned way.
Training of trainers in youth work curriculum - This curriculum was designed to train trainers to deliver workshops on the concept of participatory science in youth organisations, youth organisations and beyond. It contained a detailed competency framework and working methods aimed at setting up a structure for the continuous delivery of training for trainers in the field of participatory science.
Online training for the use of participatory science in youth work 
- This online training consisted of:
- 6 online webinars addressing different areas of participatory science;
- 10 exercises from the workbook to get you started with the concept of participatory science integrated in the webinars

2021-1-SI02-KA220-YOU-000029326.title: Podpornik
2021-1-SI02-KA220-YOU-000029326.summary:
<< Background >>

In 2019, Lojtra has been running an Erasmus+ programme, where we work with a local primary school to form a group of 15 young people who we meet regularly between September and March, and then run an international youth exchange with them. After the experience, we involve them in the work of local youth organisations. So there have been regular meetings and trust has been built within the group. 
Then came the shock of two young people cancelling their participation. We were extremely surprised by this, as we are not used to cancellations. Not at all in our work with teenagers, where we have a lot of meetings and where we are careful to create a safe space for everyone present.  The reasons and the way of cancellation were different, but because we wanted to understand them better, we discovered through conversations with each other, with teachers and with the school management that in one case it was a person with an eating disorder, and in the other case it was an extremely difficult home situation. What struck and surprised us the most from the whole experience was the fact that the youth workers did not detect this in advance and consequently did not react to the situations. That is why we decided to apply with this project. 

<< Objectives >>

Aim: To develop an organisational approach to empower youth workers to work successfully with young people with emotional and behavioural difficulties (EBD).

Project Objectives:

1. To conduct a survey on the necessary competences for youth workers to work with young people with EBI (in relation to the competences youth workers already have and the situations they face).
2. To develop a competency model to empower youth workers to perceive the EBI of young people and to apply possible solutions to different scenarios of deviant behaviour and the youth worker's reactions to them.
3. To develop a manual for youth workers that includes a cross-section of key topics in the field.
4. Develop a training curriculum for youth workers. Three modules of 6 days each.
5. Test the designed modules on 27 youth workers.
6. Identify a support network in the local area that can support the youth worker in dealing with young people with EBI.
7. To develop organisational guidelines for the development of organisations towards inclusion and sufficient support for young people with EBI, with a particular focus on support for youth workers working with young people with EBI
8. Produce a series of 15 podcasts with different mental health professionalls

<< Implementation >>

The Supporter project has implemented a series of activities aimed at achieving its objectives, in particular improving the competences of youth workers to work with young people with emotional and behavioural problems. Activities included:

youth worker competency survey, developing a competency model,  development and distribution of the Gentle Curiosity manual,  developig curriculum and training for youth workers, pilot testing of the training modules for working with young people with EBI, building a support network, creating 15 podcasts on the topic, dissemination of knowledge and experience.

<< Results >>

1. Fidnings from the research, competency model, Gentle curiosity handbook, curriculum and training modules, podcast series. 
2. Youth workers who participated in the trainings reported significant improvements in their ability to identify and respond to young people's emotional and behavioural problems. They felt more confident and were better equipped to deal effectively with difficult situations.
3. The training and other outputs (podcasts, manual) have increased awareness and sensitivity to the complexity of emotional and behavioural problems among young people. This has fostered a more empathetic and supportive environment within youth organisations.
4. Stronger support networks. 
5. Dissemination of the results engaged a wider community of stakeholders in the field of youth mental health. The collaboration with Gradec Primary School on the multiplier event was particularly successful. In this way, we reached many more people directly and indirectly than we would otherwise have without their cooperation. 
6. Increased youth workers' awareness of their own limits when working with young people. The training sessions highlighted how to identify situations that go beyond their competences and when to seek further help.
topics: Quality and innovation of youth work

2021-2-DE04-KA220-YOU-000049467.title: What?! I'm not stressed!
2021-2-DE04-KA220-YOU-000049467.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project to address the increasing stress levels among young people, highlighted especially by the COVID-19 pandemic. Worldwide statistics show a higher rate of stress issues among the youth compared to adults, attributed to factors such as peer conflict, bullying, financial stress, and career orientation. The pandemic has increased mental health concerns, leading to social isolation, disruption in therapeutic services, and loss of structured occupations like school and work. Social media, while providing a platform for socialisation, has also led to comparison and feelings of inadequacy among the youth. 

Through the work on developing knowledge management among participating organisations, youth workers, and production of intellectual outputs as resource materials for young people, we have addressed the needs of our partnership and of our target groups of youngsters with fewer opportunities to tackle this issue and mobilise youth workers to contribute to supporting young people’s mental health.


<< Objectives >>

With the implementation of this project we have aimed to tackle the problem of increase of stress among young people. More specifically, we aimed to mobilise youth workers in Europe to contribute to supporting young people’s mental health. The specific objectives of the project were:
-	Empower youth workers for prevention and management of stress among marginalised youngsters, through development of inspiring and innovative Curriculum, LTTA and the Online course for youth workers’ training.
-	Empower youngsters with fewer opportunities in coping mechanisms and dealing with stress and anxiety, through innovative Toolkit with multidisciplinary approach workshops for beneficiaries.
-	Exchange good practices and further develop quality strategic partnership among partners from 5 European countries with different realities in regards to youth stress management and prevention.


<< Implementation >>

The project activities of this project consisted of the following:
•	Project Management processes and activities throughout the whole project. 
•	M1 - kick-off project meeting in Serbia hosted by CNELL
•	O1 - Toolkit “What?! I'm not stressed!”- lead Realization and CNELL; Produced in 6 languages.
•	M2 - second meeting in Italy hosted by LINK DMT
•	O2 – Curriculum “What?! I'm not stressed!” - lead LINK DMT and JuBuK; Produced in 6 languages.
•	M3 - third meeting in Germany hosted by JuBuK
•	O3 - Online course “What?! I'm not stressed!” - lead Wizard and OTB; Produced in 6 languages.
•	C1 - LTTA - Training for trainers in Croatia hosted by Realization and Wizard
•	E1 – National conference and workshop  in Novi Sad, RS  by CNELL
•	E2 – National conference and workshop in Modena, IT by LINK DMT
•	E3 – National conference and workshop in Zagreb, HR by Realization and Wizard
•	E4 – National conference and workshop in Essen, DE  by JuBuK
•	E5 – International conference and workshop in Brussels, BE  by OTB
•	M4 – Final evaluation meeting in Belgium hosted by OTB


<< Results >>

Intellectual Outputs

O1 Toolkit “What?! I'm not stressed!” - an innovative (pdf and digital) publication and resource material for youth workers, purposely developed to recognise stress and stressors and support the needed youngsters in practicing different relaxation and mindfulness techniques, from the multidisciplinary approach of psychology, social pedagogy, youth work and art (music and photography). 

O2 Curriculum “What?! I'm not stressed!” - a resource material for youth trainers to organise a 7-day long training course on empowering youth workers to develop alternative competences and methods of prevention and managing stress that is happening in every day face-to-face and online situations amongst youth and in youth work nowadays. The curriculum consists of detailed session designs, as well as annexes and other needed materials for easier multiplication purposes.

O3 Online course “What?! I'm not stressed!” - an innovative and up-to-date digital tool / online course for relevant topics and with tools for prevention and management of stress that is happening in every day face-to-face and online situations amongst youth and in youth work nowadays. The online course allows for bigger impact of our project, as it is free and easily accessible from any community, country.

The intellectual outputs are all originally produced in English, and further on translated and available also in German, Croatian, Serbian, French, and Italian. 

Other results of the project consist of the following:

LTTA organisation and empowerment of youth workers
•	A total of 16 staff and youth workers participated in the Learning, Teaching, and Training Activities (LTTA), enhancing their skills in conducting training sessions for other youth workers based on the project's intellectual outputs.

Intellectual Outputs (O1 Toolkit, O2 Curriculum, O3 Online Course) usage
•	15 multipliers, including youth workers, volunteers, and management staff (3 from each partner country), utilised the project's intellectual outputs in their youth work activities. They engaged with at least 75 youngsters (15 per partner country) to test the effectiveness of these outputs both on a personal and organisational level.

Organisation of multiplier conferences and local impact
•	120 local multipliers and youth workers in 5 countries were empowered during the multiplier events. They learned about the significance of youth work in promoting the prevention and management of stress among young people.

Expected results were two-fold: (1) the organisations developed publications to be used to provide quality NFE about stress management and prevention among youngsters with fewer opportunities; (2) we have also developed online course that can be used by target groups who are not able to physically attend educational activities and/or who we had no chance to work with before. Thus, our project, besides impacting our organisations and current beneficiaries of ours, allows us to reach new beneficiaries and target groups, which will further contribute to bigger impact and effectiveness of our work in our communities and Europe-wide.
topics: Creating new, innovative or joint curricula or courses

2021-2-DE04-KA220-YOU-000050925.title: Youth work for career management with different abilities’ youngsters
2021-2-DE04-KA220-YOU-000050925.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project to address the critical need for comprehensive career management education, especially following the significant impacts of the 2008 financial crisis and the recent COVID-19 pandemic. These events notably intensified unemployment rates among young individuals, who are at crucial stages of career development and often lack the skills and orientation necessary for sustained professional growth. Additionally, common shifts towards new operational trends demand continual skill development, posing challenges for youth uncertain of their career paths. Developing educational approaches on career management was the core of this project, hence the project partners gathered to develop new methods to address the needs and constrains of their target group – youngsters and young adults with different abilities

This project addressed these needs and gaps by empowering youth, particularly those with disabilities, who face heightened barriers to employment and social inclusion. Through innovative educational methods and cross-sectoral approaches, we aimed to equip young people and youth workers with effective career management tools, enhancing their ability to navigate and succeed in the evolving job market.


<< Objectives >>

With this project, we aimed that our beneficiaries, youth with disabilities, to improve their skills of career management, and we also aimed to empower more youth workers for organising adequate career orientation, planning and development programmes, in line with the newest updates and cross-sectoral approach. Specific objectives of the project were:
•	Empower youngsters with disabilities for quality career management through development of inspiring, innovative and up-to-date handbook, as well as the online course.
•	Empower our youth workers and improve knowledge management of our organisations for building competences of educators in career management for youth with disabilities, through LTTA, innovative curriculum and useful toolkit with workshops for beneficiaries.
•	Exchange good practices and further develop quality strategic partnership among partners from 5 European countries with different realities in regards to career management possibilities and realities.


<< Implementation >>

The project consisted of the following activities:

•	Project Management processes and activities throughout the whole project. 
•	M1 - kick-off meeting in Zagreb, HR - hosted by Domas
•	O1 - Handbook - lead Domas, Iteccion, OTB. Produced in 6 languages.
•	M2 - second meeting in Modena, IT – hosted by LINK DMT
•	O2 - Curriculum - lead LINK DMT, CNELL, OH. Produced in 6 languages.
•	M3 - third meeting in Novi Sad – hosted by CNELL
•	O3 - Toolkit - lead CNELL, Realization, OH. Produced in 6 languages.
•	M4 - fourth meeting in Zagreb – hosted by Realization
•	O4 - E-learning course - lead Domas, LINK DMT, Realization. Produced in 6 languages.
•	C1 - LTTA - Training for trainers in Serbia - hosted by Iteccion
•	E1 – National conference and workshop – Novi Sad, RS by CNELL + iteccion
•	E2 – National conference and workshop – Modena, IT by LINK DMT
•	E3 – National conference and workshop – Zagreb, HR by Realization + Domas
•	E4 – National conference and workshop – Hannover, DE by OH
•	E5 – International conference and workshop – Brussels, BE by OTB
•	M5 – Final evaluation meeting – Online, hosted by OH


<< Results >>

Intellectual Outputs developed:
-	O1 Handbook "Exploring Youth work for career management with different abilities' youngsters": This innovative publication serves as a crucial resource for youth workers and young adults with disabilities, providing up-to-date information and tools needed for effective career management. It is developed as a foundational theoretical and conceptual resource for further empowerment within this field.
-	O2 Curriculum "Empowering youth workers for quality youth work for career management with different abilities’ youngsters": This curriculum has been used to organise a comprehensive 7-day training course, equipping youth workers with the skills needed to support career management for youngsters and young adults with disabilities in both online and offline settings.
-	O3 Toolkit "Mentoring and supporting youngsters with different abilities for career planning and management": The toolkit, comprising general concepts, recommendations, and a series of workshops, directly aids youth workers in enhancing the career management competences of their beneficiaries.
-	O4 E-learning course "Career planning and management course for youngsters with different abilities": This e-learning course extends the reach of our project, making career management tools accessible to individuals and communities across Europe, regardless of their ability to attend in-person training.
All intellectual outputs are produced in English and translated into partners' national languages (FR, DE, IT, HR & RS), enhancing accessibility and user-friendliness.

Other results of the project:
•	A support of competence development of 18 staff and youth trainers through the LTTA. These individuals are now better equipped to deliver effective training aligned with our intellectual outputs.
•	23 multipliers from partner organisations (youth workers, adult educators, volunteers and management staff – 4-5 from each country) were using our intellectual outputs in their work with at least 70 beneficiaries (10-15 per country) and testing their effectiveness locally both personal and on organisational level (related to the application of the outputs on our organisations’ procedures and practices when organising such education activities).
•	Additional 178 youngsters with fewer opportunities were empowered through dissemination efforts by community leaders and partnerships with local organisations across five countries. They had the chance to test the online course, benefiting from its content and support.
•	Empowered 117 multipliers in 5 countries through the multiplier events, which have significantly enhanced the capabilities of local youth workers to promote effective career management for youngsters and young adults with disabilities.

The project results were two-fold: (1) the development of publications and resources that provide quality non-formal education about career management tailored to the needs of youngsters with disabilities; (2) the creation of an online course that extends educational opportunities to those unable to attend physical events or previously unreached by our efforts. These outcomes have not only impacted our organisations and current beneficiaries but have also enabled us to reach new groups, contributing to a larger and more effective impact across our communities and Europe-wide.
topics: Cooperation between educational institutions and business

2021-2-EL02-KA220-YOU-000050030.title: Prevention and Support for Cyber Gender Based Violence
2021-2-EL02-KA220-YOU-000050030.summary:
<< Background >>

The project was launched in response to the EU Commission's Strategy for Gender Equality 2020-2025, which highlights gender-based violence as a major social challenge rooted in gender inequality. Cyber-violence, which is particularly exacerbated by the pandemic COVID-19, disproportionately affects women and remains insufficiently addressed in terms of its impact on victims. The project aims to address this emerging form of violence by focusing on the needs of two main target groups: young people aged 18-29 and professionals in victim support services. Needs Addressed
Youth in the 18-29 Age Group: This group is particularly vulnerable to cyber harassment due to their high internet usage. The project intends to provide training to help them protect themselves online, recognize and report violence, and access resources and support.
Youth Workers and Victim Support Professionals: The project will develop a training curriculum to enhance the ability of these professionals to support victims of cyber gender-based violence effectively. This includes recognizing, responding to, and guiding victims to appropriate services.
The project aims to provide comprehensive support and tools to these groups to combat and mitigate the effects.

<< Objectives >>

The project had the following specific objectives:

Prevention, Recognition and Early Intervention against Cyber GBV: The project aimed to contribute to the prevention, recognition and early intervention against cyber GBV.

Increasing the Capacity of Youth Workers and Victim Support Services: the project sought to increase the capacity of youth workers and victim support services to respond to the specific needs of victims of cyber violence through an innovative and transferable training program.

Improving Digital Skills: the goal was to improve the digital skills of the target groups so that they could protect themselves online, seek help and take action to break the cycle of violence online and offline.

Awareness raising: The project aimed to raise awareness about cyber violence.

Involvement of Professionals: Involvement of professionals from different countries in the fight against cyber violence.

Knowledge Dissemination: to provide knowledge on best practices and effective actions implemented to prevent and support against cyber-gender violence.

Contribute to a More Inclusive Cyber Space: Contributing to a more inclusive cyberspace


<< Implementation >>

The project included the implementation of the following activities:

Creation of an e-Platform against Cyber-Violence: Development of an online platform that serves as a resource centre on cyber-divorce.

Mapping Best Practices at EU level: collecting and analysing best practices at European level to address cyber violence.

Digital Handbook on Cyber-Violence for Young People: Create a manual aimed at young people, providing information and guidance on protection from cyber violence.

Training Programme for Victim Support Services and Youth Workers: Develop a training program aimed at increasing the capacity of workers to support victims of cyber violence.

Self-assessment in the form of an interactive quiz: creating an interactive quiz to self-assess users' digital skills and knowledge about cyber violence.

Final Research Paper: produce a final research paper that includes data on the effectiveness of the project's interventions.

In addition, four transnational meetings were held, two of which were conducted in person and two online. Finally, three multiplication events were organised in Bulgaria, Cyprus and Greece to communicate the project results and raise awareness on the phenomenon of cyber violence. 

<< Results >>

The project produced the following concrete results and other important outcomes:

Electronic Platform against Cyber-Violence: An online platform was created that serves as a resource centre for professionals working with young people in victim support and social care services, as well as for young people themselves. The platform hosts all project outputs, including best practices, training curriculum, manual and interactive self-assessment quiz.

Mapping of Best Practices at EU level: best practices from different European countries in addressing cyber violence were collected and analysed.

Digital Handbook on Cyber-Violence for Youth: A digital handbook was created to provide information and guidance on protection from cyber-gender violence.

A training programme for Victim Support Services and Youth Workers: A training program was developed that increases the capacity of workers to support victims of cyber-violence through innovative and transferable training modules.
Self-assessment in the form of an Interactive Quiz: an interactive self-assessment quiz was created that allows users to assess their knowledge of identifying and responding to cyber violence. Final Research Paper: data on the effectiveness of the project's interventions were collected, providing a comprehensive and up-to-date description of the current situation of the target groups and policy recommendations to combat cyber violence.

Other Key Results
Awareness raising and public debate: The project contributed to raising awareness about cyber violence through awareness campaigns and public events held in different countries.

Creating International Networks: the platform and training materials created helped to create international networks and facilitate cooperation between professionals in different countries.

Strengthening Digital Skills: participants developed their digital skills and gained the ability to protect themselves and their identities online.

Improving Victim Support: victim support service professionals and youth workers improved their ability to identify and support victims of cyber violence and guide them through the necessary legal steps.
