2022-1-HR01-KA220-YOU-000088701.title: Powered by V - Engaged Volunteering for the Future of EU Values
2022-1-HR01-KA220-YOU-000088701.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project to address the need for stronger youth engagement in strengthening EU values through volunteering. Volunteering is not only about helping others but is a powerful form of civic participation that can reinforce democracy, solidarity, peacebuilding and social inclusion. The COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine highlighted the urgent need for supported, value-based youth engagement. Our project responded to the lack of structured support for youth organisations to promote civic competences through volunteering. It focused on strengthening the capacity of organisations and youth workers to develop programmes that move beyond charity, helping youth understand their role in building resilient, inclusive and democratic societies. By joining expertise across countries, we aimed to create new knowledge, tools and a common European narrative on volunteering as an expression of EU values, countering extremist and populist narratives and empowering young people as active citizens for the future of Europe.

<< Objectives >>

The project aimed to encourage a better understanding of the cultural, social and political context of the relationship between youth engagement through volunteering and EU values. We wanted to support youth volunteering as a transformative force for strengthening EU values, resilience and sustainable communities. Another objective was to strengthen the capacities of youth organisations to develop more impactful volunteer engagement that promotes democratic principles, solidarity, inclusion and human rights. Finally, we aimed to unlock the potential of national, transnational and EU cooperation by building a common narrative and practical tools that foster youth civic participation and affirm fundamental EU values.

<< Implementation >>

The project activities included focus groups and interviews with youth and organisations, leading to the development of the EU Comparative Report on solidarity and EU values. National conversation saloons were organised to create the Feasibility Kit for strengthening value-based volunteer engagement. Based on research and dialogue, Policy Recommendations were developed to support youth volunteering and democratic participation. We produced the Guidebook "Pathways to Solidarity and Other EU Values" and a Curriculum for youth volunteer engagement, followed by national training sessions in Croatia, Ireland, Slovenia and Poland. Promotion and dissemination activities included the production of promotional videos, materials and organisation of dissemination events at national and EU levels to share project results widely.

<< Results >>

The project resulted in improved knowledge, skills and practices of volunteer-involving and youth organisations to better support youth engagement in volunteering and solidarity actions that strengthen EU values. Concrete outputs include the EU Comparative Report “Solidarity and Other EU Values in Focus”, the Feasibility Kit “Treasure Hunt of EU Values”, the Policy Recommendations on youth engagement and volunteering, the Guidebook “Pathways to Solidarity and Other EU Values”, the Curriculum for youth volunteering and civic participation, which was piloted through national trainings and two promotional videos containing good practice, as well as views on the topic by young people and representatives of CSOs. The project developed innovative and practical approaches encouraging greater synergy between EU values and youth volunteer engagement and created a common EU narrative for policymakers to promote an enabling environment for youth volunteering and civic engagement.
topics: Quality and innovation of youth work

2022-1-NL02-KA220-YOU-000089336.title: Empowering Youth Work for the Green Debate
2022-1-NL02-KA220-YOU-000089336.summary:
<< Background >>

We designed EYWGD to address several connected needs identified across youth work organisations in Europe. Many youth workers wished to engage young people in climate and sustainability topics but lacked structured, discussion-based materials and confidence to facilitate such activities without polarisation or misinformation. Smaller organisations, especially in rural or remote areas, faced additional challenges such as weak digital connectivity, limited budgets, and isolation from professional networks. Existing online tools were fragmented, difficult to maintain, and not adapted to youth work realities. We therefore recognised the need for an integrated approach that would combine debate methodology with environmental education, build a shared digital environment for training and cooperation, and strengthen links among dispersed youth workers and organisations. Through EYWGD, we aimed to improve the quality of youth work, support digital transformation, and make access to learning, mentoring, and peer exchange possible regardless of location or resources.

<< Objectives >>

EYWGD aimed to strengthen the quality and inclusiveness of youth work by equipping youth workers with the knowledge, tools, and methods to facilitate structured dialogue on climate change and sustainability. We focused on integrating debate methodology into environmental education and improving youth workers’ capacity to manage disagreement, identify misinformation, and guide evidence-based discussions. We aimed to make these competences widely accessible through digital solutions and blended learning. We also set out to create a permanent digital environment where youth workers could learn, cooperate, and share materials without geographic or financial barriers. Another objective was to connect organisations from different regions into a functioning network that supports continuous learning, mentoring, and dissemination of good practice. Through these goals, we wanted to make climate-related youth work more informed, participatory, and resilient, while ensuring equal opportunities for those working in remote or low-connectivity areas.

<< Implementation >>

While working on E-learning (WP 2) we developed, tested, and refined courses combining debate methodology and sustainability education. Partners co-created and reviewed lessons through more than twenty national evaluation sessions and improved clarity, inclusiveness, and accessibility before final publication. 

The result is a full learning sequence of main courses, deep dives, and exercises built around dialogue-based learning, structured reasoning, and de-escalation of disagreement.

Under WP3, we created a digital manual of debate-based case studies on sustainability and green transition issues. Each includes background, mapped arguments, facilitator notes, and options for different delivery formats. The content was drafted, field-tested in youth debate clubs and with youth groups, and adapted for both urban and rural users.

Under WP4, we developed and launched the Greenbox platform and mobile applications, built in-house by youth workers and volunteers. It provides one digital space for learning, cooperation, and activity management, ensuring safe, inclusive, and long-term access.

We also orgnaised two in-person educaitons, for young climate ambassadors and for youth workers to act as multiplers of our digital content.

<< Results >>

E-learning environment with 10 courses for individuals and 11 courses for groups with over 23.000 course enrollments happened by the end of reporting period

https://learningbase.idebate.net/climate-courses-for-individuals/
https://learningbase.idebate.net/climate-courses-for-groups/

Assembly of 38 case studies in arranged in 4 topics, available in digital manual with over 200.000 online visits during duration of project 
https://climatedebate.idebate.net/

Online platform developed by young people for the management of youth debate clubs and educational content that is already used by hundreds of youth workers and with organisations from 22 countries committing to use it in their everyday work
https://greenbox.idebate.net/

2 in person trainigs, with 24 youth climate ambassadors trained and 20 youth workers serving as multipliers.
12 live and online dissemination events organised by partners with additional 8 dissemination events organised by associated partners
Over 2000 young people and over 200 youth workers included in the process of development and testing of project results
Long term cooperation agreements by project partnership and dozens of MoUs on project result utilisation by other youth orgs.
topics: Quality and innovation of youth work

2022-1-NO02-KA220-YOU-000088146.title: Experiential Entrepreneurship Labs
2022-1-NO02-KA220-YOU-000088146.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project to make entrepreneurship education more practical, engaging and inclusive for young people from diverse backgrounds. To illustrate, at Fagskolen Rogaland, traditional approaches to entrepreneurship felt irrelevant to students in technical fields like maritime and engineering. This served to highlight the need for hands-on, problem-solving methodologies aligned with their studies.
Our partners faced similar challenges, with educators lacking tools to teach entrepreneurship effectively in informal and non-formal settings. The partnership felt that existing resources were too theory-heavy and didn’t account for diverse learning styles or the expansive vision of entrepreneurship outlined in frameworks like EntreComp.
Thus, this project endeavoured to address these gaps by creating tools like the Experiential Entrepreneurship Labs and the Starter Kit, which would ultimatley enable educators to inspire students through real-world, practical learning experiences. These resources are meant to empower young people with entrepreneurial skills, foster innovation, employability, and promote active citizenship.

<< Objectives >>

By implementing this project, we aimed to transform entrepreneurship education into an engaging, practical and inclusive experience that equips young people with essential entrepreneurial skills and mindsets. Our goal was to move beyond traditional, theory-based approaches and instead focus on experiential learning, empowering students to identify opportunities, solve real-world challenges while creating value in their communities.
We wanted to bridge the gap between policy expectations for entrepreneurial education and the readiness of educators to deliver it effectively. This included providing youth educators with the tools, knowledge, and confidence to teach entrepreneurship in informal and non-formal settings, making it accessible to learners with diverse backgrounds and learning styles.
Ultimately, we sought to foster entrepreneurial competences among young people, such as creativity, problem-solving, and teamwork, while enhancing their employability and sense of active citizenship. By achieving these objectives, we envisioned creating a lasting impact on both educators and students, inspiring them to apply entrepreneurial thinking in meaningful and transformative ways.

<< Implementation >>

We implemented activities to introduce EELs which offered young people hands-on opportunities to develop transversal skills through interactive, community-focused challenges. Participants chose real-world challenges, tackled micro-tasks to build entrepreneurial competencies and engaged in peer collaboration and reflective learning. There is no doubt that this approach supported diverse learning styles, boosted confidence and integrated digital skills. For youth educators, we delivered a Starter Kit with practical tools like case studies, digital tools and implementation guidelines, enabling them to facilitate EELs effectively. An Orientation Day allowed educators to test these resources and gain confidence in their new role as facilitators.
We also developed OERs and a digital hub to support resource sharing and peer learning. These tools provided the foundation for scaling and replicating the project, ensuring sustainability and broad impact. In one Lab, students addressed food waste by creating a campaign to redistribute surplus food. It helped them build key entrepreneurial skills like collaboration and problem-solving. One student said, "This gave me the confidence to act," showcasing the Labs' real-world impact.

<< Results >>

The project's concrete outputs included the development and distribution of the EELs Starter Kit as a comprehensive set of digital resources. This included a review, multimedia case studies, a digital toolbox for educators, and guidelines for implementing Orientation Days. These materials provided educators with knowledge and tools to apply experiential learning in their classrooms, offering practical methods for engaging students in entrepreneurship in a hands-on way.
Beyond the materials, one of the most rewarding results was the direct impact on educators and students. Over 40 youth educators participated in training workshops and Orientation Days, gaining confidence and skills to implement EELs. Over 300 educators and stakeholders downloaded the Starter Kit, reflecting its reach and relevance to the community. A meaningful result was seeing young people, often from diverse and disadvantaged backgrounds, engage in real-world challenges, develop their entrepreneurial mindset, and present innovative solutions to local problems. These experiences transformed educators’ approaches to teaching and students’ self-confidence and problem-solving abilities, leading to a tangible shift in how entrepreneurship is taught and learned.
topics: Overcoming skills mismatch and addressing the needs of the labour market

2022-1-PL01-KA220-YOU-000088903.title: Think Mindful Manage Your Anger
2022-1-PL01-KA220-YOU-000088903.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied  this project because it responded to the critical need for supporting young people (18-24) in managing anger and emotional well-being. This age group faces significant life transitions, such as entering the workforce or becoming more independent, which can create stress and emotional imbalances. The project aimed to provide practical tools, including mindfulness and self-help strategies, to help young people manage anger and prevent escalation.
The project addressed the lack of support from social circles, where mental health struggles are often stigmatized or dismissed as weakness. By participating, we aimed to contribute to breaking this stigma and empowering youth to handle emotional challenges effectively.
Youth workers needed both theoretical knowledge and practical tools to support young people. The project provided training in non-formal and experiential learning methods, enabling youth workers to implement anger management strategies. Access to digital resources further supported ongoing learning and application of these techniques in their work.
The project met the needs of partner organizations by developing a long-term strategy to train youth workers and promote mental health awareness. 


<< Objectives >>

The project aimed to empower young people to manage and prevent anger-related behaviors by equipping them with tools to cope with emotional challenges and mental health issues. To achieve this, we enhanced the competencies of youth workers, focusing on innovative mindfulness techniques and modern communication tools.

We developed a comprehensive booklet on anger management through mindfulness. It included practical strategies and theoretical insights to support youth workers in preventing anger behaviors.We designed and implemented a training program for youth workers, trainers, and mentors. This program enabled them to apply the project’s outcomes in youth organizations, NGOs, and youth councils.
A flexible online learning platform was created, featuring small learning units for youth workers. This resource provided continuous support and enhanced the learning process.
We produced an e-learning system offering self-help tools designed to assist young people in managing and preventing anger independently.


<< Implementation >>

Besides the activities that were necessary to achieve the project deliverables we also organized many meeting along the duration of the project not only the ones in persons such as in Tarnów, Zagreb, Izmir but also lots of on line meetings fostering the work dynamic of the consortium. 
We organized LTTA in Spain which was dedicated to testing the Training toolkit before the pilot testing in youth centres and plan for the pilot testing implementation
Workshops /local multiplayer events) – every partner prepared and carried out workshop to make the topic more understandable and aware of the possible impact. The workshops were part of each dissemination event. They were promoting the interaction of participants and exchange of experiences, good practices, and contacts to create future partnerships and synergies.
In Izmir, Turkey we organized a final dissemination event – international conference.  Partners of the consortium were able to attend and shared their experiences with the general public.


<< Results >>

1.	Multilingual Educational Content:
We developed a booklet featuring 32 good practices in anger management, offering youth workers, leaders, and trainers a resource to implement anger prevention activities without needing additional training. This content promoted self-reliance, self-awareness, and emotional coping skills among youth. Its effectiveness was assessed through national-level focus groups with experts.
2.	Training Program:
A comprehensive training program was created to help youth workers apply anger management techniques in daily work with young people aged 18-24. It included methodologies, needs assessments, pre- and post-assessment tools, and supplementary materials, enhancing professional development and knowledge.
3.	Online Educational Resources:
We provided nano learning content, including videos, exercises, and mini-articles, integrated with popular social networks. These bite-sized units allowed youth workers to easily access and apply the materials.
4.	E-Learning System:
An innovative e-learning platform for young people was developed, offering self-help tools focused on anger management through mindfulness techniques.

2022-1-SI02-KA220-YOU-000090117.title: Težke teme
2022-1-SI02-KA220-YOU-000090117.summary:
<< Background >>

The Hard Topics project is a response to the growing social polarization and increasingly conflictual atmosphere in society.

Youth workers, young people, and educators across various fields are witnessing this tense atmosphere on multiple levels: within groups, in educational institutions, in youth work, and most notably, in society at large.

We believe that the best response to rising polarization is DIALOGUE. Through this project, we aimed to strengthen the dialogical competences of young people—as well as those of youth workers and educators—in an engaging and interactive way.

Our goal was also to contribute to active citizenship and youth initiativeness. We focused our activities around shared European values, which remain one of the few starting points with broad consensus and acceptance. We sought to involve a diverse range of young people, youth workers, and organizations in our dialogical activities.

However, our identified needs extended beyond youth and organizations. We also aimed to make a systemic contribution—by influencing the teaching of civic education in the partner countries.


<< Objectives >>

We set seven key objectives for the project:

G1: Young people are able to manage potentially conflictual situations — both online and in real-life interactions — that stem from social polarization.
G2: Young people gain a deeper understanding of key concepts related to civic literacy, become more resilient to disinformation, and more inclusive in their civic engagement.
G3: Youth workers and youth leaders are trained to address conflicts arising from social polarization and are motivated to work for peace and mutual understanding.
G4: Other educators and youth allies are equipped to address conflicts among young people that stem from increasing social polarization.
G5: The youth sector is recognized as a relevant and competent stakeholder in tackling challenges related to social polarization, civic literacy, and youth initiative.
G6: Spaces for dialogue are established — fostering genuine conversations among young people and others at personal, organizational, local, national, and international levels.
G7: EU citizens develop a deeper understanding of the Union’s values and actively engage in promoting and upholding them.


<< Implementation >>

As part of the project, we carried out the following key activities:

DEVELOPMENT OF TOOLS FOR YOUNG PEOPLE, which included:
•	Creation of 10 guidelines for dialogue, serving both as a project framework and a didactic tool;
•	Development of the HardTopics web application, designed to invite participants with the most divergent views into dialogue;
•	Design of three training curricula aimed at preparing young people for meaningful dialogue.

TRAINING OF YOUTH WORK PROFESSIONALS, which included:
•	Exploration of dialogical concepts;
•	Development of a handbook for working with youth on dialogue;
•	Creation of a training model for youth work;
•	Implementation of training sessions.

IMPLEMENTATION OF ACTIVITIES TO STRENGTHEN DIALOGICAL COMPETENCES IN LOCAL COMMUNITIES, which included:
•	Delivery of dialogue training sessions for young people;
•	Organization of dialogue events among youth;
•	A campaign highlighting the importance of European values.

SYSTEM-LEVEL ACTIVITIES, which included:
•	An initial study on the presence of dialogue in current curricula;
•	Recommendations for civic education, based on consultations;
•	Establishment of a Dialogue Network;
•	Organization of the project’s final conference.


<< Results >>

The project delivered the following key results:

HardTopics Web Application – a tool for youth workers, leaders, and educators to conduct dialogue-based activities using the “opinion-opponent speed dating” method.
“Hard Topics” Handbook – a resource for those working with young people, presenting the most practical dialogue concepts and methods for enhancing dialogical competences.
Three Dialogue Training Programmes for Youth – 2 in-person and 1 online.
Recommendations for Integrating Dialogical Approaches into formal and non-formal education.
Didactic Tool: “10 Guidelines for Dialogue” – a practical resource for working with young people on dialogue.
Dialogue Network – open to individuals and organizations interested in continuing work in this field.
30+ Trained Facilitators – 15 trained during the main training, with more trained in later stages of the project.
Youth Participation – 950 young people in dialogue trainings, and 630 in dialogue events.
European Values Campaign – including materials that can be reused or adapted for future campaigns.
Final Project Conference.
Project Website: https://hardtopics.eu, along with a wide range of dissemination activities.
topics: Bridging intercultural, intergenerational and social divide

2022-2-BG01-KA220-YOU-000098776.title: Youth Going Back to Nature - Engage, Connect, Empower
2022-2-BG01-KA220-YOU-000098776.summary:
<< Background >>

It is the surrounding environment that gives life and protects us. If one possesses the appropriate tools and facilitated access, the outdoors offers endless opportunities for personal and professional growth, for ways to care for the community, and to sustain the environment. That potential of the environmentally sustainable outdoor activities (ESOA) must be unleashed. 
Many international (e.g.UN Sustainable Development Goals), EU (e.g.EU Youth Strategy 2019-2027 and the 11 Youth Goals), and local bodies are alerting for the needs of young people with fewer opportunities for development, mental and physical health improvement as they transition to adulthood. There is also the need to promote sustainable interaction and care for the environment that is incorporated in ESOA. 
Applying the potential of ESOA and the benefits for the youth are the motivation to initiate the project ‘’Youth Going Back to Nature’’. In searching for ways to develop the potential of the idea we were inspired by and addressed the European Union Youth Strategy and the 11 European Youth Goals. Thus, we decided to ‘’Engage, Connect, Empower’’ young people with fewer opportunities to go back to nature and embrace the potential of ESOA.

<< Objectives >>

The YGBN project aimed to support young people with fewer opportunities (YPFO) in reconnecting with nature through ESOA, guided by the partner organizations. Its main objective was to make sustainable outdoor activities accessible and effective for YPFO, reaching 2322 (initially targeting 2000) members of the youth community across Bulgaria, Italy, Belgium, Croatia, Estonia, and Lithuania – YPFO, youth workers and organizations. The objective was divided into three parts—Engage, Connect, and Empower—aligned with the EU Youth Goals.
The project first sought to engage vulnerable youth (WP2), resulting in case studies from three Learning Exchange Events, three short documentaries, and three ESOA toolkits. The second goal was to connect the youth community (WP3) by creating the Youth Outdoor Portal (YOP) and the European Youth Outdoor Network (EYON). The third goal was to empower YPFO and the youth community (WP4–WP5), involving over 200 participants in discussions, training 28 youth workers to apply the toolkits with 80 local young people, and reaching over 500 individuals through large-scale events such as the Online Youth Outdoor Conference and the European Youth Outdoor Festival, complemented by dissemination actions by partners.

<< Implementation >>

On the path to reaching the YGBN project objectives the consortium partners organized a number of activities. We began by gathering a total of 49 youth workers from the 6 partnering countries for a series of 3 Learning Exchange Events(LEEs) where they developed 3 sets of innovative ESOA for young women, youth at risk, young people with disabilities. The ESOA became part of the toolkits and documentaries. 
Second, in September 2023 the 6 partnering organizations founded the European Youth Outdoor Network – a non-formal organization dedicated to facilitating access to young people to the outdoors in Europe. In 2024 we organized an European BACK TO NATURE day, its first initiative. 
Third, we developed the youth outdoor portal www.outdoorportal.eu. 
Fourth, in March 2025 we organized the international online conference Youth Going Back to Nature for 492 members of the youth community, including youth with fewer opportunities. 
Fifth, in June 2025 we organized the first European Youth Outdoor Festival for 110 participants from the partnering countries. 
Finally, at the end of the project interactive dissemination events were organized in Bulgaria, Italy, Belgium, Croatia, Estonia, and Lithuania reaching wide audience of 321 people.

<< Results >>

Aiming to promote ESOA for youth with fewer opportunities with the project and beyond its end we developed educational materials, interactive online platform, and reached a wide audience through the project activities. 
Within the LEEs youth workers developed 21 innovative environmentally sustainable outdoor activities that were described in details in the 3 YGBN Going Back to Nature Toolkits dedicated to young women, youth at risk, young people with disabilities. To illustrate the ESOA and show part of the development process the 3 LEEs were captured on camera in 3 documentary movies. 
Another result was the newly established European Youth Outdoor Network. 
The toolkits, documentaries and resources from partner organizations are available in the Explore section on the free youth outdoor portal www.outdoorportal.eu. The platform also features a section where the youth community can Connect. The platform hosts the EYON and information about the YGBN project. Within the project the platform reached 1322 unique visitors and nearly 3400 views.
Through the online and in-person events the YGBN project reached 2322 members of the youth community including young people with fewer opportunities, successfully spreading ESOA across Europe.
topics: Quality and innovation of youth work

2022-2-ES02-KA220-YOU-000092224.title: MENTORÍA JUVENIL DE CALIDAD PARA LA INCLUSIÓN: UN GRAN HERMANO PARA SUPERAR BARRERAS COMPARTIDAS
2022-2-ES02-KA220-YOU-000092224.summary:
<< Objectives >>

The objective of this project is to create a network of European rare disease national entities to design and implement a training process for young people who suffer from these obstacles so they become mentors, guardians, “older siblings” of other youth and children who suffer from the same obstacles -anywhere in Europe-, to guide them virtually so they can develop their self-esteem, learn about their situation and consequences, and discover mechanisms to achieve their full inclusion.

<< Implementation >>

In order to develop this project, monitoring, quality, and exchange of good practices activities will be carried out, as well as activities for the constitution of a European network, activities for the generation of results, training via non-formal education, pilot tests, awareness activities, activities for the promotion of the project’s results in the 4 participating countries, and on-site and online meetings of the network used to strengthen it and monitor the project.

<< Results >>

The project’s main results will be:
‒ A European network with dialogue capabilities with the European Commission.
‒ A methodological guide for training to become older siblings.
‒ Non-formal resources for inclusion and to overcome the barriers derived from their illness.

‒ A European dissemination campaign: AN OLDER SIBLING TO REACH THE FUTURE.

2022-2-FR02-KA220-YOU-000100784.title: Peace Awareness through Volunteering and Education
2022-2-FR02-KA220-YOU-000100784.summary:
<< Background >>

De nombreux jeunes Européens ont grandi en considérant la paix comme allant de soi et n'ont donc pas apprécié ce que le projet européen commun leur a offert en termes de sécurité personnelle et d'harmonie sociale. Mais, comme l'a récemment montré l'invasion russe de l'Ukraine, des environnements pacifiques et démocratiques peuvent potentiellement être détruits à tout moment par des événements inattendus et des revirements politiques extrêmes. Cela a rappelé à toute l'UE la nécessité absolue d'une culture de la paix, qui est essentielle  à la fois comme mécanisme préventif contre les conflits potentiels et comme remède aux conflits existants. Le même événement tragique a également mis en garde contre le potentiel destructeur de nombreuses formes de conflits passés et présents non résolus dans toute l'Europe. Le projet souligne l'importance de soutenir les jeunes générations pour lutter contre l'intolérance et l'indifférence, en les aidant à faire l'expérience directe de formes de conflits qui pourraient autrement être considérées comme "lointaines" et vagues. Cela peut être le cas en raison d'un manque général d'intérêt et de connaissances, dans de nombreux cas également en raison du peu d'opportunités d'éducation à la paix.

<< Objectives >>

PAVE vise à : 
- OS1 : Éduquer et sensibiliser la jeunesse européenne à l'importance des relations pacifiques entre les États, les communautés et les individus 
- SO2 : Permettre aux jeunes d'Europe de se familiariser directement avec les conséquences des conflits passés et en cours, et d'acquérir de l'expérience dans la gestion des situations d'urgence et du passé conflictuel.
- SO3 : Encourager le volontariat des jeunes, en particulier dans les situations de conflit et de crise, et soutenir le sens de la solidarité européenne

<< Implementation >>

Les activités suivantes ont été mises en œuvre :
- Gestion du projet : signature de la convention de subvention et de l'accord de consortium, désignation d'un gestionnaire de projet principal, d'un gestionnaire financier, d'un gestionnaire de la communication et d'un comité de pilotage, coordination continue du projet.
- Création d'une communauté d'intérêt : 
- Académie internationale de la paix : un événement international de formation où la paix et la guerre ont été explorées sous de nombreux angles et perspectives, favorisant la construction de la paix, le dialogue interculturel et la gestion des conflits. 
- Trois ateliers en ligne sur le volontariat à la suite de l'Académie internationale de la paix 
- Développement d'un programme de volontariat dans quatre pays
-Mise en œuvre de 8 séries de semaines de volontariat dans quatre pays du consortium 
- Formation en ligne sur le plaidoyer
- Campagne vidéo de communication #peace_is_not_for_granted
- Événement final à Paris : Forum international de la paix
- Activités de communication : messages sur les médias sociaux, articles, bulletin d'information.

<< Results >>

Sensibilisation accrue aux différentes situations conflictuelles qui sont souvent négligées ou mal connues par de nombreux jeunes citoyens de l'UE Connaissance accrue des thèmes de l'éducation à la paix et des relations interculturelles Sentiment accru de solidarité et d'empathie à l'égard des pairs vivant dans un état de tension et/ou de conflit armé.

2022-2-HR01-KA220-YOU-000096214.title: Digitalna transformacija inkluzivnog youth worka
2022-2-HR01-KA220-YOU-000096214.summary:
<< Background >>

The "DTIYW" project was created in response to the lack of innovative tools and systematic strategies for digital development in youth work, especially in rural areas and for marginalized groups. The Studio B association, with years of experience working with youth from isolated environments, recognized that traditional approaches are not sufficiently adapted to digital generations, which limits access to educational and social opportunities. A needs analysis showed that organizations often use outdated methods, lack digital competencies, and young people with fewer opportunities (e.g., NEET youth, individuals with disabilities) do not participate in the creation of public policies.
Through collaboration with partners from Germany, Sweden, and Austria, the aim was to develop standardized models for digital inclusion and enable young people to actively participate in society. The project was designed to address geographical barriers, the lack of expertise among youth workers in using digital tools, and the insufficient representation of marginalized youth voices in strategic documents. Previous experience in ESF projects for the employment of marginalized groups and Erasmus+ trainings served as a foundation for this initiative.

<< Objectives >>

The project aimed to achieve several key objectives: to develop standardized strategies for digital development in youth work across Croatia, Sweden, Germany, and Austria, including needs assessment and guidelines for tool application. It also aimed to create five multilingual training programs for youth workers to enhance their digital and inclusive competencies. A Virtual Inclusive Center (VIC) was established as a platform for sharing resources, tools, and best practices tailored for young people with fewer opportunities, featuring all project materials and an accompanying mobile application. The project sought to empower organizations through mentorship, action plans, and seminars for implementing digital solutions. Additionally, it included marginalized youth in policy creation via focus groups and strategy development, strengthening their advocacy potential. Concrete results included trained youth workers and the active involvement of young people in decision-making processes. The project successfully developed a platform and mobile app, setting the groundwork for sustainable digital transformation in youth work across Europe through international cooperation and standardized approaches.

<< Implementation >>

As part of the "Digital Transformation of Inclusive Youth Work" project, the following activities were carried out: Workshops were held to develop strategies for digital transformation in youth work, focusing on inclusivity and improving practices. Five multilingual informal training programs were implemented, covering topics such as digital skills, sustainability, youth in virtual environments, social inclusion, and stress management (Work in Progress training). Other organizations and individuals working with youth were empowered through the creation of action plans and seminars (Short Term Practice and seminar "Let’s Do Digital"). A platform was developed to offer resources and tools for youth workers, facilitating the exchange of information and best practices, along with a mobile application. Collaborative activities with partners from Sweden, Germany, and Austria enriched the content and methods used (transnational meetings, EduLab). Continuous evaluation of activities was conducted throughout the project, gathering participant feedback to ensure program relevance. These activities strengthened the capacities of organizations and improved the quality of youth work.

<< Results >>

The "DTIYW" project achieved several concrete results: Four strategies for the digital transformation of youth work were developed, emphasizing inclusivity and practical improvements. Action plans were written for eight organizations, and youth workers were empowered through seminars. Five informal training programs for youth workers were designed and implemented, during which participants gained skills in digital literacy, social inclusion, sustainability, stress management, and virtual work with youth. A handbook was created for each program, translated into four languages. Implementation webinars were recorded for each of the five programs. A platform was developed to provide resources and tools for youth workers (including a digital nomad map, five e-learning systems, a mobile app, a "Sharing is Caring" tool, and a Virtual Study Buddy), facilitating the exchange of information and best practices. A mobile app was developed to accompany the platform. Partnerships were established with organizations from Sweden, Germany, and Austria, enabling knowledge and experience exchange. Conferences (in-person and online) were held to disseminate project results. Evaluation activities were conducted  to ensure relevance and effectiveness.

2022-2-HR01-KA220-YOU-000098445.title: COMMUNITY LEARNING POINT
2022-2-HR01-KA220-YOU-000098445.summary:
<< Background >>

This project answered our identified needs for integrating innovatively and efficiently the use of ‘space’ as an active learning tool, and this in all its dimensions. With results applicable in different sectors: non-formal & formal education, as well as informal and family contexts. Our partnership, composed by different format youth work actors: grass root youth work, social youth welfare, institutional youth work, schools and youth work service providers, joined experience and expertise to answer the following:
Main needs identified and answered:
conscious use of space and spatial elements as educational tools;
activities in the wider local communities, more efficiently answering identified problems/challenges;
a tool to connect different stakeholders in the community towards a common action plan.
Additionally, this project provided the different partners the empowering process to act within their community in an innovative and different approach, hereby re-considering the previous underuse of ‘space’ as a strong educational tool, impacting directly the learners involved within their ‘learning space’.


<< Objectives >>

The Community Learning Point project aimed to enhance community-based learning  by developing tools that promote active learning, critical thinking, and social engagement. The project achieved the intended results as answers to our needs. This in a twofold manner. 1. The creation of the interactive manual which critically lays out how to use ‘space’ as an enriching educational element in our personal and community learning.This manual includes concrete suggestions, solutions, ideas and references to explore more in depth. The manual is intended to inspire
youth workers to think out of the box and be creative in the way of learning. Translated into 5 languages to enlarge the reach and dissemination.  2.  The creation of an educational board game with a combination of existing methods structured in a way to make a complete action plan. The use of gamification makes it easier to think open and free.
This methodological approach, focusing on need assessment, stakeholders roles, proactive engagement, structured construction of action plans which cover also  the -often ignored/forgotten- spaces and areas important to effectively
implement the changes in personal and community life. Available in 5 different languages.

<< Implementation >>

The different project activities supported the phased project design of deeper research, conceptualisation, testing, evaluation, production and promotion of the innovative learning tools. ‘Space’ as a central feature given in the learning tools, taking in account the wide range of stakeholders. Resulting in the interactive manual ‘Space as a learning tool’ and the educational board game / exercise ‘Community space Intervention’. Activities supporting this flow were 1 kick off meeting, 3 transnational partner meetings, 5 multiplier events, >10 test workshops in 2 different test phases (>120 participants), development of prototypes, >5 workshops on both the manual and the board game involving different stakeholders, >20 online zoom meetings, besides the multiple specific task force group meetings (e.g. board game development, manual development, communication and more).  

<< Results >>

The concrete results of the Community Learning Point project are:
- Educational Board Game ''Community Space Intervention”
- Interactive Manual "Space as a learning tool"
- WEB page CLP for the needs of distribution and free access to materials for the realization of the game and the use of the manual
- Created more than 20 action plans, and implemented 10
- Conducted a two-phase examination of the participants of the board game test group
- Realized more than 20 expert interviews for the needs of analyzing the interactive manual
- Made a design for the game
- Made a design for the manual
- Manual and board game translated to 5 languages
- Design for the web page
- 50 Manual produced (printed) in 5 different languages
- 50 board games sets produced in 5 different languages
Additional:
an increased cooperation level between the 5 partners
increased visibility and recognition of our expertise in non-formal education in our different realities

New learning and teaching methods and approaches

2022-2-HR01-KA220-YOU-000101337.title: Eco-patrols 4 environmental goals
2022-2-HR01-KA220-YOU-000101337.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project to strengthen the strategic cooperation of our organizations in the field of youth and environment, and to increase the transnational impact of our work. Through research and needs analysis, we identified low environmental awareness and unsustainable daily habits among youth and local stakeholders during the application process. This motivated us to share and upscale the successful Croatian “Eco-patrol” model to other countries. Our goal was to expand it for older youth (14-18 years) and add a digital dimension through a mobile educational game, fostering sustainable habits and climate action.

By building on existing results and working in a transnational, multidisciplinary team, we aimed to contribute to long-term behavioral change, promote active citizenship, and strengthen environmental education across Europe.

We achieved to address key needs by developing the Eco-patrol Manual for educators, youth workers, and teachers. The lack of local extracurricular eco-activities was tackled by forming five local Eco-patrol groups. Additionally, Generation Z’s preference for mobile learning was met through the Eco-patrols in 24 Zones educational app, making environmental topics accessible via smartphones.



<< Objectives >>

By implementing this project, we aimed to enhance the competencies of environmental and youth organizations in effectively raising awareness among diverse target groups about environmental and climate change challenges. Our goal was to foster long-term behavioral changes by equipping our organizations with an innovative green skill method — the Eco-patrol program. Through this approach, we wanted to empower youth to make environmentally conscious choices in their daily lives and to provide organizations, youth workers and educators with practical multiplying tools.

The project aimed to bridge the gap between awareness and action by providing methods and practical tools, skills and knowledge that organizations can use to inspire sustainable habits of youth. By fostering collaboration among project partners and strengthening organizational capacities, we aimed to create a spilling effect that extends beyond the project's immediate participants, contributing to a wide range of stakeholders internationally. Our objective was to build a strong foundation for non-formal environmental education through the Eco-patrol method. 


<< Implementation >>

Activities implemented in WP1: Project face-to-face meetings (kick off and final) and regular monthly online project meetings; Financial administration and project reporting; Regular communication, promotion and dissemination activities; Continues evaluation and monitoring; 

Activities in WP2: Eco-patrol Manual development through online and face-to-face cooperation (International workshop held in Macedonia); Testing of the Eco-patrol Manual in National Seminars for youth workers in all partner countries; Eco-patrol concept piloting in each country and implementing the program locally; Design and publication of Manual and translation in all languages of the partner countries; Implementation of 4 dissemination events per country.

Activities in WP3: E-educational game design through online cooperation between experts and International e-game workshop held in Hungary; Testing game activities implemented locally; National and International Eco-game events; Web-site design and regular content creation; Implementation of 4 dissemination events and 1 National conference in each country; Organization of the Final project meeting in Croatia.
Regular visibility an evaluation activities were part of all WPs. 


<< Results >>

Concrete outputs of our project are: Eco-patrol Manual for non-formal environmental education of youth, consisting of 8 modules and 48 activities, in 6 language versions (English, Croatian, Serbian, Macedonian, Italian and Hungarian); Online educational eco-game - mobile application “Eco-patrols in 24 zones”, consisting of 24 tasks each in 3 levels, guiding us around the globe and building players environmental awareness in fun and interesting way; Eco-patrols - corresponding board game. 

Other results are: Straighten cooperation among 5 partner organizations from 5 different countries to work in youth non-formal environmental education and built their capacity for transnational work and cooperation; Eco-patrol youth groups formed and Eco-patrol Manual tested with more than 100 youngsters across five countries; Main outputs widely disseminated through more than 25 multiplying events and accessible online at https://eco-patrols.eu/ and other EU platforms as open source resource for non-formal environmental education of youth.

2022-2-IE01-KA220-YOU-000097037.title: Building environmental awareness and sustainability values through the Head, Heart, Hands Model for Transformative Learning.
2022-2-IE01-KA220-YOU-000097037.summary:
<< Background >>

The decision to apply for this project was driven by the ongoing climate crisis which is affecting countries across the globe. Temperatures are rising notable alongside a sharp rise in sea levels and climate related catastrophes. It was recognised by the consortium that now more than ever we are living an interconnected world where a systemic change is required. To do so, there is a whole of society approach needed with particular attention paid to the role that young people can have in creating innovative approaches to tackling such issues. However, to do so responsibly, the consortium recognised the need to ensure that people not only understand the effects of climate change, but also the cause. It was recognised by the consortium and those involved in the need’s analysis that a holistic approach to tackling climate change is needed and utilising a Global Citizenship Education methodology offered that. 

BEST as a project united young people and youth workers from across Europe to act on climate change and become advocates for change in their local and national communities. 


<< Objectives >>

The overall objective of the BEST project was to support young people to gain a deeper understanding of climate change and take concrete action to combat it. The primary objectives of the project were: 

-	To support young people to develop their awareness into the cause and effect of climate change;
-	To provide young people and educators with a range of tools, ideas and initiative’s which can be used to combat climate change;
-	To empower young people to become agents of change and become active citizens in their local and national communities; 
-	To educate young people and educators on the role of cognitive, socio-emotional and behavioural competences so that they can respond effectively and implement sustainable practices in their lives;
-	To create informative and open spaces to create dialogue and communication with regards climate change. 

<< Implementation >>

The BEST project led by Meath Partnership and comprising of Judend Am Werk Steiermark GMBH (JAW), Right Challenge, Callidus, Quality Culture SRLS and CSI Centre for Social Innovation LTD have developed, piloted and implemented a suite of resources and training targeted at young people, youth workers and community practitioners. 

The following activities were implemented: 

- Active research conducted with young people to identify key challenges facing young people with regards to climate action;
- A range of materials were developed, include youth education programmes and youth worker capacity building programmes were developed, piloted, updated and translated; 

- A substantial amount of pilot and transnational training took place across Europe regarding the BEST training materials;
-A number of Climate Action Seminars and Conferences were held to showcase the project results.

<< Results >>

The following results were developed as part of the BEST project: 

-	A 17-page Eco System Mapping Transnational Report that details the research conducted in 6 European countries with 131 young people. It includes the accompanying graphic harvested findings;
-	The development of a 4-part online training course (inclusive of a facilitators manual) that was tested with 96 young people and translated into all partner languages;
-	A 21-hour Inservice Training Programme (ISTP) was developed on topics connected to Environmental Sustainability and Transformative Education.  This was tested with 37 youth workers;
-	150 ‘Bank of Sustainable Ideas for Combatting Climate Change’ was developed and freely available for download;
-	A suite of communication activities was developed include videos and newsletters with project updates;
-	Climate Action Seminars were hosted in all partner countries.
topics: Creating new, innovative or joint curricula or courses

2022-2-PT02-KA220-YOU-000093609.title: SDG4Youth
2022-2-PT02-KA220-YOU-000093609.summary:
<< Background >>

The world today is marked by a series of problems that affect all citizens, without exception, and which relate to issues such as health, poverty, hunger, gender, education, work, inequalities, the environment, etc. In order to create a global model capable of combating cross-cutting social problems, 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were created. As representatives of the future, young people are naturally at the forefront of this process of building a cohesive, fair and sustainable society. It is clear, therefore, that there is still a long way to go and that multiple efforts need to be made to encourage youth participation for the development of society. 

PROBLEM
Low levels of youth participation in the various spheres of society.

NEEDS
a) Raise community awareness of existing social problems (in relation to the SDGs);
b) Promote the involvement and active participation of citizens in responding to the social problems identified (the responsibility cannot lie solely with the central states);
c) Strengthen European cooperation as a response to the social problems identified (instill the idea of GLOCAL).

<< Objectives >>

Based on the social problem identified and the needs raised, the aim of this project was to:
(OG) Encourage youth participation, particularly in issues that directly affect young people and society in general.

(SO1) Bring together European youth workers to identify, debate, co-create and test participatory and socially innovative solutions in the field of youth participation (which could be replicated, contributing to innovation in the sector);
(SO2) Develop the key competences of young people (especially those with fewer opportunities) for entrepreneurship, ensuring that young people are able to develop and implement their own projects and actions that respond to the problems of youth and society;
(SO3) Disseminate and explore the SDGs of the 2030 Agenda, so that young people can act in favour of building a more cohesive, just and sustainable society;
(SO4) Contribute to the enhancement of the territory, identifying problems, debating answers and presenting solutions to favour the construction of each community and society in general;
(SO5) Promote European values.


<< Implementation >>

VM-YW: through digital platforms, the TJs developed collaborative work (exchanged information, debated ideas, shared data, established points of situation, co-constructed materials as the output of the project).

STATE-OF-THE-ART ANALYSIS
TJ identified and shared:
-Good practices at European level regarding youth participation;
-SDG needs assessment;
-Structuring local actions with the possibility of global implementation;
-Community empowerment.

VM-Y: through digital platforms, the JWs developed their work with young people and were in constant cooperation, exchanging ideas and sharing information.

SDG4YOUTH Workshops: after TWS 1, the intervention program was tested with the young people. In these sessions, the young people developed skills and learning that led them to be participatory in solving society's problems. The result was proposals for local intervention in line with the SDGs, where the solution to global problems involved empowering young people. These were local laboratories with a physical and virtual component.

SDG4YOUTH Online Seminars: in addition to the workshops, there were international seminars with all the young people to explore the skills developed.

<< Results >>

a. TANGIBLE RESULTS 
- Output SDG4YOUTH: guide for youth participation in the SDGs;
- Project booklet;
- Content and materials developed throughout each phase of the project (e.g. planning documents: checklists, Action Plan, etc.; preparation documents: project value profile, Partnership Agreement, Infopack, etc.; follow-up documents: checklists, activity reports, evaluation reports, audiovisual resources, etc.).

b. INTANGIBLE RESULTS
In particular, the 8 key competences defined in YOUTHPASS on Key Competences for Lifelong Learning. These competences were continuously developed by the participants through working together, in co-learning and co-creation: literacy; multilingualism; mathematical competence and competence in science, technology and engineering; digital; personal, social and learning to learn; citizenship; entrepreneurship and cultural awareness and expression.
topics: Quality and innovation of youth work

2022-2-RO01-KA220-YOU-000096603.title: FOOD-4-THOUGHT: CULTIVATING THE PATHWAYS TO GREENER AND FOOD SECURED CITIES BY ENGAGING YOUTH IN URBAN AGRICULTURE
2022-2-RO01-KA220-YOU-000096603.summary:
<< Background >>

The FOOD-4-THOUGHT idea came to life as a result of the actual crisis which we are currently facing, in terms of environment and climate change, more specifically related to food insecurity. Our project wanted to provide young people with more tools, skills and most importantly, knowledge on urban agriculture (UA) and how effective it can be in combating climate crises, food insecurity (exacerbated by the Russian invasion in Ukraine) and improve sustainability.
Our initiative focused on the following needs:
a) Building more resilient food systems
b) Reducing food waste 
c) Increasing youth participation in agriculture
d) Enhancing urban resilience and food self-sufficiency
e) Promoting urban agriculture to help young people overcome economic and mental health challenges worsened by the pandemic and ongoing food crises
f) Addressing climate change anxiety, prevalent among youth globally by engaging them in agricultural activities that positively impact mental health.
g) Equipping youth workers with updated skills, knowledge, and methodologies related to urban agriculture and food security, enabling them to better support young people in addressing modern social challenges. 


<< Objectives >>

The primary goal of the project was to introduce young people (YP) to UA and motivate them to take an active role in creating and maintaining vegetable gardens. UA served as a tool to foster sustainable, resilient, food-secure, and inclusive urban communities.
More specifically, the project intended to:
Inspire YP to adopt sustainable habits and ways of living
Promote UA and agricultural literacy as a means to improve food security and environmental protection
Provide support for urban communities
Make agriculture more appealing to urban youth
Empower YP to become advocates for organic food production
Build collaboration among civil society organisations and a variety of stakeholders
Equip youth workers (YW) with modern agricultural and environmental skills 
Encourage the intergenerational sharing of agricultural knowledge 
Challenge and overturn negative stereotypes about farming as a profession
Bring farmers and academics together to jointly involve more youth in agricultural initiatives
Support YP in cultivating initiative and responsibility
Develop a network of YP, YW, and professionals who understand food security
Promote YP’s mental health and resilience through their involvement in UA practices
Introduce YP to local food

<< Implementation >>

During the project, the consortium formed of 6 partners from 6 European countries, worked on implementing the following activities:

1. did research by creating an evaluation survey + a map with 60 best practices in UA from each country;
2. created a comparative report in the form of infographics with the results;
3. managed an expert advisory board with agriculture experts from each country;
4. created and translated a training pack with 6 modules (learning nuggets) including activities, PPTs, non-formal exercises etc which focused on UA for young people;
5. launched a project website and an interactive platform with multiple interactive tools for the people;
6. collaborated with agriculture experts to create 18 short video tutorials on how to grow different vegetables and herbs;
7. developed a training programme with activities in each partner country to engage local young people into UA workshops, presentations, study visits and similar engaging events;
8. promoted UA and our project through several dissemination and promotion materials and channels (social media, flyers, newsletters, conferences, local events);
9. evaluated the progress of our project by gathering people's answers in valuable evaluation forms.

<< Results >>

The concrete outputs of our project are: 
1. A 5 pages INFOGRAPHIC with results from our research on UA;
2. A multimedia TRAINING PACK for YP;
3. A MULTIPURPOSE PORTAL that operates as an Open Learning Environment offering the following functions: eLEARNING for introducing YP to vegetable production, e-MAPPING, for promoting best practices at the EU level, e-SKILLS ASSESSMENT where YP are able to assess their knowledge and skills, and e-COMMUNITY, online space where all participants can exchange opinions, questions etc.
4. 18 “HOW TO GROW” VIDEO TUTORIALS that are posted on the project’s YouTube account;
5. FOOD-4-THOUGHT TRAINING PROGRAMME which included FARMERS IN THE CITY workshops for encouraging YP to get involved in local agricultural activities, where YP visited rural farms, were encouraged to develop their own vegetables in their home and learned how to plant different plants
6. A TRAINING FOR TRAINERS were youth workers from the 6 countries shared knowledge, skills and activity ideas with their peers
7. A Blended Mobility Activity, where YP in transnational groups had the opportunity to exchange experiences and learn more about the topic.
topics: Quality and innovation of youth work

2022-2-RO01-KA220-YOU-000098604.title: CAPSULE / CArreer Path Support for young women UnLocking Entrepreneurial spirit
2022-2-RO01-KA220-YOU-000098604.summary:
<< Background >>

The idea of this project started from the systemic barriers that young women (YW) face when it comes to entrepreneurship, career development, and professional growth. A consistent part of the partners’ team is composed of women, who have experienced, in one way or another, these kinds of constraints over time, namely limited access to resources, mentorship, or a supportive ecosystem. Furthermore, our previous experience in working with YW showed us that they are facing challenges like mental barriers, lack of role models, or cultural expectations that discourage alternative career paths outside of traditional employment.
This project was designed to bring awareness to entrepreneurship as a viable career choice, provide a structured system, and empower YW to take control of their professional journey. It aimed to close the gender gap in entrepreneurship, by fostering an inclusive and digitally transformative approach, in alignment with EU priorities. The project directly addressed the underrepresentation of women in business, as reflected in EU reports, and supported YW in overcoming self-doubt, fear of failure, and low-risk tolerance.

<< Objectives >>

The main objective of this project was to empower YW in entrepreneurship, equipping them with the necessary skills, confidence, and network to become active change agents in their communities. The project’s activities were designed to address the key barriers that are limiting YWs’ participation in entrepreneurship such as fear of failure, lack of role models, and restricted access to tailored support. Through the current project, we wanted to provide training, coaching, mentoring, and consultancy in order to help YW to develop and implement their entrepreneurial or community projects. Also, we aimed to create a strong and supportive network of YW entrepreneurs in order to enhance collaboration, knowledge-sharing, and peer support.
Another key objective of the project was to raise awareness about YW entrepreneurship as a viable career path and a driver for social change, achieved through a large-scale communication campaign meant to inspire and inform YW about the available opportunities, and advocating for inclusivity and gender equality in entrepreneurship. 
By implementing the project, we contributed to the EU priorities on youth and women’s entrepreneurship, self-employment, and active citizenship.

<< Implementation >>

The project consisted in providing a space for continuous learning & engagement among YW by establishing communities of practice, mastermind sessions, and an international bootcamp. 
These 3 key components were designed to empower 105 YW entrepreneurs:
-capacity building: developing a self-leadership e-course & handbooks, translating them into multiple languages, alongside with 4 e-courses already available before the project’s start, running a hybrid learning program with 6 in-person & online cohorts, covering entrepreneurial mindset, business model canvas, financing, pitching, storytelling etc.
-community support: creating 3 communities of practice for YW, thus ensuring long-term peer support; organizing an international bootcamp on business expansion; hosting 5 mastermind sessions for  international community; engaging 14 influencer ambassadors to amplify project visibility.
-tailored support & impact measurement: offering mentorship, coaching & consultancy for YW in order to start/grow their business, producing 6 impact stories showcasing YW entrepreneurs, implementing impact tracking via surveys, interviews & personal tracking diaries; and publishing an insight paper with recommendations for fostering YW entrepreneurship.

<< Results >>

As part of the capacity-building efforts, the project created a self-leadership e-course and provided a total of 5 guided e-courses available in 4 languages. YW benefited from 6 structured training programs, combining online and in-person experiences, consisting also of 18 residential weekends. 85 Youthpass certificates were awarded, recognizing the skills acquired. 71,8% of YW were reporting improved entrepreneurial knowledge and 86,11% recommended the program to their peers.
In order to foster an international community, 3 CoPs were established across 3 countries, with 22 meetings & 5 international mastermind sessions. The project engaged 14 influencer ambassadors who actively promoted its activities through 34 articles & posts. Additionally, an international bootcamp for 10 YW was organized, providing the chance to explore new business opportunities, and a network of coaches & mentors was helping participants to overcome mental barriers and refine their business ideas. 6 inspiring success stories were documented, highlighting the impact of entrepreneurship on YW, and an insight paper summarizing key learnings. 72,95% of participants reported overcoming mental barriers and felt more prepared to launch their business.

2022-2-SE02-KA220-YOU-000098716.title: DOCC: Debate on, change community
2022-2-SE02-KA220-YOU-000098716.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project to facilitate youth involvement in civic engagement, with a focus on marginalized communities such as the immigrant-origin youth. We have witnessed decreasing political participation in the young generation of Europeans, which has resulted from lack of knowledge and little space to articulate opinions.
Youth in immigrant communities in particular have additional challenges, including social isolation and cultural barriers that inhibit participation in the community. Our many efforts showed that it was essential to use more open approaches so they could express their concerns and interact with those who make the decisions.
The project also seeks to employ debating and discussing as strategies for bridging that gap, enhancing understanding and confidence, and creating a sense of being part of something. We aim to empower young people by giving a voice and public speaking opportunities so they become socially active citizens who will speak up and defend their rights as well as the issues that matter to them.

<< Objectives >>

We have long sensed the need to provide high-interest activities that motivate young people (including youth from immigrant backgrounds) to stay committed to programs over time. These young people are often excluded and unaware of their rights and opportunities to participate. Our consortia aims to design a model on youth long term programme which has increased the capacity of youth to articulate opinions and be engaged with decision makers.
European Youth Political Participation Is Shrinking, and With it Comes the Threat of Disengagement and Misinformation. Civic engagement is most commonly associated with socioeconomic status and education, both of which are less accessible to immigrant youth. We are striving to move from one off programs to regular weekly programming that will better feed the movement for young people.

<< Implementation >>

The project provided long-term non-formal education in five partner countries. Clubs in Sweden, Italy, Portugal, and Croatia engaged over 120+ youth workers and young participants to test pedagogical materials. We created and validated 21 lesson plans based on the ERR framework during an event in Croatia. Five deliberation events led participants to develop policy recommendations on mental health, urban safety, and climate issues. Additionally, we developed two e-learning courses on AI and updated the "Your Priorities" platform for youth engagement. Monthly meetings helped maintain coordination among partners, and four toolkits were translated into five languages, with results shared with over 110 youth workers. All resources are archived at: https://doccplatform.com/.

<< Results >>

The DOCC project achieved notable outcomes in methodology, digital innovation, and community engagement. We developed and translated four key toolkits into five languages, creating 21 structured session plans based on the ERR framework for deep learning. We launched two e-learning courses on AI ethics and fact-checking and updated the Your Priorities platform based on feedback from young testers for improved accessibility.
Additionally, we established four debate-based youth clubs in Sweden, Italy, Portugal, and Croatia, engaging over 120 youth workers and young people. These clubs hosted national and international deliberation events, leading to formal policy proposals presented to mayors that influenced local governance. All educational resources are available at our hub: https://doccplatform.com/
topics: Quality and innovation of youth work

2022-2-SI02-KA220-YOU-000097309.title: You(th)App
2022-2-SI02-KA220-YOU-000097309.summary:
<< Background >>

The main motive of Institute Nefiks and project partners to participate in the Key Action 2 project was the desire to strengthen our international outreach and respond to a need we identified among our youth workers and youth workers from other organisations: to develop a mobile application that would contain more support options for the implementation of youth work (evaluation, sound effects, timer, group divider) and would not only be used as a library (example of the Pika STOP application already developed at Nefiks). 
With this project, we did not want to replace the traditional "in vivo" forms of youth work with virtual youth work, but we wanted to support these forms of youth work with digital tools that would always be available to the youth worker, regardless of the time and place of the youth work. If a youth worker found himself in a remote place without a mobile signal, leading a group of young people, and needed an idea how to divide the group, a countdown timer, an evaluation model or other tool, he should have a simple solution at his disposal - an 'offline' app that combines all this and more, and that fully supports the demanding work of the youth worker.

<< Objectives >>

The goal of the project was to raise the quality of youth work by using alternative methods;
- to strengthen the capacity of youth workers in their offline work and, as a consequence, to strengthen young people's competences for participation and implementation of youth work;
- strengthen the knowledge and competences of 30 youth workers;
- Promote the visibility of the youth work profession and youth work among young people, relevant stakeholders and wider society.

<< Implementation >>

The following activities were carried out:
- Analysis of the state of the art and existing materials, tools and tools for youth workers;
- training (online module and live&online training);
- development of a mobile application;
- Communication and dissemination of results.

<< Results >>

The results of the You(th) App project are:
- A new online module to train youth workers to work effectively and efficiently with young people using the app;
- 30 trained youth workers from three countries participating in an international training course (partly online, partly face-to-face);
- 4you(th)Work, an offline mobile app for youth work, containing tools and tools for working with young people;
- networking and new partnerships established between participating organisations and youth workers in the participating countries to exchange knowledge, experience and good practices in the field of youth work.
topics: Quality and innovation of youth work

2022-2-SI02-KA220-YOU-000099917.title: Opolnomočenje mladih in mladinskih delavcev za prepoznavo in informirano odzivanje na spletno nasilje s preseganjem spolnih stereotipov
2022-2-SI02-KA220-YOU-000099917.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for the MEDUSA project in response to the increasingly pressing phenomenon of online gender-based violence among young people. Research shows worrying trends - girls and young women are disproportionately exposed to harassment, sexual pressure, revenge pornography and invasions of privacy online, which often leads to withdrawal from public space, self-censorship and deepening psychological distress.
We identified two key gaps:
1) young people do not have enough knowledge about recognising and stopping online violence and about the impact of gender stereotypes that normalise such violence;
2) youth workers need more competences and tools to support victims and develop a safe environment to talk about experiences that are often gender-based.
The project aimed to fill these gaps and establish a long-term system of support, education and awareness-raising. Our aim was to empower young people to recognise and respond to gender-based violence, and to enable youth workers to take effective and confident preventive action. We were therefore looking for a path to change at the level of understanding, behavioral patterns, and society's attitude towards the digital space.

<< Objectives >>

With the MEDUSA project, we wanted to establish a systematic, gender-sensitive approach to understanding, preventing and addressing online violence. The main aim was to create high-quality and accessible content that would encourage young people to recognise harmful online behaviours, to understand the role of gender stereotypes in the normalisation of violence and to respond actively when they encounter or witness violence. At the same time, we wanted to empower youth workers; not only with information, but also with useful methods, practical tools and greater confidence in supporting victims and in preventive action in the community. An important part of the goals was also a wider impact on society, so we aimed to raise awareness among professionals and the general public that online violence is not neutral, but is closely linked to gender norms and power relations. Through the development of a multilingual online platform, educational approaches and communication activities, we wanted to contribute to a safer, more inclusive digital space and encourage a long-term change in the understanding of and tolerance for online gender-based violence.

<< Implementation >>

Within MEDUSA, we implemented a set of activities that comprehensively linked research, prevention work and dissemination. We first carried out a research part that combined a review of existing literature, focus groups and a questionnaire, with which we analyzed the experiences of young people and youth workers and identified key patterns of online gender-based violence. Based on the findings, we developed prevention programs: i) workshops for young people on gender stereotypes, recognizing online violence and safe use of the Internet; ii) a summer school that enabled young people to engage in in-depth experiential learning and reflection on digital risks; iii) training for youth workers to introduce them to methods for supporting victims and for community prevention work. We also established an interactive multilingual online platform with information, materials and learning modules that enabled wider access to the content. We supported the project throughout with communication and dissemination activities - media announcements, online awareness campaign, sending newsletters, and public events (a conference on the establishment of the platform and a final conference where we presented the effects of the project).

<< Results >>

The results of the MEDUSA project included both concrete products and broader achieved effects that remain accessible even after the end of the implementation. The most visible result was the multilingual interactive MEDUSA platform, which combines educational modules, information on online risks and gender-based violence, advice for safe operation in the digital space, and materials prepared throughout the project. In addition, we developed a handbook for youth workers, which offers practical tools, work methods, examples of activities and guidelines for empowered support for young people and for the implementation of prevention programs. We also prepared recommendations for political decision-makers, with which we highlighted the systemic challenges related to online violence and proposed solutions for more effective regulation and treatment of violence in the digital space. In addition to the core products, research reports and analyses were created, based on the conducted literary research, focus groups and questionnaire, as well as numerous dissemination materials, including media publications, a promotional campaign, public events and information notes, which contributed to the recognition of the topic.
