2023-3-DE04-KA210-YOU-000176692.title: Giving Europe a Soul – Responsibility for the Next Generation
2023-3-DE04-KA210-YOU-000176692.summary:
<< Background >>

The partners applied for NextGenResp to work on the sustainable positioning of their personnel resources for youth work on social topics (volunteers, freelancers, part-time staff) and in their European perspective. On the one hand, dealing with this issue required coordination among the organisations and joint learning and development, which benefited enormously from the Erasmus+ support; on the other hand, locally specific measures helped  to develop further in the requested area and reach a holistic formation of the young future staff/volunteers.
The need for this measures is especially visible regarding the consequences for the Covid 19 pandemic on local youth work, which made it even more difficult to lead the generation transition in local youth work. Furthemore, activation of youth work alumni for the coorganisation of different youth work offers on social topics was (and still is) considered challenging due to the volatile life situation of the young people (graduation from school, vocational training, university studies, first job etc.). The project therefore adressed both the need of the partner organisations and the prospective participants developing a holistic pilot scheme to advance youth work participation.

<< Objectives >>

Within the framework of NextGenResp, the partner organisations identified the qualification, sustainable involvement and assumption of responsibility by alumni as multipliers/youth workers as common key challenge to address in the joint project realisation. 
Especially their volatile life situation between finishing school, university or apprenticeship or moving to other cities makes it hard to reach mid- and long-term commitment. 
The project activities want to achieve the implementation of new recruitment and training possibilities that combine, theoretical, practical and reflection-based elements towards an individual qualification and motivation - in a European exchange network, that grows stronger.


<< Implementation >>

NextGenResp was constructed by four main activities. The first three of them directly addressed the future youth workers of the partner organisations, while the fourth was more concentrated on the overarching partnership development_
In Activity 1, selected alumni, wanting to qualify and take responsibility received both local and transnational training on their role as multipliers/youth workers. Furthermore, they had the chance to participate individually in externally offered trainings.
In the second Activity these trainings were contextualised by individual coaching and possibilities for peer-exchange both on local and European level, online and offline.
To put their learnings into practise, Activity 3 gave participants the opportunity to realise their own mini-project and have a possibility for international job shadowing mobility getting to know the youth work of the partner organisations.
Lastly, Activity 4, was focussed on a steering group, supervising and evaluating the project steps, at the same time assuring the sustainability of the project and the European networking.

<< Results >>

As a result of the activities in NextGenResp, the youth social engagement and education programme areas of each participating organisation have access to several young, motivated and in-depth trained multipliers/youth workers. 
Already during the project lifetime some of the trained “young leaders” took on responsibility in the structures and started to draw on their newly established network developed during the project. The success of the combination of approaches but also learnings for structural change have had concrete consequences in the partner network: the job shadowing mobility programme will be institutionalized, as well as the coaching opportunities. Future trainings will take NextGenResp experiences into account.
Also the European networking had concrete results. The hoped cooperation beyond the NextGenResp is already part of new projects and applications - also bilateral cooperations have been strengthened.
topics: Promotion of alternative forms of participation
Bridging intercultural, intergenerational and social divide

2023-3-DE04-KA210-YOU-000176749.title: Young Climate Professionals (YCP) 2.0 – Empowerment project for “Green literacy and civic education for a sustainable Europe”
2023-3-DE04-KA210-YOU-000176749.summary:
<< Background >>

THE CIVICS applied to create a space for European youth passionate about climate action to enhance their green literacy and sustainability competencies by strengthening communication and project management skills, while also boosting the organisational capacities of all consortium partners in youth work. Recognising the urgency of youth involvement in climate action to achieve the European Green Deal goals, we aimed to equip young people with the knowledge, skills, and networks needed to drive local sustainability initiatives. Our focus was on bridging the gap between passion and practical, action-oriented climate education, particularly in Eastern and Southeastern Europe, where young changemakers often lack structured support and cross-border collaboration opportunities. Through expert inputs across environmental and sustainability topics, peer learning, and the development of their own project ideas, participants were encouraged to build their agency as multipliers. The project also enabled partners to exchange best practices and refine youth-focused learning methods.

<< Objectives >>

With this project, we aimed to promote active citizenship and social entrepreneurship by empowering 30 young people across Europe with the knowledge, skills, and networks needed to drive local sustainability initiatives and contribute meaningfully to climate action in the realisation of the European Green Deal. By enhancing their green literacy, communication, personal development and project management competencies, we sought to bridge the gap between passion and practical implementation, particularly in regions where structured support for youth-led climate initiatives is limited.
Beyond youth capacity building, we also aimed to strengthen the organisational competencies of all consortium partners in youth work and climate action, equipping them with better methodologies and approaches to  fostering active participation and long-term engagement, and delivering high-impact youth centred projects. 
Ultimately, our goal was to develop a network of motivated young changemakers capable of translating their climate ambitions into tangible, community-driven projects while fostering stronger inter-organisational collaboration for future youth-centred initiatives.

<< Implementation >>

The YCP programme consisted of four main activities. The first three were online sessions, each lasting four hours and held on Saturdays (28.09.2024, 19.10.2024, and 18.01.2025) via Zoom. Delivered through interactive formats such as speaker talks, brainstorming exercises, and practical workshops, these sessions covered key themes from the European Green Deal, including food systems, green entrepreneurship, biodiversity, resilience, and adaptation. They aimed to build participants’ climate action knowledge, skills, and networks to support youth-led initiatives. To ensure smooth collaboration, we used Padlet, WhatsApp community channels, Google Forms, and Slack. Between the second and third sessions, we partnered with the NECE project of THE CIVICS to host a webinar on intergenerational dialogue in climate action, providing the YCPs the opportunity to practice their communication, presentation, and project design skills while engaging in meaningful discussions with older generations on climate issues.

The final activity was a three-day in-person YCP Campus in Zagreb (13–16.02.2025) with expert talks, training, pitches, a green-themed treasure hunt, workshops, and a site visit to a sustainability action centre.

<< Results >>

At the core of our project was training participants to translate their climate action interests into tangible and feasible project concepts. By the end, 23 youth-led climate projects were developed for implementation across Europe. One standout output too was a sustainability tool created by a YCP participant to track carbon footprints and assess travel choices, which was widely used for the Campus and adapted by others to suit their local contexts.

Some YCPs also introduced interactive alternatives to traditional feedback forms, later incorporated into the programme. These feedback innovations allowed partners to adjust content and methods in real time, refining our interactive learning approaches. This iterative process strengthened programme quality and improved partners’ capacity to deliver impactful capacity-building activities. Beyond formal sessions, participants stayed active through tools like WhatsApp and Padlet, sharing climate insights and resources. As a result, an open-access digital library/toolbox was created and is available on THE CIVICS website, offering curated content to boost sustainability competencies and green literacy for all those interested.

2023-3-HR01-KA210-YOU-000178853.title: Više od PR-a: razvoj strategija za borbu protiv greenwashinga i youthwashinga
2023-3-HR01-KA210-YOU-000178853.summary:
<< Background >>

Centre Miko Tripalo and its partner organisations applied for this project because their previous work with young people had revealed a growing need for a better understanding of greenwashing and youthwashing. Although an increasing number of organisations and companies formally embrace principles of sustainability and youth inclusion, these values are increasingly used merely as a marketing strategy to improve reputation and increase profit, without any real impact on actual business practices. Young people had identified these phenomena as important for their future, but lacked the knowledge and tools to recognise and critically evaluate them. At the same time, the partner organisations themselves were not entirely immune to latent tokenisation practices, which is why the project was also conceived as an instrument of institutional learning and self-reflection for the consortium.

<< Objectives >>

The core idea of the project was to empower the partner organisations — Centre Miko Tripalo, Bernays University of Applied Sciences and Förderverein Europa Zentrum Baden-Württemberg — to recognise and prevent negative practices of greenwashing and youthwashing, and to raise awareness of the importance of ethical conduct. The project was also directed at young people, with the aim of providing them with knowledge and concrete tools for critically evaluating educational institutions and future employers. The transnational dimension of the project, combining experiences from Croatia and Germany, was intended to enable a more comprehensive insight into the prevalence of these practices and to support the development of higher-quality educational and organisational tools.

<< Implementation >>

The project comprised four main activities. The first activity produced a double comparative analysis of greenwashing and youthwashing practices in Croatia and Germany, preceded by focus groups with young people in both countries. The result was the published study Greenwashing and Youthwashing: Manipulation of Environmental and Generational Awareness in Contemporary Society, available in Croatian and German. The second activity involved the development of an educational curriculum and the delivery of workshops for young people in Zagreb (21 participants) and Stuttgart (15 participants), where young people critically examined real-life examples of manipulative practices. In the third activity, all three organisations conducted an internal risk assessment of greenwashing and youthwashing in their own work, developed prevention guidelines, updated their strategic documents, organised internal seminars for staff and members, and ran a social media campaign. The fourth activity was the final conference, held on 24 November 2025 in Zagreb, at which project results were presented with the participation of experts and young people from both countries. 

<< Results >>

The project yielded a range of concrete outcomes. A comparative analysis of greenwashing and youthwashing practices in Croatia and Germany was published. An educational curriculum for youth workshops was developed and field-tested, and is now available to partner organisations and other interested organisations working with young people. Each of the three partner organisations developed its own internal guidelines for preventing greenwashing and youthwashing and incorporated them into its strategic documents. Particularly noteworthy is the fact that the guidelines were presented to the senate of the newly established Algebra Bernays University, resulting in the introduction of a course on these topics — the first of its kind in Croatia. Young participants from Germany who participated in activities in Germany, in the final conference in Croatia, and in an additional activity in Zagreb (final workshop) were issued Youthpass certificates. The project also achieved a broader dissemination impact through a social media campaign, guest lectures and an additional workshop held after the final conference, with EU funding visibility prominently featured across all communication materials.
topics: Quality and innovation of youth work

hr.name: CENTAR ZA DEMOKRACIJU I PRAVO MIKOTRIPALO

2023-3-HR01-KA210-YOU-000180491.title: A.S.P.I. Agile Sustainability Practices and Innovation
2023-3-HR01-KA210-YOU-000180491.summary:
<< Background >>

The ASPI project was initiated in response to the growing need among youth organizations for more adaptable, efficient, and sustainable approaches to project management—especially when working with young people with fewer opportunities. Traditional methods often lack the flexibility needed to respond to complex and changing realities in youth work. Through national-level surveys with NGOs, we confirmed that many lack structured project management methodologies, digital tools, and capacities to sustain long-term initiatives. By introducing agile methodologies, we addressed gaps in digital readiness, inclusive project design and management. Our aim was to build the capacity of youth organizations to deliver impactful, flexible, and youth-centered projects. The need was especially evident among smaller, newer NGOs and those supporting marginalized groups. This project empowered them with tools, training, and methodology to improve their youth work sustainably.

<< Objectives >>

The ASPI project aimed to build the capacities of youth organizations by introducing agile project management methodologies adapted to the needs of youth work, especially for engaging young people with fewer opportunities. We wanted to develop a practical guidebook that translates agile methods into tools youth workers can use in planning, executing, and evaluating projects. Our objectives included: (1) developing and testing a new agile-based methodology tailored to youth NGOs; (2) enhancing the digital readiness and adaptability of partner organizations; (3) supporting a newcomer organization in its first Erasmus+ project; (4) conducting research to identify current practices and gaps in youth project management; and (5) fostering cross-border cooperation and knowledge exchange. By achieving these goals, we aimed to increase the overall quality, sustainability, and responsiveness of youth work in diverse contexts across Europe.


<< Implementation >>

We implemented a series of interlinked activities designed to build capacity and introduce agile methodologies to youth organizations. The project began with project management coordination and a kick-off international meeting in Croatia, where we aligned expectations, roles, and tools. We conducted research with 15 NGOs across partner countries to understand existing project management practices and challenges in youth work. Based on findings, we developed a comprehensive guidebook introducing agile methodology and digital solutions for youth workers. An international evaluation meeting in Greece helped finalize the guidebook and plan next activities within the project. We then organized Agile Laboratories—three national-level training sessions for 51 youth workers in Croatia, Bulgaria, and Greece, focusing on practical application of agile methods. Finally, we carried out broad dissemination activities, including Agile Cafés and sharing the guidebook via Erasmus+, Salto, and partner networks. The project closed with a final transnational meeting in Bulgaria.


<< Results >>

The ASPI project produced several concrete outputs and impactful results. The main intellectual output was the guidebook, a practical and open-access resource tailored for youth organizations to implement agile methodologies in their work with a variety of strategies, methods and tools. The guidebook was based on findings from research conducted with 15 NGOs and includes adaptable tools, digital solutions, and step-by-step agile practices. We also delivered three national training sessions (Agile Laboratories) for 51 youth workers through which they gained knowledge, tools and methodology to implement agile in their organizations. Through Agile Cafés, we reached 72 additional stakeholders, raising awareness and sharing best practices Dissemination actiovities reached over 30,000 people and number of downloads was 1,062. All participants received Youthpass certificates, enhancing their recognition of learning. Internally, partner organizations significantly improved their digital readiness, cooperation methods, and project sustainability practices. The project built a strong foundation for future Erasmus+ collaboration and long-term impact.
topics: New learning and teaching methods and approaches

2023-3-HR01-KA210-YOU-000180977.title: I dig STEAM in youth work
2023-3-HR01-KA210-YOU-000180977.summary:
<< Background >>

The I dig STE(A)M in Youthwork project was developed in collaboration with partner organisations, and we applied for the project in response to the common need to strengthen the competencies of youth workers in the fields of digital literacy, creative thinking, and the use of innovative learning methods, particularly in STEM and scientific literacy.  Analysing joint activities, we discovered that our partner organisations have strengths in different areas and complement each other with thematic differences. However, a large number of youth workers and facilitators within partner organisations lack experience in using integrated methods that connect STEM with the digital and artistic fields.  Young people, particularly those with fewer opportunities, frequently lack access to quality non-formal education that focusses on strengthening critical and creative thinking, so the goal of the project was to develop practical tools and a manual that will enable youth workers to include STEAM activities in their work, connect through European cooperation and exchange of experiences in order to contribute to a more inclusive, digitally empowered, and creative youth.

<< Objectives >>

The initiative aimed to strengthen partner organisations' work with young people by developing youth workers' STEAM competencies to encourage them to use innovative methods and digital tools.  We did this by empowering youth workers to use creative and experiential learning methods in specific thematic areas on which the project relies to promote critical thinking, problem solving, and collaboration in activities with young people and to help them informally learn about basic natural science concepts, which young people usually find difficult and complicated.  We supported the involvement of underprivileged youth and the closure of digital skills gaps between youth workers and the youth they serve in all project activities.  Partners created a manual and online platform as long-term tools.  We created a sustainable network of youth workers from 3 countries who use the STEAM approach to work with youth and improved competence prerequisites through training and educational materials. This opened up new collaborations, ideas, and mutual support.

<< Implementation >>

In total, 18 partner meetings were held.  We also held three international trainings in Croatia, Estonia, and Spain, each with 15 participants, utilising experiential, research, problem-based, and collaborative learning approaches on specific topics that reflect each partner's capabilities.  We developed a website and a manual navigation system for the STE(A)M world, which we tested and improved based on participant input.  Meanwhile, as collaborators in another project, we helped produce a manual for using reflective methods in adolescent work in Cyprus.  We took advantage of the chance and received a lot of feedback on our platform and manual, allowing us to improve the reflective parts in both depending on what we learnt.  Each partner organised one dissemination activity in their local neighbourhood.  In addition to the handbook, we created and tested an online platform at an international hackathon called DIGI EDU-HACK.  In addition, we advertised the project at two conferences (PCST 2025, Aberdeen and EARLI 2025, Graz), at Scientix's STEM DISCOVERY CAMPAIGN, and on social media and the project website.

<< Results >>

With 45 participants, Croatia, Estonia, and Spain hosted three successful and high-quality international trainings.   Youth workers developed digital and creative competencies through experiential, research-based, problem-based, and collaborative learning in each training themed to the participants' capacities and main quality segment of the host organisation (OUI / Croatia - STEM, Cultura Creativa / Spain - arts, and Project Spirit / Estonia - digital skills).   Navigation through the STE(A)M world, a manual in English, Croatian, Estonian, and Spanish, provides practical exercises and techniques for incorporating STEAM into non-formal education.   Three dissemination activities (picnics as multiplier events) were held in each partner country to disseminate the findings, recruit new youth workers, and share best practices and educational materials with non-parent organisations that work with youth.   At an international Hackathon, we piloted an online network for youth workers to share experiences and help.   We presented the concept at two conferences and made new connections.
topics: Quality and innovation of youth work

2023-3-IT03-KA210-YOU-000176681.title: Ascolta i giovani e proteggi gli adolescenti online
2023-3-IT03-KA210-YOU-000176681.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project because we recognized the urgent need to improve the online safety of teenagers, especially those aged 13–17, who are increasingly exposed to risks such as cyberbullying, grooming, disinformation, and identity theft. Although tech-savvy, young people lack the life experience to critically navigate the digital world. This situation has alarmed parents, educators, and youth workers, who often feel unprepared to support them. The project has addressed a growing digital divide and the lack of digital literacy and awareness, particularly among disadvantaged youth. Inspired by EU initiatives like BIK+ and the European Youth Strategy, we have aimed to empower young people, enhance media literacy, and promote safer digital environments. We believed that by creating tools, raising awareness, and involving all key stakeholders, we could contribute to a safer, more inclusive internet for all.

<< Objectives >>

We aimed to improve the digital safety and the psychophysical well-being of teenagers, especially those aged 13–17 and from disadvantaged backgrounds. We sought to increase the knowledge of young people, parents, and educators about online risks such as cyberbullying, grooming, and disinformation. A key goal was to promote the active involvement of youth workers and young people aged 18–25, including those with fewer opportunities, by engaging them in meaningful learning and exchange. We also wanted to raise public and policymaker awareness of the urgent need to protect minors online. Finally, we aimed to strengthen our partners' skills on the topic of digital safety and enhance their ability to collaborate in international contexts. These objectives have been achieved through educational activities, international cooperation, and awareness-raising efforts aligned with EU priorities on digital transformation, youth participation, and inclusion.

<< Implementation >>

We implemented a set of activities designed to improve online safety for teens and build capacity among youth workers, educators, and families. First, we conducted surveys in Italy, Croatia, and Portugal involving teenagers, their parents, and teachers. These surveys assessed their knowledge of online risks and their current practices to prevent and manage digital threats.
Based on the survey data, we organized a transnational mobility workshop in Lisbon for youth workers and young people (18–25), including participants from rural areas and those with fewer opportunities. During this workshop, participants shared experiences, reflected on survey results, and co-designed concrete educational materials.
Following this, we developed a digital safety guide, a decalogue of practical tips for teenagers, and a website to make these resources accessible to a broad audience. We also organized an online public conference, which allowed us to reach parents, teachers, youth organizations, psychologists, journalists, and policy makers at national and international levels.
Finally, a closing meeting in Rome and a dissemination eventi in Lisbon helped evaluate impacts, share feedback, and discuss strategies for sustaining project outcomes.

<< Results >>

Key outputs included a digital safety guide, a teen-created decalogue, a dedicated project website, and national survey reports from Italy, Croatia, and Portugal. The online conference increased awareness and policy interest. Evaluation data from the workshop in Lisbon showed a strong impact: 75% of workshop participants rated it 5/5, highlighting new skills and empowerment to share knowledge in their communities. All participants in the Lisbon workshop received the Youthpass certificate, validating the competences gained in non-formal education. Schools agreed to include project materials in their 2025/2026 calendars, ensuring sustainability. The dissemination event in Lisbon Book Fair, where the project's results were presented, and the ongoing dissemination by psychologists and educators further expanded reach. The project also built new networks, inspired follow-up proposals, and strengthened partners’ capacity to work internationally, fully meeting and even exceeding original objectives.

2023-3-LV02-KA210-YOU-000170610.title: Environmental awareness-raising of young people from protected areas
2023-3-LV02-KA210-YOU-000170610.summary:
<< Background >>

The possibility of undertaking a small-scale partnership, dedicated to youth activities, in a cross-border cooperation among European protected areas immediately arose as an improvement of usual educational practices. We applied for this project to address the need for stronger youth engagement in nature conservation and protection, especially in protected areas where the gap between youth and environmental issues had grown. Young people lack structured opportunities to participate in environmental actions, to connect with peers from other countries, and to learn about nature protection through practical and motivating activities. This project aimed to overcome these challenges by developing a motivation system, engaging Junior Rangers and scouts, and sharing best practices across partner countries. A more direct and outgoing cooperation between protected areas at a national and European level is welcome and by setting an example this project’s outcomes could inspire others to connect and develop youth activities dedicated to Nature.


<< Objectives >>

This project aimed to raise environmental awareness among young people at a EUROPEAN level, strengthen their involvement in nature-protection organisations, create a motivation system for long-term engagement, support the development of Junior Ranger (JR) programmes, and encourage youth cooperation between Latvia, Finland and Croatia.


<< Implementation >>

The project implemented all planned activities, including publicity and visibility actions, three best practices study visits, development of the Junior Ranger programme motivation system, youth activities in nature across all partner territories, and the establishment of a new Junior Ranger group in Krka National Park (also the first JR group in Croatia based on a signed agreement with the EUROPARC Federation). Moreover, the project’s final event had an international character and interactive educational activities equally dedicated to all partners. Additional activities were also implemented, based on the best practices collected, including a youth forum in Latvia and expanded nature-based learning sessions in all partner countries, an art contest and workshops organised to collect drawings for the project visualisation as well as the creation of three promotional videos and a digital game about invasive species.


<< Results >>

Results included: 
3 successful study visits and an international final event;
Developed Junior Ranger (JR) program and motivation system for youth;
Strengthened JR and scout involvement among JR of the National Parks (NP) of Gauja and Ķemeri, and Finnish scouts;
3 new JR and 7 volunteers in Gauja NP, 10 new JR in Kemeri NP; 20 new JR in Krka NP,  together 33 new new Junior Rangers applied for the programme;
New youth cooperation networks -  Gauja NP Rangers and “Cēsis Jauniešu Dome” (The Junior Council of Cēsis municipality), Ķemeri NP, Krka NP, and Sepra have now established a new network of Coastal Leader Youngsters 
A cooperation network created with Southern coastline Leader youth groups in Finland
A new Junior Ranger group established in Croatia, cooperation agreement with the EUROPARC Federation signed and the group registered in EUROPARC network, new logo and substantial communication activities; 
Improved environmental knowledge (5 JR workshops held in Croatia, 4 in Latvia, 3 in Finland);
Visibility materials (art workshops conducted, visualisation of our nature values, usable merchandise for Junior Rangers)
Digital game about invasive species and promotional videos

2023-3-NL02-KA210-YOU-000184111.title: Healing Digital Wounds: A Psychosocial Support Guide for Youth
2023-3-NL02-KA210-YOU-000184111.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project in response to the increasing psychosocial effects of digital wounds among young people, including cyberbullying, online harassment, hate speech and digital addiction. These experiences often lead to anxiety, depression and social isolation. At the same time, youth workers lack practical tools, structured guidance and psychosocial approaches to support affected youth. Existing initiatives are fragmented and rarely combine digital safety with mental well-being, mindful media use and emotional healing.

Through needs assessments and SWOT analyses, partner organisations identified limited funding, resources and expertise to respond to these challenges in a holistic way. Youth are spending more time online and those who are vulnerable or marginalized face even higher risks of exposure to harmful content.

We recognised the need for solutions that not only heal the negative impacts of digital wounds but also promote digital minimalism, mindfulness and healthy digital habits. This project aims to provide accessible resources, psychosocial tools and capacity building to strengthen resilience, emotional intelligence and safe online engagement.

<< Objectives >>

The project aimed to strengthen digital well-being and psychosocial resilience among youth and youth workers by addressing the impact of digital wounds such as cyberbullying, harassment and overuse of digital media.
Our main goal was to equip young people with knowledge, skills and emotional tools to navigate the digital world safely and consciously.

To achieve this, we focused on the following objectives:

>Develop practical and accessible resources, including a pocket-sized guide that provides psychosocial support, digital safety tips and strategies for healing digital wounds.

>Create an interactive online platform promoting mindful media consumption, digital minimalism, digital detox and emotional well-being.

>Increase awareness and understanding among youth and youth workers about different forms of digital wounds and their psychosocial effects.

>Empower youth workers to act as psychosocial advocates for digital well-being by offering training and capacity building.

>Foster empathy, peer support and open dialogue about mental health and digital experiences within youth communities.

>Ensure long-term impact by developing strategies for sustainability, partnership collaboration and wider dissemination of project results.

<< Implementation >>

The project was implemented through four main activity phases. First, we established a Steering Committee, created a project plan, defined risk management and quality assurance measures, and held regular coordination meetings, including a kick-off in France and a final evaluation in Croatia.

In the second phase, we developed the Digital Guardian Pocket Guide. Partners organised focus groups with youth and youth workers, analysed needs, and co-created content. The guide was designed, translated into partner languages, piloted with users and refined based on feedback.

The third phase focused on building the Mindful Tech Oasis online platform and capacity building. The platform integrates tools on mindful media use, digital detox, minimalism and psychosocial support. A two-day training for youth workers was organised in Breda to enhance skills in digital resilience and the use of project outputs.

In the final phase, dissemination and exploitation activities were carried out. These included social media campaigns, project website updates, 2 webinars, three multiplier events, promotions, creation of visual materials and an open-source repository to ensure sustainability.

<< Results >>

The project delivered several tangible and measurable results.
A key output is the Digital Guardian Pocket Guide, developed in 4 languages, containing psychosocial strategies, digital safety guidelines and healing practices. It was distributed in digital and printable formats and piloted with youth and youth workers.

The online platform Mindful Tech Oasis was created as an open-access hub offering tools on mindful media use, digital detox challenges, digital minimalism, resilience exercises, updates and resources.

A capacity-building training for 10 youth workers took place in the Netherlands, equipping them with practical skills in psychosocial support and digital well-being. Youth workers now act as multipliers in their communities.

In total, more than 550 individuals were reached through dissemination activities, newsletters, social media and multiplier events. Through youth worker networks and partner channels, an additional 200+ young people were engaged. Over 30 youth workers and learners took part in piloting and testing activities.

Additional results include a project plan, sustainability and dissemination plans, visual materials, translations, two webinars, strengthened partnerships.

2023-3-PT02-KA210-YOU-000176401.title: EmpowerCanvas: Cultivating Resilience in At-Risk Youth through Art and Mindfulness
2023-3-PT02-KA210-YOU-000176401.summary:
<< Background >>

The EmpowerCanvas project was developed to respond to the urgent challenges faced by at-risk youth across Europe, many of whom struggle with poverty, migration, minority status, unemployment, and discrimination. These factors increase vulnerability to social isolation, poor mental health, and limited employability. We applied to create innovative and accessible tools that build resilience, emotional well-being, and transferable life skills. By integrating art and mindfulness, the project fosters coping strategies, agency, and confidence, directly supporting the EU Youth Goals 2021–2027 to Engage, Connect, and Empower young people. Research such as Arts and Mindfulness Education for Human Flourishing (2023) and Mindfulness as Art Education, Self-Inquiry, and Artmaking (2023) highlights the potential of this approach for socio-emotional learning, resilience, and critical thinking. EmpowerCanvas addresses unmet needs by: (1) developing creative resources linking art, mindfulness, and resilience; (2) providing training and tools for youth workers; (3) equipping youth with employability skills like teamwork, problem-solving, and communication; and (4) fostering transnational cooperation to share knowledge and best practices.

<< Objectives >>

The EmpowerCanvas project was designed with the overarching goal of empowering at-risk youth by strengthening resilience, emotional well-being, and employability skills through art and mindfulness. The project’s objectives are: (1) Engage at-risk youth in mindful art activities and mindfulness resources to enhance emotional well-being, resilience, and both personal and professional growth; (2) Design and develop a resilience-building board game that integrates art and mindfulness into an interactive and engaging tool; (3) Create a digital platform that equips youth workers with innovative tools, resources, and methods for supporting resilience in vulnerable young people; (4) Organise a participatory visit in Portugal to exchange good practices, validate identified needs, and consolidate the project’s outputs; (5) Deliver three workshops to train youth workers and educators on the effective use of the platform and board game; (6) Disseminate project insights, methods, and best practices to at least 1,500 stakeholders to ensure long-term impact and sustainability; (7) Actively support the EU Youth Goals 2021–2027 by contributing to Engage, Connect, and Empower, reinforcing the project’s alignment with European youth priorities.

<< Implementation >>

The EmpowerCanvas project was implemented through a structured sequence of activities. A kick-off meeting in Germany aligned partners on objectives, roles, and Erasmus+ guidelines. Resources were then developed, including a resilience-building board game combining art and mindfulness and the ARTMIND online platform offering tools and resources for youth workers and young people. A participatory visit in Portugal engaged at-risk youth, gathering user-centered insights and adapting outputs to real needs. Three international training workshops brought together 45 youth workers and educators to build capacity in using both the board game and platform. Piloting activities with young people tested and refined these tools, ensuring quality and relevance. Dissemination actions included multiplier events, a project handbook with sustainability, risk management, and evaluation plans, and outreach campaigns that reached over 1,500 stakeholders. Ongoing project management covered coordination meetings, reporting, financial and quality monitoring, eco-friendly practices, and compliance with data protection. The project concluded with an online final meeting to evaluate results, share lessons learned, and plan sustainability.

<< Results >>

The EmpowerCanvas project delivered concrete and sustainable outputs that strengthened youth empowerment and the capacity of youth workers. The ARTMIND online platform was created in EN, PT, DE, and HR, providing accessible tools and resources to build resilience through art and mindfulness. A resilience board game, produced in EN, PT, DE, HR, RU, and UA, integrated art and mindfulness into an engaging activity for at-risk youth. Three workshops across partner countries trained 45 youth workers and educators to effectively apply these tools. A participatory visit in Portugal with 10 participants enabled user-centered insights and validation of project outputs. Piloting activities with over 45 at-risk youth refined the board game and platform, ensuring their relevance and impact. A comprehensive project handbook was developed, covering sustainability, risk management, and evaluation strategies. Dissemination actions reached more than 1,500 stakeholders through three newsletters, two posters, 30+ social media posts, and a SALTO entry. Finally, the project reinforced transnational cooperation, fostering strong, long-term partnerships between Portugal, Croatia, and Germany to ensure sustainability and ongoing impact beyond the funding

2023-3-RS01-KA210-YOU-000170300.title: Women Empowerment in Wages Equality Rights
2023-3-RS01-KA210-YOU-000170300.summary:
<< Background >>

Project directly addresses deeply rooted issue - gender pay inequality, which remains one of the most persistent forms of discrimination against women worldwide. Although the problem is evident and leads to the violation of other human and social rights, very few legal cases have been initiated in Serbia and Croatia, largely due to the lack of transparency in wages and limited awareness among women of the tools and mechanisms available.
Project responds to the need to build the capacities of those working with young women, whether from civil society, the public, or the private sectors, in order to reinforce educational activities. Actors relevant to the subject must first strengthen their own understanding of the topic in order to transfer that knowledge effectively. Through this project 1) comprehension of the gender pay gap has been deepened, 2) non-formal education methods have been learnt to communicate this issue in a relatable way, and 3) broader target group (young women) was encompassed through on-field knowledge application.
Initiative also provided opportunity for networking ,to learn from good practice examples, apply knowledge on the topic among young women, and gain broader understanding of the educational process.

<< Objectives >>

Main objective was to strengthen the capacities of civil society organisations and other relevant actors, including those from public and private sectors, working with or for young women in Serbia and Croatia, equipping them to address the issue of unequal pay for equal work, through knowledge of legislation, mechanisms for achieving wage equality, and the use of non-formal education.
By doing so, the project aimed to:
- empower youth workers to transfer knowledge directly to young women as their target group, who often remain unaware of their right to equal pay for work of equal value;
- practice knowledge through field work by engaging young women from local communities participants were coming from;
- build future regional network of equipped advocates across sectors, capable of promoting wage equality and encouraging active female citizenship; 
- elevate the topic on the social agenda by increasing public awareness of the issue through a targeted promotional campaign and dissemination event;
- enable networking among stakeholders of relevance for the subject.
Ultimately, the project aimed to strengthen democratic participation, support inclusion, and improve the rule of law by fostering long-term engagement on gender equality.

<< Implementation >>

Following key activities were implemented in Serbia and Croatia:
1) Initial capacity building training for 24 participants on gender (in)equality in the workplace, providing them with tools to advocate for equal pay for work of equal value.
2) Field activities/workshops with 142 young women, as practical implementation of knowledge by trained participants, who conveyed insights into the laws and mechanisms ensuring the right to equal pay for equal work.
3) Mini-research among 110 women on their acquaintance with the right to equal pay and workplace discrimination, conducted during the workshops as added value to the project.
4) Consultative meeting with 24 participants for gathering feedback, sharing impressions from the field, and drafting conclusions and recommendations.
5) Final conference with 67 stakeholders of relevance to give the issue of the gender pay gap greater visibility and place it higher on the social agenda.
6) Online toolbox as permanent value of the project, prepared by experts from various sectors, serving as a practical guide to support the understanding and implementation of gender pay equality principles in the workplace.
7) Promotional digital and PR campaign reaching a total audience of 1,139,912 people.

<< Results >>

Outputs and results are:
- 24 participants equipped to transfer knowledge and advocate for equal pay for work of equal value, through initial capacity building training on gender (in)equality in the workplace.
- 142 young women engaged in field workshops, where trained participants applied and shared knowledge about laws and mechanisms securing the right to equal pay for equal work.
- 110 young women’s awareness of equal pay rights and workplace discrimination assessed through mini-research, adding valuable data to the project outcomes.
- 24 participants shared feedback and impressions from field activities during a consultative meeting, leading to conclusions and recommendations drafting.
- 67 stakeholders of relevance gathered at the final event, visibility of the gender pay gap issue increased and raised on the social agenda.
- online toolbox developed by experts across sectors, as a lasting resource to support understanding and implementation of gender pay equality principles in the workplace.
- 10 videos produced and distributed, including a central one serving as a multimedia project report.
- 1,139,912 people reached by a promotional digital and PR campaign, raising awareness of the project’s goals and gender pay equality.
topics: Human rights and rule of law

2023-3-SK02-KA210-YOU-000183253.title: Narrative video game for climate participation
2023-3-SK02-KA210-YOU-000183253.summary:
<< Objectives >>

We aim to educate youngsters about EU environment and climate policies thanks to a specially created narrative video game. In turn, we aim for this medium to support youngsters’ participation to EU environment and climate policies. We will deveop inclusive material to support the participation of all.

<< Implementation >>

We aim to create a narrative video game to teach about climate change, the EU green policies and how they can have an active role. We will connect the educational notions and approach in the game to the European programmes, thanks to creating a short pedagogical guide for trainers and supporting learning activity to make the most of the game. We will test the resources with at least 125 youngsters and 15 educators and specialists.

<< Results >>

Concrete Results:
- 1 pedagogical guide on game-based learning for environmental education
- 1 narrative video game on EU climate policy participation
- 8 supporting training activity scenarios
- 1 testing phase with 125 youngsters and 15 educators and specialists

Impact:
Increased knowledge of youngsters to understand and participate in EU environmental and climate policies, increased ability for youth trainers to implement activities about the environment and climate change.

2024-1-EE01-KA210-YOU-000252869.title: Reflective Youth Work
2024-1-EE01-KA210-YOU-000252869.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project because we identified a clear need to strengthen self development and reflection practices in youth work across the partner countries. The project responds to the lack of awareness, skills, and practical tools for self analysis among youth workers and youth leaders, despite reflection being recognised as an important competence in youth work at both European and national levels. Research and policy documents highlight that youth work contributes significantly to personal development, yet the sector struggles with insufficient evaluation practices and limited use of existing self analysis tools. Surveys and partner experiences revealed that professional standards related to reflection are often not taken seriously and available support materials are underused, while many youth workers feel they lack concrete guidance on how to reflect on their practice. This project addresses these needs by raising awareness, mapping existing practices, and developing a practical self development workbook that supports reflection and improves the overall quality of youth work

<< Objectives >>

By implementing the project, we wanted to raise awareness among youth workers and youth leaders about self development and reflection in youth work and thereby contribute to improving the quality of youth work in all partner countries. Specifically, we aimed to map existing opportunities for self development and self reflection in youth work, increase awareness of the importance of reflective practice, and develop a tangible and practical self development workbook for youth workers and youth leaders.

<< Implementation >>

- Project management activities ensured coordination, communication, and quality throughout the project.
- A kick off activity in Estonia aligned partners, clarified roles, and planned project activities.
- Local studies were conducted through surveys and focus groups to identify self analysis practices and needs of youth workers and youth leaders.
- A workbook development seminar in Cyprus focused on creating the structure and content of the self development workbook.
- An online design competition involved youth workers and young people in shaping the workbook’s design and usability.
- The first version of the workbook was developed collaboratively by all partners.
- Local workshops tested the workbook in practice and collected feedback from youth workers and youth leaders.
- The workbook was improved based on workshop feedback.
- An inspiration day and final meeting in Croatia presented the workbook and raised awareness of reflective youth work.
- Evaluation and dissemination activities ensured visibility and sustainability of project results

<< Results >>

The concrete outputs of the project included the creation of a practical self development workbook for youth workers and youth leaders that contains reflection models, scenario descriptions, guiding questions, and easy to use self analysis tools. The workbook was developed based on surveys, focus group interviews, seminars, and testing workshops, ensuring that it responds directly to the real needs of the youth work field. It was tested in local workshops, improved based on feedback, and translated into all partner languages as well as into English, making it accessible to a wider audience beyond the project partners.
In addition to the tangible workbook, the project resulted in increased awareness and understanding of self development and reflection in youth work among youth workers and youth leaders in all partner countries. Participants strengthened their ability to analyse their work, reflect on their professional role, and recognise the value of youth work. The project also mapped existing self analysis practices and gaps in the field, strengthened cooperation between partner organisations, and increased the visibility of reflective youth work practices within local communities and youth work networks.
topics: New learning and teaching methods and approaches

2024-1-HR01-KA210-YOU-000250951.title: Our Earth, Our Voice
2024-1-HR01-KA210-YOU-000250951.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project to address clearly identified needs among youth workers and young people related to environmental awareness, engagement, and inclusion. Our initial needs analysis showed that youth workers lacked practical skills, tools, and methodologies to effectively implement sustainability-related activities, while young people demonstrated low motivation and limited opportunities to actively participate in addressing ecological challenges. Also, many young people, including those with fewer opportunities, faced barriers to participation and felt excluded from community initiatives.
The project responded to these needs by strengthening the competences of youth workers through targeted training and providing them with practical resources, such as the booklet of green methodologies. At the same time, it created engaging opportunities for young people to participate in environmental actions through local events, campaigns, and awareness-raising activities. The project also ensured inclusive participation by actively involving young people with fewer opportunities.
The project addressed gaps in knowledge, engagement, and inclusion, contributing to more active, informed, and environmentally responsible youth.


<< Objectives >>

By implementing the project, we aimed to strengthen the competences of youth workers in environmental sustainability by providing them with practical tools, methodologies, and non-formal education approaches to design and deliver engaging activities. At the same time, we aimed to increase young people’s motivation and active participation in addressing environmental challenges within their communities, fostering a sense of responsibility and active citizenship.
Another key objective was to raise awareness and promote behavioural change among young people by encouraging eco-friendly lifestyles and reducing their environmental impact. Particular attention was given to the inclusion of young people with fewer opportunities, ensuring equal access, active participation, and empowerment.

In addition, the project aimed to strengthen the capacity of partner organisations in youth engagement and environmental advocacy, through cooperation, exchange of practices, and joint implementation of activities. Overall, the project sought to contribute to more active, informed, and environmentally responsible young people, as well as more capable and resilient organisations in the youth sector.


<< Implementation >>

The project implemented a coherent set of activities designed to achieve its objectives:
A1. Project Management: Ongoing coordination among partners, including regular meetings, planning, monitoring, and evaluation to ensure effective implementation and quality of all activities.
A2. “Green Generation” Training Course: A 7-day international training for 16 youth workers, focused on sustainability, climate change, eco-friendly lifestyles, and non-formal education methods for engaging young people.
A3. Environmental Local Events with Youth: Organisation of 6 local events involving around 120 young people, promoting active participation in environmental initiatives and community-based actions.
A4. Booklet Development: Creation of a booklet containing green methodologies, tools, and best practices for youth workers.
A5. “Green Talks – Building a Better Future” Podcast: Production of 6 podcast episodes addressing sustainability topics and promoting eco-friendly behaviours.
A6. Dissemination Events: Organisation of physical and online conferences to share project results and increase visibility.


<< Results >>

The project delivered several concrete outputs and measurable results. Key tangible outputs included the implementation of the “Green Generation” training course for 16 youth workers, the organisation of 6 local environmental events and 4 ecological campaigns, the development of a Booklet of green methodologies and best practices, the production of the “Green Talks – Building a Better Future” podcast (6 episodes), and the organisation of 4 dissemination conferences (online and physical).
Also, the project achieved significant intangible results. Competences of 16 youth workers increased by 51.9% in implementing engaging sustainability activities, while motivation of 121 young people increased by 34.4% to become more active and civically engaged. At least 1,320 young people were reached, with an estimated over 37% increase in knowledge and awareness. 60 young people with fewer opportunities were successfully included and empowered. Partner organisations also enhanced their capacities in youth engagement and environmental advocacy by 35% to 42.5%, strengthening cooperation and international networks, as confirmed by evaluation surveys.

2024-1-HR01-KA210-YOU-000252309.title: Design locally, apply it globally
2024-1-HR01-KA210-YOU-000252309.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project to strengthen the capacities of our organization and our partners in the field of permaculture education, specifically made for the youth sector. While we possess expertise in permaculture, we recognized a gap in our ability to deliver this complex content in a way that is engaging and modern for young people. By integrating the Design Thinking methodology, we wanted to innovate our youth work practices and move beyond purely theoretical teaching. Our goal was to equip our youth workers and educators with a mindset focused on adaptability and innovation, ensuring that permaculture becomes a practical tool for sustainable living rather than just a concept. Our application was a natural progression of a successful long-term cooperation between partners, which was solidified during the 2023 training course "Learning from S.P.A.R.R.O.W.S.". Having discovered a strong alignment in our missions, values, and geographical proximity, we applied for this project to transform our mutual trust into a concrete, transnational network. We recognized that permaculture is not just an environmental tool but a powerful resource for peacebuilding and regional unity, where youth play a central role. 

<< Objectives >>

The project aimed to increase the quality, innovation and recognition of youth work, in line with the priorities of Erasmus+, while addressing environmental sustainability and green skills. It focused on strengthening the capacities of the partner organisations active in permaculture education to deliver engaging and high-quality non-formal learning content for youth workers, youth leaders and young people. We integrated Design Thinking approach into youth work, with a focus on developing green and sustainable skills and bridging the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application. 
A key objective was to enhance their ability to communicate permaculture concepts in a practical, accessible, and youth-friendly way. Ultimately, we wanted to create a broader impact beyond the immediate participants by contributing to a cultural shift towards sustainability. Through improved youth work practices, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and alignment with EU priorities, the project aspired to empower young people and communities to become active contributors to a more sustainable future.

<< Implementation >>

The project was implemented through 5 main and interconnected activities ensuring effective management and quality results. Project management was coordinated by ZMAG, responsible for overall planning, coordination, and monitoring, while partners ensured local implementation. Regular communication was maintained through online and in-person meetings with core team and in teams that were dealing with activity A3. The kick-off meeting in Croatia aligned partners on methodology and project goals, complemented by study visits to permaculture and community initiatives. The development phase focused on creating DLAG methodology practiced through an educational toolkit and a social-educational board game, combining permaculture principles with Design Thinking in a collaborative and iterative process.
An online platform was developed to share all outputs, including the toolkit and game, available in four languages to ensure accessibility and wider impact. A training activity in Slovenia enabled participants to test the methodology and game, ensuring relevance through participatory feedback. All partners organized multiplayer events at national level the project, aiming to promote the project and share its results with wider audiences.

<< Results >>

The main outputs are the development of an educational toolkit, an educational board game designed for young people aged 12+, and the DLAG methodology, which innovatively combines permaculture principles with the Design Thinking approach. An open-access online platform was created to host project results. The full set of materials was developed in 4 languages (English, Slo, Cro and Serb), increasing accessibility and inclusiveness across the region. The platform attracted over 4,000 visitors and engaged more than 400 active users, demonstrating strong relevance.
Partner organisations strengthened their competences in delivering innovative non-formal education and have opened new cooperation for partnerships, particularly in the fields of permaculture and sustainability. The integration of the DLAG methodology into practice improved the ability of organisations to engage young people in meaningful and interactive ways. The project reached at least 120 members of the target group. The project itself demonstrates sustainability, as all developed outputs remain available to be used in youth work. With strong scalability, it created a solid foundation for continued development, wider use and long-term impact in the field of youth work.
topics: New learning and teaching methods and approaches

2024-1-HR01-KA210-YOU-000255908.title: Atelier Pelikula
2024-1-HR01-KA210-YOU-000255908.summary:
<< Background >>

The project was launched to strengthen the capacities of all partner organisations working with young people from diverse, often vulnerable backgrounds, and to introduce structured, transferable methods based on film. We identified a lack of accessible, high-quality programmes in our local contexts, especially in rural areas, as well as the need for a joint curriculum, methodological tools, and clear processes for quality management. Another key need was transnational cooperation and closer involvement of local authorities to ensure sustainable practices and inclusive policies. Each partner aimed to both share its expertise and learn from others – combining experiences in film education, intercultural dialogue, and community engagement. Together we also relied on SALTO resources and digital tools to strengthen collaboration. The project additionally addressed barriers linked to mobility, language, and access to culture, with a strong focus on inclusion and environmental awareness.

<< Objectives >>

The main goal was to strengthen organisational capacities through: (1) developing and testing a methodological guide and curriculum for work with heterogeneous youth groups; (2) establishing operational processes (coordination, monitoring, evaluation, dissemination) and digital collaboration; (3) reinforcing cooperation between NGOs and local authorities for long-term community impact; (4) empowering a network of mentors through learning from international experts; and (5) contributing to horizontal priorities (inclusion, green transition, digital transformation, youth participation). A secondary goal was to empower participants through practical film production and the development of transversal competences, serving as evidence of the applicability of the developed methods.

<< Implementation >>

Clear management structures were established, including designated coordinators, defined roles, monthly reporting, and a communication plan. A kick-off meeting and needs analysis were conducted in Trieste, ensuring that subsequent decisions were tailored to the specific contexts of the target groups. International experts delivered masterclasses, complemented by a dedicated mentoring block, whose insights were systematically integrated into the curriculum. In parallel, the curriculum and methodological guide were iteratively developed, refined through regular reflections and adjustments.
Workshops with young participants were implemented in Croatia and Italy, applying the newly developed methods in practice. The project concluded with a public film screening and panel discussion, providing visibility to the outcomes and voices of participants. Collaboration was supported by digital tools (Google Meet, Drive, Slack, Viber) and SALTO resources, which ensured effective coordination across borders. Evaluation combined quantitative indicators with qualitative feedback from mentors and participants, offering a comprehensive assessment of the project’s success.

<< Results >>

The project achieved clear and lasting results. Three key documents were developed - a methodological guide, curriculum, and recommendations, all tested in practice, transferable, and publicly available for wider use. Standardized processes for coordination, reporting, and evaluation were introduced, strengthening management capacities across partners. Mentors enhanced their pedagogical and intercultural skills, especially in working with diverse youth. Eight short documentary films were produced (instead of the planned four), addressing identity, migration, inclusion, and environmental issues. A total of 23 young participants gained technical competences (camera, sound, editing) and transversal skills (teamwork, responsibility, tolerance). All outputs are available online, ensuring open access. Films and documents were presented at public events, shared via media and social networks, and will be included on the Erasmus+ Project Results platform, securing European visibility and long-term impact.

2024-1-HR01-KA210-YOU-000255996.title: Sustainable future of organisations
2024-1-HR01-KA210-YOU-000255996.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project because we observed that many environmental youth organisations successfully promote sustainable practices through activities, but often struggle to ensure the long term sustainability of their own organisations. Common needs included clearer values based decision making, realistic capacity and workload management, financial resilience, and practical models for involving volunteers and young people, including those with fewer opportunities, in a way that is fair and sustainable. As a young and growing organisation, we also needed structured learning from experienced partners and a safe space to reflect on real organisational challenges. Through transnational cooperation, we aimed to exchange practices and test a regenerative approach that connects environmental impact with organisational wellbeing and quality youth work, and to turn this learning into practical tools that can be used by other NGOs beyond the partnership.

<< Objectives >>

Specific objectives of the project were:
- to promote the exchange of knowledge, the best practices and EU perspectives among partners in order to improve their everyday operations and achieve greater impact to young people;
- to raise awareness about the sustainability and regenerative approach in NGOs;
- to provide youth organisations with the tools and knowledge necessary to implement sustainable practices and regenerative approach, presented in a Guidebook - Sustainable future of organizations;
- to build long-term international partnerships to enable further collaboration and joint development of innovative environmental projects;
- to develop methodologies for inclusion of youth through environmental projects based on permaculture and cleanup actions;
- to support a newcomer in the implementation of an E+ project.

<< Implementation >>

We implemented a full learning cycle combining online coordination, transnational mobilities, tool development and dissemination. The project started with online meetings to set roles, timelines and working procedures and to develop a holistic context for each partner organisation. We then carried out three study visits in Croatia, Greece and Germany, each including a presentation of the host organisation’s holistic context, identification of key challenges, peer exchange, co creation of solutions and an action plan. Throughout the project we ensured project management, monitoring, evaluation and dissemination. Based on the learning from the study visits, partners jointly developed and published a Guidebook - Sustainable future of organizations and prepared training materials. The project concluded with an international training course for youth workers, supported by local workshops and online promotion of results.

<< Results >>

The project produced a published Guidebook for regenerative organisations as the main tangible output. It consolidates the tested methodology, practical tools, worksheets and examples from the study visits and training, enabling other youth organisations to apply a regenerative approach in their work. Additional concrete results include three implemented study visits and one international training course for youth workers, with documented programmes, session outputs, action plans and evaluation reports. Participants reported improved competences in values based decision making, holistic context analysis, prioritisation and realistic capacity planning, and many planned follow up actions within their organisations. Partners also strengthened their project management and cooperation practices and expanded networks for future collaboration. The Guidebook was shared through Erasmus+ and SALTO Youth platforms, partner websites, social media and direct outreach to relevant NGOs to support wider uptake beyond the partnership
