2019-1-RS01-KA204-000854.title: Rural Women to Sustainable Food and Farming - Fresh Food from Farm to Table
2019-1-RS01-KA204-000854.summary:
<< Background >>

The project is designed to follow the identified needs at the participating organisations’ level and social needs identified at the national/regional levels.
The World’s population is rapidly growing, and more and more people are joining the middle class. As a result, food demand is expected to increase by as much as 98% by 2050. Agriculture already accounts for 1/3 of land use (with 40% of degraded agricultural land), while modern agriculture brings out a broad range of social challenges, health and safety issues and a more difficult economic environment for all but the most successful farms. Environmental issues and the benefits of grown food to people's health also matter to Europe and the region's economy. All this emphasises the importance of sustainable and healthy food. In January 2019, Euromonitor International published a report on trends "The Future of the meal: mapping a new fresh food economy" with one of the key findings that a new “Fresh Food Economy” is emerging.
Taking into account modern trends, the partners are ready to share their rich experiences to contribute to empowering and teaching rural women and enhancing rural development.

<< Objectives >>

RWSFF targets social inclusion and access to disadvantaged learners, such as rural women, small-scale farmers in less-favoured areas, who feel social exclusion and limited market entry.
THE AIM
To contribute to rural women’s empowerment by encouraging new trends “Fresh Food Economy” and agricultural entrepreneurship, as well as additional farm-related segments of the rural economy, contributing to generating income and employment, taking into account the adaptability of methods and technologies to meet local conditions in each partner's country.
THE OBJECTIVES
To put in place a sustainable process of empowerment and self-initiative of rural women (involved in agriculture or the agriculture supply chain) which will continue to evolve after the project’s completion
To promote the consumption of local and quality food from small producers
To share innovative models within rural areas and create a bridge between similar characteristics areas by diffusing project outcomes, learning tools and methods at local, national and international levels
All the set goals are intertwined and strongly include the creation of conditions and educational materials for adult teaching, with a special focus on women in rural areas.

<< Implementation >>

RWSFF lasted 30 months and contained 3 stages.
Activities:
- Preparatory and preliminary research
- 3 Transnational Meetings, 4 Multiplier Events and a Short-term joint staff training
- Preparation and development of Intellectual Outputs, including their publication and commissioning:
* Startup the Network of Women from Rural Communities (NWRC) and formulation of accompanying documents
* Creation of the Platform Community Access to Fresh Foods
* Creation and publication of a Guide Access to Fresh Foods
* Production of a structured RWSFF ToT with 4 modules
- Enactment in the practice of RWSFF ToT through C1 for adult educators
- A range of events with rural women in each partner country (online or in the presence):
* meetings, discussions and raising awareness of interest in participating
* local educational events
* piloting ToT
- Promotional events for a wider audience
Throughout the project, activities also included:
- Joint online work and cooperation to the achievement of the results
- Enlargement and implementation of NWRC by attracting stakeholders
- Project Management/Coordination
- Informing and communication
- Capacity building and networking
- M&E, Risk and Quality management
- Dissemination and exploitation

<< Results >>

1. Rural women increased knowledge about new trends “Fresh Food Economy” and agricultural entrepreneurship
2. Designed effective practical solutions to help women in rural areas who are small food producers
3. Improved access to nutritious, fresh foods for all citizens by promoting health, protecting the agricultural assets and natural resources
4. Improved competencies and upgraded the skills of adult facilitators/educators belonging to community groups and grassroots organisations
5. Successful dissemination of project results that are available for use throughout Europe
Envisaged significant positive results in terms of rural women:
- Newly acquired or reinforced key competences
- Increased abilities to plan, develop, and management of small businesses in agroindustries
- Increased opportunities for getting income, self-employment and employability thanks to the relevant skills gained
TANGIBLE RESULTS - Intellectual Outputs (in 5 language versions: Serbian, Croatian, Italian, Greek and English):
- The Network of Women from Rural Communities (NWRC)
- The Online Platform Community Access to Fresh Foods
- Guide Access to Fresh Foods
- RWSFF Training of Trainers Course (RWSFF ToT) with 4 modules

2019-1-SE01-KA204-060368.title: CREative MAking for Lifelong Learning
2019-1-SE01-KA204-060368.summary:
<< Background >>

The maker movement is a growing phenomenon in our society. People want to create, with digital tools as well as traditional arts and crafts. A lot of museums have creative spaces that offers activities related to their programs and exhibitions, using cultural heritage as a starting point for creative making. Often, cultural heritage organisations which work with maker spaces do this in order to address the key competences through informal learning. This is important work, since the threshold for people to engage in informal learning is low, and you can reach diverse groups of people. At the same time, many museums have huge collections that aren't available to the public. Using them for making and creativity could be one possibility for institutions to work more actively and with their collections and making them more accessible. Also, even though creative spaces and activities are common in European museums, they are mostly intended for children and families. This project is aimed towards adult and intergenerational groups.

<< Objectives >>

The CREMA project aims to develop and inspire creativity in adult learning. Through the development of innovative methods the project will make use of cultural heritage collections in museums for creative making. Many museums are increasingly working with a variety of creative spaces or maker spaces - places where you can make things, create and innovate. We wanted to build on methods for creative making and combine that with knowledge, collections and skills found in museums. The project has several objectives:
- Promoting social cohesion by reaching out to marginalised groups, people with special needs and working with intergenerational learning. 
- Opening up the museum and the collections by offering new ways of working with museum material for making and innovation.
- Enhancing entrepreneurship and innovation by particular focus on these aspects in the activities developed by the project.
- Train staff to provide learning opportunities through creative making.

<< Implementation >>

Pilot activities: 12 creative making workshops for the public (plus additional workshops at the multiplier event) were carried out to test the guidelines produced.
Kick-off meeting: We had a startup meeting in Copenhagen and Kristianstad to discuss the project.
Online LTT: There was an online training event for representatives from the partner organisations, as well as for other interested parties invited by the organisations. 
Webinar: "Designing a makerspace", an online seminar/project meeting
Project meeting in Szentendre/Budapest: The progress of the project was discussed as was the formalia of the outputs and pilot activities. We also tried out a workshop related to the subjects of outputs 4 and 5.
Project meeting in Bologna: The drafts of the outputs where discussed as were the performed pilot activities and their outcomes, and plans were made for moving forward. 
Multiplier event in Helsinki: In the multiplier event, the project was disseminated to an audience of people working with museums, learning and cultural heritage. 
Final meeting in Helsinki: In connection to the multiplier event, there was a final meeting to discuss the shape and content of output 6.

<< Results >>

Output 1: Museum collections and creative making (handbook)
Output 2: Audience development and engagement (handbook)
Output 3: Guidelines for entrepreneurship and innovation (handbook)
Output 4: Guidelines for intergenerational learning (handbook)
Output 5: Accessability and makerspace = MakeAbility (handbook)
Output 6: Creative Making for Lifelong Learning in Museums: A Guide (handbook/final report, still not finished because it's yet to receive layout, but will be published on the project website soon)
Mapping: An overview of creative making in museums from 7 European countries
Online articles, results, exercises and toolkits from the LTT event: "Makerspace goes digital. What we learned in 2020" (article), "Accessability and makersapces = MakeAbility" (recommendations and toolkit), "Atraining on audience development" (toolkit and exercises), "Makerspaces and museums: The culture of makers" (article) and "Intergenerational learning and examples from Finnish museums" (article and exercises).
A website that gathers all the resources: cremaproject.eu
A satisfaction survey of participant experience in making activities

2019-1-SI01-KA204-060564.title: The key: Developing methodology for younger adults education
2019-1-SI01-KA204-060564.summary:
<< Background >>

Two years before the project application (2017, 2018), we noticed young people (YP) between the ages of 25 and 35 have problems with transition to adulthood, and the problems are not necessarily related to their personal circumstances. Although better educated than their parents, they still don`t reach milestones that used to follow each other in the past: finishing school, long-term partnership, stable employment, buying a home, children. The sequence of mentioned milestones is different today, but strongly related to social reality - unsupportive environment. In all partner countries, partners have noticed the aforementioned problem and the growing number of YP who are no longer young nor adults, due to the failure to reach the previously mentioned milestones. We naturally looked for the cause in specific socio-economic circumstances, which make the path to adulthood difficult, as YP they reach milestones in a different sequence, incoherently, often even unconnected, as stable employment is quite remote for many YP (and does not necessarily enable independency), housing are unattainable... Considering the new reality and conversations with other adult educators, we concluded it is necessary to prepare tools for the target group.

<< Objectives >>

With the project we wanted to support youth workers and better prepare them for the target group of young adults aged 25-35 with specific needs. As a result, we wanted to offer young people in the mentioned age group support in the transition to adulthood, especially by raising the competencies that can help them in this. At the same time, we wanted to influence politicians to prepare programs that would enable us to carry out such activities and support non-formal educators in offering suitable programs for the aforementioned target group.

<< Implementation >>

Partner organizations first shared their practices and approaches for working with the target group in the field of non-formal education; in all partner organizations we tested and implemented 30 activities to address the activation of younger adults and their empowerment - 12 young people/country; we prepared guidelines for working with the target group of younger adults and descriptions of methodologies that we identified as key; we prepared a manual with examples of activities that professionals can use to work with the target group; on the Moodle platform we offered all created documents, training examples and also international recommendations to decision-makers.
We conducted two trainings for youth workers; we improved the competences of 400 adult educators to address younger adults on their transition to adulthood; we increased the number and quality of activities aimed at young adults in the four partner countries and advocated for young adults also by informing various stakeholders and decision-makers about the problems faced by young adults and proposing some solutions to them.

<< Results >>

O1 - Methodology for young adults activation and empowerment, with educational theories, approaches and methods that support young people on their way to adulthood.
O3 - Manual for  young adults activation and empowerment with instructions for carrying out 30 activities and instructions for educators of young adults.
O4 - The Moodle platform enables the widest range of individuals to use the results.
O5 - 5 memorandums for decision-makers and stakeholders - 4 national and 1 international.
12 adult educators participated in the first training, 20 in the second; we implemented the methodology in all 4 countries (48 young people total), at least 250 adult educators used the Moodle platform.
9 newsletters - we sent the newsletter to over 1000 organizations in 4 countries.
According to the results of the evaluations, the young people from the target group developed and strengthened their competencies and would recommend the training.
Users report that the intellectual results are useful, they come in handy and are happy to share them with colleagues.
All partner organizations have strengthened their competences in their areas and areas where partner organizations operate, cooperation within the partnership has partially strengthened.

2019-1-SI01-KA204-060567.title: Education accessibility through a digital audio library for the blind and visually-impaired
2019-1-SI01-KA204-060567.summary:
<< Background >>

Visually impaired are undoubtedly among the most vulnerable and least visible members of society. For the most part they are at the bottom end of the earnings league. Poverty and social exclusion are inextricably linked and are caused by a complex combination of factors: poor education and housing, unemployment, inaccessible information, negative attitudes and prejudices... 
The success of visually impaired is highly determined by the level of their personal readiness and motivation, by the environment, as well as the level of technical support they have access to. 
Prior to this project they were - among others - lacking the technological support, which would help them use audio materials without the support of librarians, mentors and family members; 
Libraries for visually impaired mostly rented CDs with audiobooks, catalogues of audio books were not available in sound, online audio books required assistance of a person with good vision…
The holders of audiobook copyrights were reluctant to share their books, even though the visually impaired have the legal right to free access, because the existing platforms didn’t ensure safety and didn’t prevent the unauthorized transfer of books.

<< Objectives >>

Objectives of the project: 
- To increase the accessibility of learning materials and literature for the visually impaired by providing free and independent access to them 
- To equip librarians / mentors of visually impaired with the knowledge, skills and competences to be able to support the use of the Audiobook library for visually impaired long-term objective: to spread the use of the application among all EU countries

<< Implementation >>

For the Erasmus+ project we implemented activities ranging from research, development, training and dissemination.

We researched the necessary national and international legislation, which sets the boundaries in which the project needed to be implemented. Blinda project grants autonomous accessibility for blind and partially sighted persons to learning materials in accessible formats in the form of audiobooks. 

A lof of research activities were also carried out in the field of accessibility tools and technologies, which enable blind and partially sighted users autonomous use of mobile applications. 

Based on the research, we then carried out the development of both the Blinda mobile application and the CMS platform.

Once the intellectual outputs were produced, we began with the dissemination activities and training of mentors. During the dissemination, we informed the general public, potential end users, other organizations of the blind and partially sighted and publishers about the project results.

We also carried out training activities, during which we equipped mentors with the knowledge needed, so they can further teach end users how to use both the Blinda CMS system and the mobile application.

<< Results >>

We produced three main outputs:

1)	Blinda CMS
Blinda CMS (content management system) is the back end system for the Blinda mobile application. This is the user interface, where organizations of the blind and partially sighted upload audiobooks and enter all relevant information, such as title, author, narrator, description. These audiobooks, which are uploaded into the Blinda CMS, are then available to the end users through the Blinda mobile application.
2)	Blinda mobile application
Blinda mobile application offers blind and partially sighted users free access to thousands of audiobooks in German, Slovenian and Croatian languages. At the moment of launch, more than 7000 audiobooks are available. With the use of Blinda mobile applications, users can access audiobooks anywhere and anytime with the use of their mobile device. Blinda is developed specifically for the blind and partially sighted and is completely accessible. Users can navigate through the entire application using voice synthesis.

3)	Training programme and learning materials
During the project, we developed and implemented a detailed training programme, which will allow the training of mentors inside the organizations of the blind and partially sighted. These mentors will be equipped with the necessary skills and knowledge about the CMS platform and mobile application, which will enable them to teach end users how to use these technological solutions and tools. We also developed learning materials - detailed instructions for use, which cover all aspects of the Blinda CMS and mobile applications on 103 pages.

2019-1-SK01-KA204-060641.title: The path to the independent life
2019-1-SK01-KA204-060641.summary:
<< Background >>

The partners of this project were organizations dedicated to the education of people with disabilities in the field of education and social care.
The aim was to increase the professionalism and skills of employees of special schools and social services facilities in the field of alternative ways of teaching for adults with disabilities on the international level.
The main goal of lifelong learning of people with disabilities is:
1. Social education - Social rehabilitation - support of independence through development and training of skills, strengthening of self-confidence and basic social activities,
2. Occupational therapy - Development of occupational skills under professional supervision to maintain or develop physical and mental condition in a way to integrate the client into society,
3. Cognitive learning - alternative communication, help in expressing clients' ideas, perception of time, working with memory.
The output of the project is innovative approaches in lifelong learning with respect for people's rights by slowing down
 in the field of alternative methods - art therapy, music therapy, occupational therapy, basal stimulation and alternative communication.

<< Objectives >>

The main output of the project are innovative approaches to lifelong learning through exchange
experience on international level in the field of alternative methods - art therapy, music therapy,
ergo therapy, basal stimulation and alternative communication. 

The participants of project team are working with young people and adults and supporting them and
helping them be more independent. We tried to find better approaches in life long education
through alternative methodologies , looking for the ways how to involve to this process parents, how
to cooperate with another institutions and how to share experiences with another professionals .
Each country has different experiences in alternative methodologies of life long education,that why is
very important to meet transnational.
Good quality of education is conditioned with good quality training of professionals.The main project
outcomes are recommendation of alternative methodologies , which they can help support life skills
of people with disabilities in their life and social inclusion.
 
New innovative learning processes will help improve the quality of education for people with disabilities - helping them to be independent and be
part of the community.

<< Implementation >>

time schedule of meetings, forms of communication, promotion, determine who is responsible and agree on the program
meeting.

We had to wait a year for the next  2nd training meeting due to the pandemic. 
It took place in Greece 10/2022.Partners from Portugal attended the meeting online and the missing partners from Croatia and Cyprus were unwell due to the severe course of COVID-19, so they were not caused to attend the meeting even online.
3rd training meeting took place in Croatia 12 / 2021- The Portuguese side still did not have a permit for foreign trips and were participants online
The final Transnational Meeting was in Cyprus -04/2022 - where we all participated and we evaluated our project .
Despite the difficulties, we managed to fulfill our plans and the program was always adhered to.

<< Results >>

The main project outcomes are exchanges of experiences for educators working with youngsters and
adults with disabilities, which will help transition to independent life.
Exchanges of experiences during working visits, we learned new approaches in lifelong education,
we applied it to education system in each organization.
We  prepared on line material with recommendation of alternative methodologies with new
approaches in life long education.
On line brochure is helpful in education in new approaches and can more prepare youngsters and
adults with disability for their independent life.
They will have better chance be involved to society, to social community. It increase their motivation,
self perception,person´s autonomy.
On line brochure is available on each partner´s website, we offered it to families, schools ,
institutions working with people with disability and to all professional and lay public.

2019-1-SK01-KA204-060780.title: Career Path
2019-1-SK01-KA204-060780.summary:
The objective of the project Career Path is to enable migrant workers from non-EU countries in Europe to achieve their professional aspirations and fulfil their potential. In order to allow that to happen it's important to create an environment where they have access to qualified advice and guidance and to further professional development opportunities. The goal of this project is therefore to prepare policy recommendations and toolkits for and with relevant stakeholders (public institutions, employers, adult education organisations and NGOs) that will enable them to create a more supportive environment for the professional growth and economic integration of migrants.

To fulfil this goal, we need to deeply understand the needs of our target group and the deficits of the existing environment that should be able to address them. For this reason we will map and analyse the existing situation in all partner countries by organising 30 interviews (5 interviews with public/civil servants and NGOs, 5 interviews with HR managers, 20 interviews with migrant workers from non-EU countries) in every partnership country (Czech Republic, Hungary, Croatia and Slovakia). A part of this background research will also be a report on best practices that will document the cases when migrants are getting good support in their career growth which can serve as examples to be replicated elsewhere.

After the research part, we will organize 4 study visits (one in every partnership country).  The main purpose and content of the visits will be a presentation of findings from the first phase, immersion in career guidance on the national level (explanation and showcasing), introduction of relevant stakeholders and sharing of best practices. 

Following study visits will be the preparation of the policy recommendations and compact toolkits for specific types of stakeholders. Policy recommendations will serve as suggestions and guidelines on the course of action and priorities for policymakers, public sector, employers, institutes of adult education and relevant NGOs. The toolkits will be tailor-made practical guides advising specific types of stakeholders how to translate policy recommendations into their daily reality. 

All throughout the project implementation, a special emphasis will be put on cooperation and networking amongst stakeholders. Contacts of all relevant stakeholders will be collected on a rolling basis throughout the project ́s phases and an effort will be made to engage them in the preparation of the outputs. 

During the last phase of the project, we will organize four multiplier events (one in every partner country), which will help us share and increase the visibility of the project ́s results amongst stakeholders. A database of the stakeholders ́ contacts will also be presented and shared at this event for purposes of future partnerships. All events and results will be communicated with a press release and by publishing information on partners ́ websites and social media.

2019-1-UK01-KA204-061444.title: Waste Not Want Not
2019-1-UK01-KA204-061444.summary:
<< Background >>

The ICE-CAP Project has delivered age appropriate online activities introducing the circular economy and promoting individual responses to the challenges of climate change.  The activities are available as twelve online Comics (6-10 year olds), twelve Digital Breakouts (11-15 year olds) and twelve WebQuests (16+) at www.ice-cap.eu.  The activities are supported by teaching resources aimed at exploring the understanding of family learning for parents and developing the skills and competences of educators.

The activities follow a calendar year with topics related as closely as possible to a relevant month.  The themes cover Energy, Food, Fashion, Recycling, Gardening, Sustainable Transport, Travel (Holidays), Water, Back to School, Waste, Preservation and Christmas.

The Comics introduce younger children to these concepts through the adventures of four new characters; Buzz, Honey, Vespa and Bumble.  The Digital Breakouts follow the concept of Escape Rooms with participants able to move on once a set of clues or a task has been successfully undertaken.  The WebQuests follow a similar pattern but with the addition of self directed learning opportunities to improve knowledge and understanding.

<< Objectives >>

In many ways the ICE CAP project application pre-empted the rise of news stories regarding shrinking ice sheets, the protests of Climate Rebellion and the focus of events such as COP26 held in 2021.  While there has always been an interest, the last few years have seen activism and action rise. The ICE CAP partners have used the project to explore the benefits of addressing the issues through an inter generational, family centred approach supported by the development of interactive resources that can be carried out individually but addressed collaboratively.

However, education without an understanding of the impact of personal changes, would not have been a sufficient result.  By introducing the concept of the Circular Economy through the interactive resources, participants have been encouraged to see how individual and family decisions and small changes in habits - made on subjects such as travel, food, holidays and Christmas - can lead to more sustainable behaviors that, in turn, ask for a response from market and service providers.  Practically this has been seen recently in the rise of plant based food products as a response to the demand for better quality meat-free food.

<< Implementation >>

Educating families about the circular economy utilised an inclusive approach which the ICE CAP Project Partners felt could be achieved through the design and implementation of a new comprehensive family learning programme providing bespoke learning materials and resources appropriate to different age groupings within each family context. To support the delivery of the family learning model the partners also addressed the needs of adult and community educators through the development of an in-service training programme. This in service training focuses on four key areas:
(i) an introduction to the circular economy
(ii) an introduction to family learning methodologies
(iii) working in non-traditional online environments using challenge-based educational materials - and through this providing training resources that can be re-used and adapted to suit the requirements of participants.
(iv) developing digital breakout and WebQuest resources - Partners explored the idea that educators could be inspired by the resources and use them as a template for their own.
With Covid impacting the opportunities for face to face contact, partners appreciated the value of developing the resources to be predominantly used online.

<< Results >>

The ICE CAP project has implemented a family learning approach to promote awareness of the circular economy and environmental issues through the development of age appropriate resources focusing on  issues of climate change by delivering:
12 Comic Strips (IO1) aimed at 6-10 year olds
12 Digital Breakouts (IO2) aimed at 11-15 year olds - 6 introductory and 6 intermediate levels
12 Web Quests (IO3) aimed at 16-20 year olds - 6 advanced and 6 expert levels
Each of the above resources followed a pattern of themes developed during the first partners meeting.  These themes were developed to reflect issues relating to a specific month of the year; for example Christmas in December and Travel and Holidays in July.
In addition ICE-CAP partners produced resources providing a theoretical understanding of the concepts used.  These included:
Induction Training (IO4) - a comprehensive induction training programme for parents to develop their knowledge of the circular economy
In-service Training (IO5) - building the skills of adult educators for circular economy education and challenge based learning methods
Interactive Online Portal (IO6) - a project website also providing open and continued access to all resources.
Four Partnership newsletters

2019-1-UK01-KA204-062024.title: Social (Media) Inclusion
2019-1-UK01-KA204-062024.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project after recognising the critical need to improve media literacy skills, to promote the good use of social media, to raise awareness of the huge number of digital dangers, to demonstrate how migrants, refugees and other vulnerable groups can be significantly affected by social media, and how to construct a safe and inclusive digital identity. Our project was born after seen the danger that improper use of social media can pose to both communities and to democracy itself. Moreover, our project coincided with the coronavirus pandemic, where many of these issues were felt even more acutely, and the need for our project was intensified, as global problems such as fake news, disinformation, online fraud, digital divides and other online dangers increased dramatically. It is important to teach educators practical online skills, and raise awareness of phenomena such as filter bubbles and algorithms. We also looked at how to use social media in positive and constructive ways such us social media, cultural heritage and inclusion to build up a better and more inclusive society. The success of our project demonstrates that we have addressed global needs which are felt significantly on an international scale.

<< Objectives >>

The main objectives of the project were to gather the experience and expertise of the participating organisations in topics related to the use of social media, and their effect on the individual, society, and vulnerable groups such as migrants and refugees. Through this, we achieved our aim of creating a toolkit directed at practitioners, educators, trainers, migrants who work as cultural mediators, translators and/or other roles in reception centres, local communities, community leaders and authorities. The aim of the toolkit was to give a detailed picture on the power of social media in defining who we are, who we like, what we fear and how it can destabilize and/or increase social cohesion depending on its use. This was also put in practice through two online trainings, which achieved the aim of having a direct effect on participants from partner countries. We improved their skills, raised awareness, shared experiences and used their feedback to ensure that our toolkit fulfilled the project objectives. Our toolkit covered the main topics of our project: Social (media) education and digital divides, The digital identity, Digital dangers, Online perceptions and discrimination, Social media, cultural heritage and social inclusion.

<< Implementation >>

Our project implemented several project activities to ensure the success of our project. We had regular project meetings as well as several extra online partner meetings, particularly in response to the global pandemic situation. This ensured constant communication, accountability and progress of the project. We co-created and published the Toolkit, and organised two online training events. The training was held online due to covid restrictions, and we had two of them because it was so successful and in such high demand that we needed a second one in order for all applicants to have the possibility to join. We organised several local events, mostly online due to covid, in order to disseminate and raise awareness of the project, and we followed a detailed dissemination plan to ensure that our project activities were widely communicated, and that relevant articles or resources were distributed. We created a project website, where the toolkit and presentations of the training can be accessed, as well as an online community on Facebook which is very active, and a Google classroom community for the first online training. We also implemented different evaluative activites including google forms, ahaslides, verbal and group evaluations.

<< Results >>

The first concrete output is our toolkit, accessible via our project website, which has been widely disseminated. It includes resources, activities, case studies, theoretical content & more. We also produced an evaluation of the toolkit.
Our 2nd concrete output are our 2 online trainings. We had 2 thanks to the success and high demand of our trainings, so that all applicants could have the opportunity to attend. We received very positive evaluations of the trainings, and the presentations used are freely available on the project website.
We created a lot of promotional material, including our logo, brochures, blog articles, posters, newsletter articles, and online advertisements of the trainings and toolkit on networks such as EPALE & ENTER.
We have a project website which gives free access to our resources and provides a summary of the project, project partners and meetings https://smiproject.eu/ .
We have an active Facebook account where partners post related articles on a weekly basis. 
Based on our evaluations we can conclusively deduce that we have improved the media literacy skills of participants, raised awareness of our objectives, developed innovative content during the covid pandemic, and addressed major global issues related to social media.

2019-1-UK01-KA204-062093.title: Creative Approaches to New Democracy through Innovative Inclusive Citizenship Education
2019-1-UK01-KA204-062093.summary:
<< Background >>

SDSA has coordinated school support inequality, multicultural education, student voice and democracy education for many years and been involved in European education projects since 2006. Our central involvement in NECE (Networking European Citizenship Education) included coordinating the focus group on inclusion. During these years, a debate on the working of democracy has become more public, urgent and prominent. In Europe, concern has increased over the rise of xenophobic rhetoric, extreme right-wing movements, the distorting impact of social media and the election of populist, authoritarian politicians, all of which appear to be at odds with the fundamental tenets and values of the European Union.

In sharing these concerns with many of the agencies involved in citizenship education, it was recognised that there was little or no educational attention paid to the role of creative expression in exploring the motivations and emotions behind support for populist political action. Equally, it was apparent that there was a general deficit in ready-to-use materials available to continue the implementation of the Council of Europe Reference Framework of Competences for Democratic Culture. These were the strong motivations which led us to seek partners to set up CANDIICE.

<< Objectives >>

As set out in our original bid, we believe that an improvement in the popular understanding of democracy is an urgently needed pre-requisite to a better defence of European values and the practice of inclusive democracy. Events in Ukraine have since shocked the western world and reminded us that our democracies are precious and need widespread popular understanding and support.  The central responsibility for developing understanding lies with the education sectors across Europe. CANDIICE sought to improve on the uncritical normative descriptive approach that typifies much citizenship and civics education across Europe and provide learning and training materials which would lay foundations for more informed, thoughtful and politically capable populations. Given the universal stresses on education professionals, with almost no time for research and resource production, the optimal way of supporting change in the curriculum and pedagogy is to provide attractive, ready to use, motivating learning activities and flexible training units and resources, (together with guidance) which can all be fitted into crowded timetables and meeting calendars.

<< Implementation >>

Due to Covid 19, we set out a revised programme of research and consultation to be carried out by our coordinating team. We drew up specifications for new approaches to learning to meet our objectives. These included combining exploratory and experiential methods of arts and creative learning with concepts central to democracy education. All partners activated their wider networks for ideas used to draft our suite of learning materials. This in-house process in all partner countries (drawing on experts and outside agencies who could help) replaced the planned work with artists embedded in learning settings, although dogged determination meant that we were able to set this up in some cases. After about half of our learning activities had been drafted, we were able to start designing training units to support the confidence and capacity of education staff (who often report lack of confidence in teaching citizenship topics and tackling controversial issues). We found ways to pilot and evaluate about three-quarters of our materials. Based on this work we were able to proceed writing our two major guidance documents. Additional work included website design and two conferences

<< Results >>

•	An attractive website providing easy navigation to all publications and videos plus considerable explanation (with animated videos) of the concepts and principles underlying CANDIICE
•	A suite of 27 learning activities, presented in step-by-step instructions for educators with additional resources where needed
•	Six international exemplar case studies illustrating approaches to education for democracy
•	Four adaptable training units with customisable presentation materials for use in in-house training sessions
•	A collection of training videos comprising keynote lectures from international experts and academics, interviews with experienced educators 
•	A detailed guidance document supporting education leaders in transforming learning settings to have democratic cultures
•	A guidance document with detailed recommendations explaining and advocating community-, country- wide and international engagement with progressive education for inclusive democracy
•	A toolkit with video records and detailed leader instructions for facilitation of workshop programmes on deep issues of identity, discrimination, oppression and citizenship
•	Two international conferences with CANDIICE materials and inputs from leading academics

Creating new, innovative or joint curricula or courses

2020-1-AT01-KA204-078054.title: Paths for timely interventions on trainings with male adolescents
2020-1-AT01-KA204-078054.summary:
<< Background >>

Reaching and accessing young male adults with a lack of key social competences as early as possible in order to set efficient interventions in time is THE key issue for almost every provider of psychosocial services for young male adults. Far too often we find that due to the sometimes quite severe manifestations of lack of key social skills, a lot of negative consequences have resulted for the person concerned and also for his social environment, in some cases even delinquency has already occurred. An intervention by trainings with male young adolescents with absent social key competences is the more effective, the earlier it starts. Unfortunately we have to assert very often (more than 90% of the cases) that our trainings start too late. In the meantime a very detrimental situation arose. - Not only for the concerned but also for their social environment.
Unfortunately our support in adult education reaches our target group (male young adolescents with absent social key competences) often too late. The effort would be much lower if we could reach the male young adolescents with absent social key competences timely. Belated interventions in adult education last longer and are much more costly. By a timely intervention we could minimize crisis situations and also avoid long- lasting and expansive repair work.

<< Objectives >>

A main goal of our work with male young adolescents with absent social key competences is to shape the access to our target group more effective. Besides we diminish the harm for the concerned and their social environment. Trainings with male young adolescents with absent social key competences are a very effective measure to reduce deficits in social key competences.

<< Implementation >>

Several measures and activities were taken to achieve the project's goals. This includes communicative activities, the preparation of an analytical grid for the country analysis, the production of this manual, documentation, dissemination and the conception of a follow-up project.

Communicative activities
The communication activities include the steering group meetings and the exchanges of best practice as well as bilateral communication. We communicated by E-Mail, Zoom and telephone. 

Steering group meetings
The steering group consisted of: Eberhard Siegl (IMS), Thomas Kraft (IMS), Oriol Gines (conexus), Heinrich Geldschläger (conexus), Barbara Klen (SPA), Petra Kremenjas (SPA). There was at minimum one participant per organization at the meetings. 
There were 14 steering group meetings: 21.10.2020, 25.11.2020, 18.12.2020, 27.1.2021, 23.3.2021, 4.5.2021, 24.5.2021, 8.9.2021, 17.9.2021, 14.1.2022, 9.2.2022, 4.3.2022, 27.4.2022, 6.9.2022
The steering group had the following tasks:
- Control of project status and the achieved goals 
- Control of the budget
- Clearify details of the administration
- Theoretical discussions concerning the concepts which are the base of our work
- Handling of the problems arising with the COVID-restrictions
- Organisation of the further meetings and the Exchanges of Best Practice
- Preparation of the handbook
- Documentation
- Conception of the follow-up project (this was also dealt with in various Exchanges of Best Practice)
The topics of the steering group were prepared in advance by e-mail. For this purpose, a proposal was sent out by the project management, which was completed by the members of the steering group in the course of the weeks before the meeting.

Exchanges of Best Practice
Preparation and follow-up of the meetings in the partner countries: The agendas, the framework programmes and above all the outputs of the Exchanges of Best Practice were prepared in the steering group meetings.
Holding the meeting in the own partner country: The team managed to hold a meeting in each partner country. Wherever possible, an attempt was made to involve the relevant stakeholders of the respective project partners in the Exchanges of Best Practice. Unfortunately, this was only possible to a very limited extent due to the prevailing post-Covid situation.
Travelling to the partner meetings: Wherever possible, the partner organisations sent the number of staff members foreseen in the project plan to the Exchanges of Best Practice.

Focus groups
We approached the topic in a professional way through a focus group. The focus group's discussions were guided by a guide for the focus group discussion that were continuously processed through a hermeneutic approach. This was mainly implemented in the Exchanges of good practice, as an online discussion was only applicable to a very limited extent to a clearly defined topic. The results of the focus group discussion were summarised in the handbook.  

Collaboration on the handbook
Each project team was responsible for those parts of the handbook that concerned their partner country. The final editing and the organisation of the translation of the manual was the responsibility of the project management (IMS). The current status of the handbook was continuously controlled. 

Contribution to the final documentation
The final documentation was prepared under the overall responsibility of the project management. For necessary data and information, the project team members were contacted, who then provided the requested data and information.

Participation in the conception of a follow-up project
It was to clarify, if we should work on a follow-up-project or not. We started this process after the half-time of the project, at this time the members of the steering group were alle ready and willing to work on a follow-up. The essentiell elements of the follow-up were prepared in the steerings groups and then discussed in the Exchanges of good Practice.

<< Results >>

The project produced the following outputs / results:

Transnational project meetings
Despite of the very restricting COVID-measures we were able to hold 4 of the 5  planned meetings for the exchange of good practice. At this meetings, we built up a network for the work on the current project and a possible follow-up project. 

Building up a network
We needed to exercise, how we were able to cooperate This was conducted by a clarification of the roles and tasks of each member of the team. Due to the high level of professionalism of each person who took part in the project this task was done very well. This enabled us to develop a sustainable cooperation partnership. 

Meetings of the steering-group
The meetings were the element that enabled us to work continuously on the project despite the travel restrictions. At the same time served to control the progress of the project. 

Guide for the focus group discussion
We decided to work on the topic of our project with focus groups and additionally some written additions. The initial version of the transcripts of the focus groups was prepared by the project management. The final version was then produced by means of peer review methods. The difference with a standardised peer review process was that the reviewers in this process were neither independent of the author nor anonymous. However, it was essential for us to draw on the expertise of the participants for the final version of the focus group report.

Focus group and peer review
We held focus group discussions on specific aspects of our theme. This was done on the one hand at the steering group meetings, where appropriate, and on the other hand in a planned way at the exchanges of good practice. We had 4 main outcomes of the focus group and two topics which showed the needs of professional work. 

Handbook
We created a Handbook with the central outcomes of our project, called „Work with young male adolescents – Structures, Donations and Cooperation“.  

Work on the question, if systems of adult education could help us to reach young male adolescents timely
We could not achieve any significant results regarding the question of whether adult education institutions can support us in reaching young male adults at an early stage. Contacting senior citizens or adult education institutions as planned in the application was not possible due to COVID restrictions. Furthermore, in our focus group discussions we found that there were only a few points of contact from a professional point of view as well. Secondary labour market institutions that provide vocational training for young people were seen as one possibility. 

Documentation
We created the interim and final documentation of the project. 

Follow-up-project
We produced a follow up project called „Competence in the Work with Boys“ (Acronym: CWB; Form ID: KA220-YOU-9E75CD30; Submission ID: 1366091)

2020-1-AT01-KA204-078112.title: Transnational approaches and multi-perspective methods in history teaching
2020-1-AT01-KA204-078112.summary:
<< Background >>

Seven cultural and educational institutions from Austria, Belgium, Germany, Croatia, Poland and Sweden worked on the project "Transnational History" with the aim of developing a common understanding of "transnational history" and trying out methods for looking at historical events from different perspectives. For the EU and its member countries are heterogeneous. They gather autochthonous ethnic minorities and majorities as well as people who have migrated or had to flee. Educational and cultural institutions therefore work with learning groups whose experiences go far beyond national historical narratives, because their biographies anchor them in transnational spaces. To do justice to this, we believe that "European history" must always be renegotiated. It should take into account different national perspectives, but also include the perspectives of minorities and migrants within nations. Starting from biographical narratives, we interwove scientific approaches with artistic forms of expression and tested a range of methods, which we describe and make publicly available on an online platform for imitation.

<< Objectives >>

We assumed that other educational and cultural institutions in Europe are also increasingly working with learners whose transnational life contexts correspond to an open form of history consideration that we do not find in standard history textbooks. Our aim was to develop a portfolio of learning experiences and teaching guides for adult educators, teacher trainers and arts and culture mediators that can meet these new demands. First, we had to test suitable methods ourselves and then share them with other institutions in Europe. The resulting portfolio of methods should enable learners and teachers to understand biographical narratives in their historical and social context and to integrate them into the teaching of history. Creative approaches such as editing video clips, curating an exhibition and processing in the form of a theatre performance should deepen the engagement with the narratives. The transnational comparison of textbooks also helps to put national narratives into perspective. It was also important for us to learn from the contemporary witnesses of all partner countries about their contribution to European history.

<< Implementation >>

In the course of the project, learning and training activities with numerous workshops took place in AT, DE and SE. Of the total of eight transnational project meetings, the first three were online meetings, the fourth meeting was split between Lodz and Vienna. Two meetings were held in HR, one in DE and one in AT. In addition, three bilateral meetings were held in DE, HR and AT. Throughout the project, 22 monthly Zoom meetings were held online to discuss ongoing tasks, and at the end of the project four multiplier events were held in HR, DE, AT and PL. In addition, numerous local meetings were held to prepare the work on the Intellectual Outputs (IOs) and to evaluate the methods. Nine IOs were elaborated: six historical topics were worked on, 38 history books were examined, 22 biographical interviews with contemporary witnesses were conducted, 20 video clips of the interviews and a video documentation in four language versions were produced. Work was done on an exhibition in HR and a theatre performance in DE. A method guide in six language versions, a scientific article and the method platform www.transnationalhistory.eu were published.

<< Results >>

More than 50 project results are available on the project's method platform www.transnationalhistory.eu. It contains descriptions of the methods used including materials on "Conducting biographical interviews", "Editing video clips", "Theatre performance", "Curating an exhibition" and "History book analysis" as well as its starting point "Historical topics". Additionally accessible are 20 video clips of interviews conducted with contemporary witnesses of the historical topics in the national languages and subtitled in English. Also on the method platform is a video documentation that presents the goals and course of the project. It is available in four languages. The methods developed and tested are summarised in the method guide, which can be downloaded in six languages. The theater play "Mauerläufer", which was performed in DE, was based on the interviews. In HR, the exhibition "Kome opanci, kome obojci" was curated for the project. Publications: "Mediation of complex historical facts" (BE), "Transnational History - Transnational approaches and multi-perspective methods in the mediation of history" (AT).  Project logo, flyers, brochures and press releases are available for the press.

2020-1-BE01-KA204-074914.title: SKILLS4PARENTS
2020-1-BE01-KA204-074914.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project because support for parents/families as first educators is essential yet quite underdeveloped across the EU in both social and education sectors. Parents need help to boost their understanding of the skills which they need in their parenting journey, both to help them as individuals and transmit skills to next generations, and also for overall family well-being, in line with international conventions on fundamental rights. We also wished to explore the potential of technology and digital tools to help them, as well as the help professionals. Educators also need a better understanding of the family environment of the people they work with: the challenges of parenting, the need to empower them through their different education programmes (parenthood, social support, mental health and more).

<< Objectives >>

We wanted to develop a new parenting skills model to help both parents and educators address the challenges of parenting today, boosting communication inside the family and within the wider community. This is also important in policy terms both in the education and the social fields, to help create a stream of support for upskilling of families and educators in this important field of first education of children. But also in practice terms, to make the parenting journey more visible as well as the skills needed, since this is still undervalued.

<< Implementation >>

To reach our objectives, we did the following.

IO1: We carried out research in cooperation with the target groups (parents and professionals) in the five countries of the partnership (Belgium, Croatia, Cyprus, Italy, The Netherlands) plus additional countries (Bulgaria, France, Finland, Greece, Hungary) through the European network of COFACE. Focus groups were organised both offline and online. This helped us co-produce  a European comparative report with the target groups, get validation from them, and identify new skills - all of which served as an important baseline to develop the Skills4Parents educational tools in IO2 and IO3
https://skills4parents.eu/research-methodological-framework/

IO2: On the basis of this IO1 research, we developed two educational tools available in 6 languages. A Learning Guide for parents with five learning packages (communications, empowerment, mediation, problem-solving and digital) and secondly a Handbook for professionals on how to engage with parents on different skill sets. https://skills4parents.eu/learning-resources-parents-professionals/. 

IO3: Finally, we used all the material developed under IO2 and centralized it in an online platform called the Skills4Parents Hub: Hub.skills4parents.eu The multilingual Hub hosts the five Learning Packages for parents which include articles, case studies, videos, digital resources, quizzes etc, as well as the Handbook for professionals. The aim is also to use this online hub to further consolidate the European community for parent empowerment built during the 2 years of the project, helping parents and professionals connect across countries.   https://skills4parents.eu/hub/

<< Results >>

Developed through the expertise of 6 organisations and founded on values of human rights, non-discrimination, social inclusion, gender equality, intergenerational solidarity and empowerment of all families, the Skills4Parents Learning Guide for parents contains learning packages to boost parenting skills in five areas: Communication, Empowerment, Mediation, Problem-Solving, and Digital. The guide adopts a self-learning approach, allowing all learning parents to choose the content (tips, case studies, exercises) that they need to tackle the parenting challenges they are encountering at their own pace. This educational material was developed on the basis of feedback coming from the focus groups of parents and educators in 5 countries.

The project partners have also developed an accompanying Handbook addressed to professionals working with parents and families. In other words, this handbook is for professionals who wish to use the self-learning content of the Skills4Parents Learning Guide and integrate it into their work with parents and families. The Handbook contains further explanations on how to transform the content of the Skills4Parents Learning Guide into training with a suggested learning plan for each of the learning packages, containing a mix of development activities, practicing activities, and activities for the evaluation of the knowledge and skills acquired. You will also find some tips on how to conduct training for parents and families – everything you need to get inspired and integrate the Skills4Parents learning into your activities!

Centralised online HUB: The information is available in all EU languages through an automatic translation feature which is very accurate, helping to disseminate the content of the Learning guide beyond the 6 languages of the Skills4Parents partnership, and using interactive, accessible and user-friendly digital features. The material is available in different formats in order to ensure maximum accessibility of the learning material for parents and professionals, who gave feedback during the focus groups on their different habits and learning methods (some preferred offline tools and some online).  There were discussions on whether the online platform should be set up in a training/module format, but given the self-learning non-judgemental approach to acquiring parenting skills, the material was set up to ensure easy and full engagement of parents and professionals (especially taking into account persons with low digital skills) for a more a inclusive approach. The hub also contains testimonials of the different focus group participants who are part of the Skills4Parents community, to inspire users of the Hub to join the community by signing up and connecting with COFACE (a community of millions of parents, volunteers and professionals working across 23 European countries). Hence using the full potential of digitalization to bring like-minded people together around parenting skills and empowerment, using the Skills4Parents material as a starting point for conversations and connecting people in Europe and beyond. Thanks to the automatic translation feature, the Skills4Parents partnership is using technology to break down barriers linked to language. By making the HUB content user-friendly, the aim is to empower parents, grandparents, carers to engage and use materials in digital formats (as opposed to written/printed format only). The Hub is also compatible with mobile devices, which is aiming at people who have access to a smart-phone but not a computer (hence acknowledging the digital divide still present in Europe).

2020-1-BE02-KA204-074684.title: European Senior Exchange
2020-1-BE02-KA204-074684.summary:
<< Background >>

Experience had taught us that an effort had to be made to involve the seniors more in the increasingly focused life on computer science in all its forms.
To give the opportunities for seniors to learn or improve their English. 
Obtain more knowledge about project management in Erasmus + for the Staff members

New teaching methods.  Special methods for seniors. Improving the lessons
for seniors. Discover and knowledge of different cultures. Knowing more about each others history. Common European values and history.
Bilateral help if needed. Exchange of knowledge and strengthen the own organization.

Lessons in Zagreb for seniors and staff.

2020-1-BE02-KA204-074812.title: Innovating Social Entrepreneurial Leadership Education
2020-1-BE02-KA204-074812.summary:
<< Background >>

The background analysis for the ISELE project showed that to sustain and consolidate citizen-led initiatives, new thinking and learning for leadership development and innovative approaches to social entrepreneurship were needed. Despite the acknowledgment of adult learning's importance for up-skilling, re-skilling, active citizenship, and social cohesion in the EU 2020 Strategy Executive Summary, minimal effort had been made to grasp essential active citizenship competences & create targeted education programs.
The project therefore addressed a perceived deficit in the skills, knowledge and competencies required to initiate and sustain effective community and citizen-led initiatives – and a corresponding lack of educational knowledge and provision for CSO’s, voluntary organisations, change-makers, engaged citizens & disadvantaged or marginalised groups seeking social entrepreneurial leadership skills.
It developed and disseminated new and innovative approaches to adult education for social entrepreneurial leadership training and equipped educators and CSO and community organisers staff to empower more effective forms of active citizenship and to build civil society capacities to address a range of social and ecological challenges.

<< Objectives >>

This project has contributed to an increase in the quality and reach of educational opportunities across Europe. The objectives included the development of conceptual and competency frameworks, an innovative curriculum and training methods, a repository of best practices, and blended learning resources, which all were aimed at supporting programmes for more effective social entrepreneurial leadership training.

We have built on the idea of “group-centred leadership” (Ella Baker) that can inform ‘leaderful movements’. These educational interventions were set out to promote community and active citizenship leadership which takes pride in being shared, accountable, clear and easy to spread. 

The methods were focused on the principles of inclusion, diversity and increased access for disadvantaged learners and socially marginalised groups.

Our primary target groups were adult educators and community organisers working within CSO’s and voluntary organisations. Secondary target groups included change-makers, activists, civically engaged citizens, and disadvantaged learners and socially marginalised groups who could benefit from acquiring skills for social entrepreneurial leadership.

<< Implementation >>

The central activities of this partnership involved producing the content of six intellectual outputs: 
1. Research Challenges and Review of International Best Practice
2. An Educators DIY Tool Repository
3. A Social Entrepreneurial Leadership for Active Citizenship Competency and Learning Framework
4. A Social Entrepreneurial Leadership for Active Citizenship Curriculum
5. A Training of Trainers Handbook and Practice Guide ”Towards a Leaderful Pedagogy”, translated in 7 languages (HU | SK | PL | ES | BE | HR | CAT).
6. A Blended Learning Course Resource platform

In addition to this, 6 Multiplier events were organised throughout the project duration to share this work with our target groups. These events were well attended, with more than 150 participants giving positive feedback.

Additionally, we organised a Training for trainers event.The training tested the competency and learning framework and the project's curriculum. It aimed to skill up 20 trainers from four European countries to roll-out a new educational programme across Europe and refine the handbook through their feedback.

<< Results >>

The project equipped educators and CSOs in the provision of educational programs that empower and support more effective active citizenship. The outputs and organised events have enabled citizens with new skills related to active citizenship. 
IO1: Research Challenges & Review of International Best Practice. Participatory research, in-depth interviews, and online surveys were compiled in the report “Leadership and Leaderful Organizing: Research on Building Leaderful Movements in Europe'. 
IO2: The Educators DIY Tool Repository gathered and redesigned tools for Leaderful Organizing competencies, enhancing access for educators and organizers. 
IO3: The Social Entrepreneurial Leadership for Active Citizenship Competency & Learning Framework, titled “Leaderful Organizing: a guide for educators and organizing”, serves as a reference for adult educators. 
IO4: The modular Social Entrepreneurial Leadership for Active Citizenship Curriculum covers competences with example session plans. 
IO5: The “Towards a leaderful pedagogy” Training of Trainers Handbook and Practice Guide supports leadership and is translated in 7 languages. 
IO6: The Blended Learning Course Resource platform offers digital resources and tools for flexible learning.

2020-1-BG01-KA204-078960.title: Creative Hub: Continuous Audio-Visual Upskilling among Cultural Operators
2020-1-BG01-KA204-078960.summary:
<< Background >>

The findings of Cedefop’s European skills and jobs survey emphasize the importance of developing and using employees skills in the workplace. According to Eurostat estimates based on the Adult Education Survey,employers are among the most common providers of non-formal education and training activities - more than 80%of the training provision.
The Report of the Education and Training 2020 implies that digital resources need to be more extensively used in adult education. The ‘OER revolution’ promises to make available high quality educational resources to all at a relatively low cost. According to the Institute for the Future(2016), the ideal worker in the cultural industries of the next decade is “T-shaped” - they have a deep understanding of at least one field but have the capacity to converse in the language of a broader range of disciplines. The demanding environment in which the creative labourforce is called to respond and function presupposes that creative workers should be characterised by a large variety of skills. As long as job demand remains higher than supply in the sector, the emergence of multi-skilling is becoming even more important.

<< Objectives >>

The project general objective is: Upgrading audio-visual and technical skills of adults through development of educational resources in an online Open Educational Platform for the needs of the cultural sector.
Project specific objectives are: (1)Enhancing coherence of knowledge and expertise in adult learning, through integration of existing training practices;(2)Improving the access to high quality digital learning materials in the field of audio-visual and cultural sector, through ICT;(3)Supporting the European cultural and creative sector for using the non-formal and informal adult learning, through providing interactive digital e-learning platform.
The identified groups which will be targeted throughout the project implementation are:
1.Employees in the cultural institutions and operators, responsible for the audiovisual and creative productions;
2. Unemployed adults (lowskilled, long term unemployed and NEETs) – interested in the cultural/creative field
3.Trainers and educators in audio-video and creative skills.

<< Implementation >>

The project planned the implementation of five major activities:
1. Methodology for coherence and transfer of knowledge and Assignment for OERs and software
2.  Review and analysis of existing educational resources, and shortlisting of most qualified examples of trainings.
3.  Development of pilot database and tutorials into training modules and OERs in the AV and creative sector.
4. Adult learners and trainers toolset in the field of audio-visual and creative skills, made available through development of online platform
5. European network for audio-visual and creative skills established

<< Results >>

The project achieved the following major results
1. Reviewd and analysed existing educational resources, and shortlisting of most qualified examples of trainings in all project countries. These were integrated as Glossaries to the OERs, and uploaded to the Creative Hub Platform.
2. Developed Methodology for coherence and transfer of knowledge, which is available for all creative and cultural industries stakeholders to develop their trainng potential through the use of the Creative Hub platform OERs and tools.
3. Developed pilot database and tutorials into training modules and OERs in the AV and creative sector. A total of 36 video tutorials shot and processed. OERs in 4 categories developed. All available educational content is translated into 6 languages.
4. Adult learners and trainers toolset in the field of audio-visual and creative skills, made available through development of online platform. The platform is the central focal point of the project and contains all resources developed during the project, structured into categories, containing all necessary tools for learners and trainers
5. European network for audio-visual and creative skills established by all paroject partners fo sustaining and developing the project results

2020-1-BG01-KA204-079272.title: DIGI-WOMEN, digital entrepreneurship tools and support for women entrepreneurs
2020-1-BG01-KA204-079272.summary:
<< Background >>

The United Nations (2020) warned that the economic impact of the COVID-19 crisis will negatively affect women entrepreneurs more than men when social protection plans and emergency schemes neglect constraints women face. 
1. There is the persistent gender inequality of labor and businesses spread over the different economic sectors (EIGE 2019). 
2. Women entrepreneurs represent only a third of the self-employed in the EU (European Commission 2014) and only 14.8% of start-up founders are females (2nd European Startup Monitor 2016). Only 33% of women feel they have the necessary skills, knowledge, and experience to start a business.
3. The 2018 European Commission study on Women in the Digital Age reveals that there is a decrease (with 2011 as base year) in women taking formal classes in internet and digital communication technologies.
There are programs helping women entrepreneurs implementing digital tools. Still the problem remains and is getting worse according to the European Commission 2018 study on Women in the Digital Age and the 2019 Digital Economy and Society Index report.

<< Objectives >>

The project's goal is to help women entrepreneurs because they are skilled at using digital tools for social purposes but they need help digitalizing their businesses (Aerts 2019) and since they are less in formal ICT classes (European Commission 2018 and 2019) and more in micro firms that are less digitalized (United Nations 2020), there is lots of potential for improvement.
Therefore, the project team wish is to engage in a large scale understanding of female user needs and influence or adapt training in current and new digital tools.

The overall objective is to develop a training program (IO3) that will train experts by taking the above-mentioned requirements into account in order to offer trainings and mentorship sessions that are tailored to the needs of the female entrepreneurs digitalizing their business and help them overcome the obstacles they face in the digitalization.
The final objective is to evaluate the project and to disseminate the program and recommendations (IO6) to other organizations so they can implement it to reach more women entrepreneurs and train additional experts. Information will be available to everybody free of charge.

<< Implementation >>

The Curriculum Prototype was developed based on a desk and primary research conducted by DIGI-WOMEN partners. Primary research was conducted among women entrepreneurs as target beneficiaries of the DIGI-WOMEN project and digitalization experts as target audience (participants) of the implemented Curriculum. In total, primary research included 39 women entrepreneurs and 35 digitalization experts from 7 countries. Both desk and primary research were implemented based on detailed research guidelines and checklists for semi structured interviews. 
The Recommendation Report was prepared to explain what the outcomes of all the analyses and reports, how the curriculum will be best used, what the impact is, how it can help supporting organizations and policy makers to improve the situation of women entrepreneurs facing difficult circumstances but also SMEs in general. In this stage, additional analyses were done based on the potential impact that the training, under the DIGI Women Curriculum Prototype, would have on women entrepreneurs regarding the income and the reduction in costs and time related to certain business tasks. Also, the outcomes of these forecasts by the digitalization experts became part of the report.

<< Results >>

A training program curriculum has been developed. The content of the curriculum is based on the investigation of published research from different parts of the world on the topic of digitalization and women entrepreneurship. New evidence has been added based on the analyses of interviews with 40 women entrepreneurs (WEs), of which certain percent were women living in difficult circumstances. Besides the WEs, 37 digital experts (DEs) from all partner countries were also interviewed. Country specific elements were also noted. Based on the desk research, the interviews, and the knowledge of the partners of the project, the curriculum was designed. This curriculum was then tested by presenting it to WEs and DEs. 
A recommendation report has been drafted. It outlines the findings of the analyses and reports. They can be used by education institutions, women supporting organizations and policy makers. These results can also be the starting point for even more in depth and/or larger scale research projects. Part of the report is a manual in which is explained how the curriculum is best implemented to achieve the best results. This will improve the dissemination of the training and the related outcomes on regional, national and EU level.
