2020-1-IT02-KA201-079994.title: Circular Economy Lab & Observatory
2020-1-IT02-KA201-079994.summary:
<< Background >>

Today there is a clear need to overcome the traditional linear development model, based on the consumption of non-renewable resources, to adopt a new, more inclusive, sustainable and responsible economic approach. This new model should embrace the concepts of recovery, regeneration and reuse of natural resources and produced goods, placing the circular economy at the centre. The widespread diffusion of practices related to the circular economy and related business models will strongly depend on the technical skills of the workers and entrepreneurs of the future. Therefore, it is imperative to focus on skill development in youth, including technical and soft aspects, in order to effectively support this paradigm shift. This process cannot only be promoted at a national level, but must be implemented at a European level and is fundamental to support community development and the well-being of European citizens. The CiELO partnership wanted to contribute to responding to these needs by providing the schools involved with the tools to understand, implement and promote change and making them available to all European citizens.

<< Objectives >>

CiELO aimed to transfer knowledge and skills on sustainable development, paying particular attention to the circular economy and the recovery of environmental resources. The initiative aimed to involve 160 students and their teachers from at least three European countries, Italy, Croatia, Lithuania, to which Romania was then added.
The main objective of the project was twofold. On the one hand, orienting students towards circular solutions, both in daily life with conscious choices and with practical examples illustrated during the project, inviting them to imagine their own more sustainable future and helping them to face the current challenges of sustainable development. On the other hand, stimulate active learning, personal development and the sharing of conscious behaviors in students, encouraging the formation of virtuous circles of development. In parallel, the project aimed to update and raise awareness of the teachers involved, a crucial aspect to generate a cascade effect that the positive influence of the teachers will have on other students during their careers, with the ambition of contributing to a cultural change and lasting education in Europe.

<< Implementation >>

CiELO engaged up to 189 students and 23 teachers in learning and collaboration activities. The partners created the project infrastructure, the Cloud Platform used as an interactive tool for learning, communication, archive and dissemination channel. The teachers were trained through 4 synchronous and asynchronous e-learning masterclasses created by the partners. The students participated in the Elevator Pitch, producing presentation videos then edited into a video series. They trained with specialist supports and a Flipped Classroom activity was designed for them, which saw them active in transferring the circular economy concepts learned to their classmates. They then worked both in national groups, carrying out research with the scientific method in the field and producing 48 digital dossiers, and in international groups, creating 12 Knowledge Hubs, in which their research was transformed into podcasts, videos, images and texts. 3 mobilities in Croatia, Lithuania and Italy, 4 multiplier events and other communication activities led the partners to work together even in person and created synergies that will last beyond the project.

<< Results >>

CiELO has produced a Cloud Platform (IO1), an innovative teaching tool on the circular economy and soil and water recovery accessible for students and teachers to learn in English; a cycle of 4 Masterclasses for the training of teachers and students with video lessons, support materials and verification tests, on the risks linked to the non-rationalized use of resources such as soil and water, and alternative, circular approaches and sustainable, as well as an e-library with a dynamic archive of resources useful for in-depth study (IO2); 12 videos made up of 175 student pitches that reflect their interests and opinions (IO3); information guides, documents, teachers' reports and 89 student reports on the Flipped Classroom on the project themes, with lessons learned and ideas for replicating the activities (IO4); 48 Digital Dossiers in 6 categories on water (pollution; reclamation) ), soil (contamination and reclamation; impact of agriculture) and circular economy (global processes and ecosystem services; sustainable behaviors and ecodesign of processes and goods) (IO5); 12 Knowledge Hubs on related topics, with podcasts, videos, images and texts produced with scientific rigor by students with experts.

2020-1-MT01-KA201-074241.title: Augmented Reality Enhanced Toolkit for Sustainable Education
2020-1-MT01-KA201-074241.summary:
<< Background >>

Through this ARTse project, we felt the need to address two crucial priorities within the European Union, namely the need to encourage a higher level of sustainability on our lifestyles and to promulgate digitalisation within member states. This is also reflected in the document: The Future of Education and Skills Education 2030 published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Educational institutions need to prepare students for jobs that might not even have been created but which will definitely require use of technologies. Digital literacy and data literacy are of crucial importance as also evidenced by the European Commission’s Digital Education Action Plan (2018). To equip students with the knowledge, skills, values and attitudes that will be required in the place of work, it is imperative to have educators that are conversant in creative digital pedagogical tools.  This in itself presented two issues:
a.	Gen Zers and Generation Alpha students are challenging educators to provide them with a learner centred environment that respects and caters for various learning capabilities, diversity of individuals and ways of learning. This requires a paradigm shift in our educational approach from using one- or two-dimensional educational resources to one that is more in with our physical three –dimensional world.
b.	Educators are not as conversant in creative digital pedagogical tools and therefore we needed to address the problem by, first of all, training a number of educators from partner schools on the use of AR assisted educational resources, and then propagating this innovative pedagogical tool by creating step by step guidelines to assist educators in moving beyond traditional class-based methodologies for teaching and learning.
With technological advancements, we felt that it was becoming imperative to incorporate innovative, interactive and immersive teaching methods in the classroom. We chose Augmented Reality as the platform since it is a technology that has gained considerable traction. AR is predicted to surpass the use of VR in both the social and economic aspects of life and is therefore likely to become a ubiquitous platform. With its ability to enhance the learning experience and cater for different learning styles, engage students and make learning more enjoyable, AR is considered as an emerging technology that will have a significant impact on education.
Equally important we also wanted the project to fulfil targets set in ET2020 about the need to improve the quality of education primarily by enhancing student understanding of sustainable lifestyles and help them place a higher value on common prosperity, sustainability and well-being. We took the approach of developing AR assisted resources that would be cross curricular and extend beyond national boundaries in their applicability. Through AR we wanted to increase awareness of the impact our lifestlyes has on the environment, and showcase different sustainable practices that individuals and communities can adopt, such as recycling, reducing waste, and using renewable energy. By providing students with a visual representation of these practices, AR can help them understand the impact of their actions and encourage them to adopt sustainable behaviours and become more active citizens in their communities.
This would ensure the promotion of  the four key competences as stipulated by the European Commission Directorate-General for Education, Youth, Sport and Culture: Key competences for lifelong learning, (Publications Office, 2019, https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2766/569540), namely:
•Providing high-quality education, training and lifelong learning for all
•Supporting educational staff in implementing competence-based teaching and learning approaches 
•Encouraging a variety of learning approaches and contexts for continued learning
•Exploring approaches to assess and validate key competences.
We also wanted the project to fulfil other targets sets by the European Commission by organising activities that foster more social integration by having educators and students to meet and work with their peers in different countries.

<< Objectives >>

One of the objectives of the EU member states is to reduce the rate of early school leavers (aged 18-24)at EU level to below 9% by 2030.  The path to achieving this goal (currently 10%)  is to ensure that the students’ educational experience is an engaging, relevant and beneficial one. Students currently in post compulsory education/senior classes are GenZers and GenAlpha who are technologically advanced, have an attention span that is an evolved 8-Second Filter, can multi task and tend to be independent and self confident. For Gen Alpha, there will be an increased digital literacy because of the omnipresence of technology with its underlying implication of shorter attention spans that highlights the importance of the gamification of learning.  This implies that knowledge of subject matter is no longer enough for educators. Information is available at the touch of a button and therefore educators must strive to ensure that the added value they provide in the students’ educational experience is significant and meaningful.  Educators need effective and interesting teaching methods that motivate students and incentivise them to take an active role in their learning. This necessitates the adoption and incorporation of advanced technology in pedagogy that caters for various learning capabilities, learning styles and embraces the diversity of students. Given that our physical world is three –dimensional, using Augmented Reality (AR) technology in the teaching/learning experience removes the dichotomy between the two-dimensional approach used in classrooms and the three-dimensional physical world and helps create an educational environment where physical and virtual worlds intermingle to enhance the effectiveness and attractiveness of this experience by providing more realistic scenarios. AR enhances the interactivity between student and learning and seeks to mainstream innovative practices based on collaboration and peer learning. Given the ubiquity of smartphones, schools should start embracing methodology that incorporates their use as a key educational tool. The use of assistive technology such as 3D learning tools will also balance the social/psychological divide since it allows everyone to learn at their own pace. 
Apart from focusing on using AR as a pedagogical tool, another main objective of this project is to address the issue of sustainability. Following the EU commitment to implement the UN Sustainable Development Goals in all its internal and external policies together with the 2030 Agenda adopted since 2015, this project seeks to reinforce the pedagogical importance of Sustainable Development as a cross curricular, cross-national priority. Both GenZers and Gen Alphas are more societally involved and considered to be climate crusaders.  By exploring sustainable education through cross curricular modules, students will learn about the importance of leading sustainable lifestyles and understand the implications of sustainability as seen from different perspectives. By developing outreach material using AR, this project will create a more engaging and persuasive student understanding of sustainable development. The expertise each school partner has in specific SDGs have been conducive in the creation of intellectual output and resources that address different environmental, economic and social factors that are meaningful both nationally and globally. The project also Through the transnational exchanges of both educators and students,  the viability and understanding of the resources generated on cross curricular and cross national levels will be assessed. This project also needed to create an awareness of the need for a paperless learning experience and the societal implications of an unsustainable education system.  This project started at the height of the pandemic – a phenomenon that highlighted the need and urgency for a more flexible and creative approach to education. This project therefore had the added aim of creating material that supports educators, parents/guardians and students to obtain key competencies in sustainable development and digital skills and which could be used both for classroom and virtual teaching/learning.

<< Implementation >>

The project aimed to create a ‘a people-centred and planet-sensitive’ (UN General Assembly 2014) by developing a portfolio of resources using the overarching SDG4 as the central and interlinking factor. We focused on 12 specific SDGs to create a set of intellectual outputs and educational resources that reflect the paradigm shift in the global framework for Sustainable Development as presented in the 2020 Agenda for SD and concurrently use AR as an immersive tool to create an immersive, interactive and creative learning experience for students. To this end this project devised a manual, case studies, lesson plans and an overarching curriculum for AR supported teaching/learning of Sustainable Education. Given the innovativeness of the project, partners felt it necessary to conduct a series of teaching/learning activities in home countries as well as abroad. Joint staff training was necessary for the mastering of creating and using AR supported educational material to be used in multicultural classrooms. The expertise of the Croatian partners in the development of the AR supported case studies in the bespoke app and the Maltese business partner in the use of AR supported handouts and case study material were harnessed during the transnational project meetings and served as platforms for the school partners to develop the necessary AR supported resources.
We also wanted to get a clear picture of the impact the AR supported resources would have on both educators as the primary targets of this project, and the end beneficiaries -i.e. the students. We therefore planned to have groups of students from Malta, Italy and Finland to participate in a research exercise into the effectiveness of the resources and intellectual outputs being created. This would help corroborate the multiplier effect of the project when the intellectual output and resources produced are then rolled out to other secondary and post-secondary institutions thereby ensuring the effectiveness and long-term positive impact of output developed in this project.
As the project was reaching its end, all school partners held a multiplier event targeting key people in the education sector including senior management members of the Education Department, heads of secondary and post secondary institutions, educators from different levels of schooling, and influential members of the local community in the respective areas of the schools. The aim was to disseminate new methods and pedagogical tools to support education of sustainable development. Key officials from the department of the environment were also invited to attend. During these events, attendees were given an overview of the project and were presented with all the intellectual outputs that have been created for the project. Workshops were also held to familiarise attendees with the use of AR to develop new and customised pedagogical resources.

<< Results >>

This project managed to obtain positive results on two levels:
a. Creation of outputs: Curriculum for Training Educators on AR in SD, A Guide on How To Develop AR Content for SD Education, AR Based Case Studies, E-Learning Platform with Training Material for AR in SD and An Open Digital Toolkit for Sustainable Education. Given that AR is not integrated into the education experience as VR and robotics, these outputs attempt to put AR on a sounder footing as a learning tool. Moreover, by focusing on sustainability as the underlying leitmotif this project explored sustainable goals from different educational perspectives and incorporate their understanding into a more meaningful experience through the AR platform. 
b.Creating a heightened awareness among educators and policy makers for the need of this innovative pedagogical tool. Through a series of multipliers, educators from primary to tertiary institutions were introduced to this new pedagogical tool and were given the opportunity to learn how to create new AR supported educational resources through workshops. Senior management officials from the Ministry of Education and the Directorate for SD were also given thorough exposure to this innovative pedagogical tool.

2020-1-NL01-KA201-064702.title: A Community of Ethics Teachers 2
2020-1-NL01-KA201-064702.summary:
<< Background >>

The classical approach to education, which focuses mostly on receptive learning, no longer meets our needs. In this age of mass media, we require our students to be critical thinkers and active participants in civil society. There’s no better way to develop an active role in society and a critical stance than the art of debating.

<< Objectives >>

Debating Ethical Dilemmas in the Classroom is a valuable resource for educators looking to foster critical thinking and ethical reasoning in their students. It presents a variety of thought-provoking ethical dilemmas and offers structured debate frameworks to help students develop the skills to articulate and defend their viewpoints. While debating values, principles, harms and benefits, students will not only learn how to analyze and evaluate ethical issues, but also how to respect and consider the perspectives of others.

<< Implementation >>

We researched debating ethical dilemmas in the classroom. The research by Natascha Kienstra was published in a first paper in a peer-reviewed book: Kienstra, N. (2020), Ethiekonderwijs in Europa: een Community of Ethics Teachers (COMET). In: Monique van Dijk-Groeneboer et al., Handboek Vakdidactiek Levensbeschouwing en Religie, Landelijke Expertisecentrum voor Levensbeschouwing en Religie in het Voortgezet Onderwijs (LERVO), 277-87. Secondly, a paper in a peer-reviewed journal was: Kienstra, N. (2020), Reconnecting Moral education and Philosophy/Morele vorming en filosofie opnieuw met elkaar verbinden. Tydskrif vir Geesteswetenskappe 61, no. 2:1311-1326. DOI: 10.17159/2224-7912/2021/v61n4-2a5. Thirdly, a paper was published by Floris Velema in the journal of the Italian Philosophical Society: Gabriele Münnix, Werner Busch & Floris Velema (2021). The International Association for Philosophy Teachers at Schools and Universities. A Non-profit Organization for the Promotion of Philosophical Education and its Activities. Bollettino della Società Filosofica Italiana, Nuova Serie n. 232, Carocci Editore, 63-78. Fourthly, a paper was published in the journal of the Association Internationale des Professeurs de Philosophie (AIPPh): Kienstra, N. & Velema, F. (2022), On Debating Ethical Dilemmas. In: Association Internationale des Professeurs de Philosophie (eds.), Nature / Natur, Forum Philosophie International, bulletin 71, Zürich: Lit Verlag GmbH & Co, 35-39. Based on the research, we designed a digital edition of 'Debating Ethical Dilemmas in the Classroom' that is freely available as an Open Educational Resource. The print edition of Debating Ethical Dilemmas in the Classroom is available at ISVW Uitgevers. A collection of five worksheets facilitates the effective implementation of the debate method in the classroom, as outlined in chapter 2. They are available in A4 and A3 sizes.

<< Results >>

The Erasmus+ project with the title A Community of Ethics Teachers 2 (COMET 2), coordinated by Natascha Kienstra from Tilburg University, aims at expanding the online platform and consolidate the network of ethics teachers by developing a systematic approach to debating ethical topics within a shared COMET framework. Our methods that combine the argumentative skills of debate education with central concepts in ethics can be found at https://ethics.community. On this website, we offer an Open Access book with the title 'Debating Ethical Dilemmas in the Classroom', as well as a set of practical worksheets. All intellectual outputs of the COMET project (book, worksheets, expanded website, and research papers) were developed by a consortium of three schools (Wolfert Bilingual School Rotterdam, The Netherlands; Lycée Classique de Diekirch, Luxembourg; Gymnasium Weilheim, Germany), five universities (Tilburg University The Netherlands; Sofia University Bulgaria; Oslo Metropolitan University Norway; Universidad Complutense Madrid Spain; Matej Bel University Banská Bystrica Slovakia), and three associations (Mala Filozofija, Croatia; Za in Proti, Slovenia; Institute of Educational Policy, Greece).

2020-1-NO01-KA201-076471.title: All on board! Ensuring that no child is left behind.
2020-1-NO01-KA201-076471.summary:
<< Background >>

At Verket skole, we wanted to make our school a better place for all children, and especially improve the situation for the children that doesn’t feel like they belong to the large group. 

We applied for this project, because it is an opportunity to dedicate time and resources to work systematically to better include students in school life.  

Through a project like this, it is possible to increase the teacher’s competence in a way that enable them to make the students thrive better, and hence learn more, and consequently they will be better equipped for life. The Education Act states the importance of this in the purpose of the law, § 1-1. Through the Salamanca Statement (1994), all European schools are committed to inclusion, yet we know that in real life, there is always room for improvement. 

All children need to feel included, yet we realize that students who deals with physical disabilities, have spectre disorder, reduced hearing, struggle emotionally, are gifted, struggle to learn, live in low-income families, or speak another language will be in a greater need of help.

“Early intervention” is considered good pedagogy in school, and we are mainly dealing with first till fourth grade.

<< Objectives >>

We want to achieve better practice for teachers, through increased awareness, challenged attitudes and more competence.  

The short-term objective of this project is to help the students to experience inclusion in their everyday school-life. 

The long-term objective is to save the school, its children, and families from many years of struggle and frustration. This could be a benefit for society, which might save a great deal of money in a lifelong perspective.

We wanted to work on this project with colleges from different parts of Europe, to learn good inclusive practice from each other. The distance in geography, might help us bring in new perspectives.

<< Implementation >>

At each transnational meeting we scheduled class observation, reflection meetings, coordinators meeting, lectures about the school system with the perspective of inclusion, common meals, and cultural days.

The observation var mainly in the classroom. In Norway we had one day with outdoor schooling, where the whole mobility group joined. After the observation, we would meet together with all the persons involved in observation and teaching, and we would reflect together, and discussing what we had seen, and if it was good inclusion or not. The coordinators meeting was scheduled at every transnational meeting, and there we planned for the next trip, we talked about different issues that appeared, evaluating, talking about the compendium, agreeing on how to share the work tasks, and other things that needed to be done. This was an arena for solving practical issues. At every transnational meeting we attended different lectures about the school system, with the perspective of inclusion, or other interesting perspectives on inclusion. The meals was a place where we got to know each other better, we really enjoyed that. Cultural days introduced us to each country's unique culture and heritage.

<< Results >>

The intention of better practice through raised awareness, the challenge of attitudes and increased competence is achieved, as far as it is possible to measure this within given time and resources. All activities have been strictly focused on this aim of better practice, except our cultural days and common meals, which has produced friendship, cultural understanding, and good conversations. 

We have pondered what inclusion is, and how to make it work in every class. We have looked at the Salamanca Statement, which is valid in all our partner countries, we have looked into the national legislation, we have investigated research, and of course our national curriculum, and how this can be realized in a best possible way in the classrooms. 

Our attitudes have been challenged through systematically have reflection meetings after observation. Our competence is increased through all that we have learned.

A result is also our compendium at the platform E-Twinning. It will be open and accessible for all.
topics: Reception and integration of refugees and migrants

2020-1-PT01-KA201-078680.title: Robots for STEM: building, teaching and learning
2020-1-PT01-KA201-078680.summary:
<< Background >>

This project was created to develop a low-cost mobile robotic kit aimed at children and adolescents from 10 to 13 years of age, designed to work as an interdisciplinary teaching tool that can be applied directly to a curriculum. The idea behind this robotic kit was to promote students' technical skills and allowing them to develop new skills like Computational Thinking and Problem Solving, driven by the motivation created by Robotics Competitions.
There was an urgent need related to robotics in schools and the costs of it. Robotics kits from big manufacturers cost too much for schools to be able to invest. On the other hand, if you decide to invest in low-cost robotics kits, usually you get a set of parts, and then you, as a teacher have to imagine what to do with them. This was a problem that emerged from meetings between partners, before the beginning of the project.

<< Objectives >>

The main goals of the project were to create a mobile robotics kit aimed at children and adolescents from 10 to 13 years of age that could be used as an interdisciplinary teaching tool that can be applied directly to a curriculum. T
This it, alog with the other outputs with innovative educational scenarios for teachers and students, allowed the partners and every school that follows the footsteps, to promote students’ 21st century essential skills, to develop new skills like Computational Thinking and Problem Solving by using Robotics Competition as motivation for learning.  Another objective was to improve communication in foreign language, namely, in english, the project's language.

<< Implementation >>

During the implementation of the project, and, although every on-site activity had to be delayed because of Covid, we managed to implement every activity that was originally planned. We implemented two Short-term joint staff training (C1 in Lithuania and C2 in Croatia) and three Short-term exchanges of groups of pupils (C3 in Turkyie, C4 in Italy and C5 in Portugal).

<< Results >>

In terms of outputs, the project produced everything it planned: A low-cost robotics kit was created as output 1, as it is the foundation of every other output. The project partners also collaboratively developed a training plan on Robotics and innovative methodologies to teach STEM subjects. With this training plan, the project produced a training course, also a very important part of this project as teachers involved in the project, and also others from other schools, could benefit from this source of information. Currently, the online training course is in the approval phase for official teacher training in Portugal. The project also produced a Teachers and a Students eBook with methodologies for teachers and  STEM-related activities for students by using the created robot. All activities in the student's book have lesson plans with the teacher's book to make it easier for STEM teachers to use them in their classes. As part of the dissemination strategy, the project involved other researchers and made a call for papers, blind reviewed, resulting in a paper book with scientific articles on STEM, innovative teaching methodologies and robotics. Not originally planned, the project also produced an eBook version of the paper book.

2020-1-RO01-KA201-080014.title: 4TEEN-Writing, Acting and Playing
2020-1-RO01-KA201-080014.summary:
<< Background >>

The project (4TEEN-WAP) has social inclusion as a reference point and it is a strategic partnership for the exchange of good practices between schools facing similar problems, such as reducing the phenomenon of social exclusion, school dropout and discrimination of disadvantaged students who want a friendly learning environment. The partnership includes 8 high schools from Romania, Turkey, Croatia, Portugal, Italy, Macedonia, Poland, which carry out extracurricular activities, with different experience in putting a social inclusion plan into practice, and a non-governmental organization from Italy, which is also an institute of  psychology, to ensure the complementarity of the partnership and the cross-sectoral nature of the project. The idea of the project started from the analysis of the common needs of the institutions involved in the partnership: increasing social inclusion, reducing school dropout, increasing the quality of the educational act, reducing discrimination. The local and trans-institutional context was taken into account and it was completed with the development of appropriate methodologies to identify, integrate and adapt the educational content at the curricular level in order to ensure an inclusive education.

<< Objectives >>

We pursued the achievement of the following specific objectives:
1. increasing the motivation for more than 200 students to practise sports, reading and theater as a means of social, cultural, economic, political and historical knowledge of their own country, as well as of partner countries in order to expand the space in which they feel appreciated;
2. the development of key skills, such as linguistic, digital and teamwork of more than 200 students through educational, creative and integrative activities, in order to avoid school failure and early school leaving;
3. diversification of teaching methods and computer tools of the 100 participating teachers (directly and indirectly), through a practical-experimental, active-interactive, interdisciplinary approach;
4. the training of 50 teaching staff by participating in training courses in order to achieve social inclusion.

<< Implementation >>

The activities that were implemented were the following:
- 5 Short-term exchanges of groups of pupils, which took place in Turkey/ Trabzon, Macedonia, Romania, Croatia, Italy/ Rome, in which 101 students and 62 teachers participated.
- 3 Transnational Project Meetings (Romania, Portugal, Turkey/Antalya) attended by 48 teachers.
- 3 Short-term joint staff training events (Poland, Italy/ Bologna, Antalya) attended by 49 teachers.
It should be mentioned that the Short-term joint staff training event in Antalya is an additional activity compared to the ones originally proposed, with the name of Art of Teaching, through which we achieved the need to deepen and bring together the students' integration experiences. We also supported the partner from Turkey/Trabzon to use their grant effectively. This course took place physically and online synchronously.

<< Results >>

Results obtained through this project:
- teachers' interest in international projects and the number of extracurricular activities increased by 30%.
- the motivation of over 300 students to learn has increased, being reflected in their school performance, with a direct effect in combating early school leaving.
- Partnership relations were consolidated with 3 more projects: "Innovative Digital Educational Approach" carried out simultaneously and 2 more projects for the future. 
In addition, tangible results/intellectual products were obtained, for which no funding was requested, but which were thought from the beginning as a response to the common needs of the 8 schools in the project.
- Educational materials represented by 2 books of creative texts made by students, published with ISBN.
- A guide to identifying students at educational risk.
- The procedure for supporting/integrating students with SEN.
- Multilingual conversation guide.
- Extracurricular Activities Guide.
- Exploring Inclusive Teaching Without Boundaries – a book with theoretical landmarks and good practice models in the issue of school inclusion, following the international Symposium that we coordinated.
- https://4teenwap.wordpress.com/

2020-1-RO01-KA201-080152.title: Overcoming functional illiteracy through ICT, to ensure social and professional integration
2020-1-RO01-KA201-080152.summary:
<< Background >>

We applied for this project because of the 2018 PISA results, which showed an international tendency towards lower scores, especially on math. Students all over EU were at risk for functional illiteracy. Romania was faced with this issue, as well as the other 6 countries involved in the project: Croatia, Greece, Italy, Lithuania, North Macedonia and Turkey. The statistics showed a level of functional illiteracy higher then 40% for all 7 partners. More so, Romania and North Macedonia were among the 8 countries that gave the test using paper and pen instead of digital instruments.
After hearing the news, we started researching, to learn more about functional illiteracy and to look for signs of it among our students. From the Faculty of Education Sciences, we found out that functional illiteracy is an issue for those preparing to become teachers. 
The conclusion draw was that something had to be done to make the gap between what the teachers know and what the students want to know, how teachers are teaching and how students want to be taught smaller. So we decided to write this project focused on training staff, the main goal being to create innovative school materials and tools, using ICT, for overcoming functional illiteracy.

<< Objectives >>

By implementing the OFI-ICT-PSI project we wanted to find innovative, digital and practical, ways to prevent and overcome functional illiteracy, to find answers to the following questions: WHO? HOW? WHEN? WITH WHAT?
Three topics were addressed by this project: combating failure in education, developing digital competences and creating new curricula, teaching / training / evaluating methods and tools.
We had 2 horizontal priorities (supporting educators, youth workers, educational leaders, support staff and innovative practices in a digital era) and a sectorial one (reinforcing the development of key competences).
Linked to the first one we established as objectives: conducting a scientific research to identify and define functional illiteracy and training over 70 teachers outside the partner schools, in OFI-ICT-PSI courses.  
Linked to the second horizontal priority, the objectives were: contributing to the enrichment of open educational resources for the 7 partner schools and ensuring long life learning, for at least 20% of the teachers, in the partner schools. 
As for the sectorial priority, we aimed at achieving one objective, strengthening and developing literacy skills for at least 20% of the teachers, in the partner schools.

<< Implementation >>

During these 3 years of project we had 3 transnational project meetings and 7 short term training events for teachers. We organized 21 international workshops during the LTTs and 49 local workshops to multiply the learning results.
We conducted 7 seminars on Functional Illiteracy and 21 training modules for teachers outside the partner schools, on 3 topics: Didactic games and their use in overcoming functional illiteracy, Contextualized learning or how to get through all the paperwork around me and Educational web 2.0 applications and their use in overcoming functional illiteracy. 
We created 7 note books for 7 optional subjects, the theme being digital literacy, each containing: 24 crosswords, 24 mind maps, 24 puzzles, 24 didactic games and over 24 guided reading exercises. 
We wrote a methodological guide for teachers, with directions and tools for identifying and overcoming functional illiteracy, presented in 7 multiplier events. We made good practice exchanges with sister schools and held round tables with university professors and key persons in the field of education. 
We learned how to use 21 digital apps, creating 147 open educational resources. We made an e-book, a website and a webinar portfolio for teachers everywhere.

<< Results >>

Our project produced:
- 1 methodological guide for preventing, reducing and overcoming functional illiteracy, in 8 languages
- 7 diagnostic studies and 7 presentations on functional illiteracy 
- 1 comparative study and 1 round table to discuss it
- 1 psycho-pedagogical screening on 3 levels of interest: development of language, communication, reading and writing premises; cognitive development and knowledge of the world; learning skills and attitudes
- 12 standard tests for primary, secondary and high school classes 
- 7 note books for 7 optional subjects, containing: 24 crosswords, 24 mind maps, 24 puzzles, over 24 guided reading exercises, 24 didactic games
- 1 e-book
- 1 website
- 1 face book group
- 1 eTwinning group 
- 1 portfolio of webinars
- 21 presentations of digital tools
- 147 exercises created (133 still active)
- 49 local workshops
- 7 seminars on Functional Illiteracy
- 7 training modules on Didactic games and their use in overcoming functional illiteracy
- 7 training modules on Contextualized learning or how to get through all the paperwork around me
- 7 training modules Educational web 2.0 applications and their use in overcoming functional illiteracy
- 35 webinars showing how to fill in different documents.

2020-1-RS01-KA201-065438.title: Generating Inclusive and Fair Teaching in Early Development
2020-1-RS01-KA201-065438.summary:
<< Background >>

The project contributes to innovative practices in the digital age by developing new educational resources, 
instruments and pedagogical practices in the field of working with gifted children from an early age using 
digital techniques (digitally available content) in Austria, Croatia, Slovenia and Serbia.

<< Objectives >>

It also contributes 
to the professional development of kindergarten employees, enabling them to recognize the giftedness of 
children in their work and to adapt their method of work to such children, thereby influencing the 
application of inclusion and during the earliest, pre-school education.

<< Implementation >>

The project contributes to 
innovative practices in the digital age by developing new educational resources, instruments and 
pedagogical practices in the field of working with gifted children from an early age using digital techniques 
(digitally available content) in Austria, Croatia, Slovenia and Serbia.

<< Results >>

With all of the above in mind, the project seeks to achieve the following objectives:
- Strengthening the competence of educators to work with gifted children- - Improving understanding of the concept of inclusive education in early development
- Improving the quality of provision of education and upbringing services in kindergartens
- Strengthening the cooperation of parents and educators
Dealing with this topic is of great importance for educators, as recognizing the gifted and creative and 
creating a supportive environment in which they will be able to develop and upgrade their potential is a 
great responsibility and challenge for educators and the profession in general. The ability to identify 
children's potentials and to provide adequate support to each and every one of his or her characteristics 
depends on the child's understanding, learning and development and program design accordingly. Areas in 
which we strengthen practitioner competencies relate to the context of a real-world program and the 
understanding of the child and his or her own roles through the filter of components that construct talent 
and creativity.
The project will strive to achieve the following results during implementation and at the end of the project:

2) Developed Educator's Handbook on Educational Practices for Gifted Children and Their Parents
3) Developed didactic games for preschool children that encourage further development of perceived 
giftedness and awareness of the child and parents about the existence of
giftedness and its importance in the further development of the child
4) Developed course/training on recognizing creativity and giftedness in children (for educators and

2020-1-SI01-KA201-075989.title: Professionals' Media Empowerment through Educational Suitability
2020-1-SI01-KA201-075989.summary:
<< Background >>

In the project, we aimed to develop concrete tools to counteract the negative impacts of increased media consumption among children in today's society. The lines between reality and the virtual realm shift daily. Inappropriate media exposure disrupts the healthy development of young individuals, with proven adverse effects at cognitive, emotional, and physical levels. Practitioners are also noting these impacts more frequently. This has amplified the call for media literacy.

Addressing this, we spotlighted two key Media Literacy needs:

- SCHOOLS require holistic media education to foster child growth.
- TEACHERS need empowerment to catalyze student development.

Historically, these areas saw limited attention.

Our experience and analysis reveal that media literacy is largely taught WITHOUT A CLEAR DEVELOPMENT-ORIENTED TRANSVERSAL PLAN that would COMBINE CROSS-CURRICULAR TOPICS UNDER ONE CONCEPTUAL CANOPY. Other challenges identified:

- ICT's dominance in school media curricula.
- Tertiary level's lack of structured teacher training.
- Fragmented extracurricular media initiatives.

<< Objectives >>

Addressing the highlighted needs and the gaps in addressing them, our project aimed to forge a HOLISTIC APPROACH TO MEDIA EDUCATION. Specifically:

For LEARNERS, our goal was a UNIVERSAL FRAMEWORK for media literacy, grounded in child development principles, tailored for primary and secondary students. Our envisioned approach would be:
- LEARNER-CENTRIC
- FLEXIBLE & AUTONOMOUS: granting teachers discretion in methodology.
- RESOURCE-EFFICIENT: promoting varied methods, including unplugged and plugged media techniques.
- AWARENESS-DRIVEN
- UNIVERSALLY APPLICABLE: transcending organizational, political, and cultural barriers.
- CROSS-CURRICULAR

For TEACHERS, our objective was crafting DETAILED TERTIARY CONTENT for university elective courses.

Understanding that teacher efficacy is pivotal in education, PROMETHEUS aspired to enhance media literacy training, furnishing expert guidance to educators to bolster their competency, pedagogy, and support in development-centric media education.
We aimed for a teacher empowerment strategy that accentuated:
- CRITICAL THINKING
- CREATIVITY
- ADAPTABILITY: equipping teachers to navigate evolving tech landscapes.
- STUDENT EMPOWERMENT: equipping educators to instil a sense of agency in students.

<< Implementation >>

Our implementation phase was methodical and involved a structured set of activities:

1. Planning: With Partners, laid the foundational blueprint, determining objectives, strategies, and timelines.
2. Management: Employed robust Project Management techniques to oversee timelines, budgets, and resources using different tools (Gdrive, Zoom)
3. Coordination: Engaged in both online and face-to-face meetings, ensuring seamless communication and efficient task allocation among team members.
4. Production of IOs: Focused on Output Development, crafting tangible deliverables that would serve our end objectives.
5. Evaluation: Instituted a Quality Assurance protocol, periodically reviewing our processes and outputs, ensuring the maintenance of high standards.
6. Dissemination: Proactively shared our findings, methods, and results with broader audiences to expand the project's reach and impact.
7. Multiplicative Efforts: Ensured that our strategies and results could be replicated and scaled, amplifying the benefits and expanding our project's legacy.

<< Results >>

Prometheus delivered the following key Intellectual Outputs:
IO1 - THE METACURRICULUM: An overarching media literacy (ML) curriculum tailored for primary and secondary education, underlining developmental principles. It extensively maps out DEVELOPMENTAL STAGES and nuances across learners' growth phases.
IO2 - MEDIA EMPOWERMENT TOOLKIT (MET) Stemming from IO1 insights, we introduced the MET – an online resource encompassing various theoretical ML aspects tailored for diverse age categories in different cases.
IO3 - THE PRACTITIONER’S GUIDE ON MEDIA LITERACY (PG): The PG serves as a teacher's manual, offering a practical breakdown of developmental doctrines and themes highlighted in the MC.
IO4 - TRAINING COURSE FOR STUDENTS/TEACHERS (TCT): Addressing the continuous demand for superior tertiary-level expertise, a specialized training module emerged in collaboration with partner institutions. 

Prometheus also accomplished:
- MULTIPLIER EVENTS
- SUPPORT MATERIAL: 
 • Project website: www.medialit4all.eu
 • Coordination and production worksheets
 • Online Evaluation Instruments
 • Pilot phase survey tools
 • Motivational multimedia content
- MEDIA EXTRAS: media hints to add ML character to a wide range of topics taught at school.

2020-1-SI01-KA201-076035.title: Training programs for teaching and support professionals in primary schools and kindergartens in child abuse cases
2020-1-SI01-KA201-076035.summary:
<< Background >>

Background of the project:
• Aside from providing education, kindergarten and schools have principal responsibility for care and welfare of children and youth. A kindergarten and a primary school is a privileged setting to prevent, recognize and intervene on situations that threaten children's well-being and development.
• Kindergarten and school personnel are sometimes the only persons in a position to recognize that a child is in need of protection. Children who come to school with injuries (physical and emotional) can be identified if kindergarten and school staff is aware of the indicators of abuse and neglect. For some children, their school may be the only place where they feel safe.
• Teachers in primary schools and kindergartens are requested to detect child abuse and/or neglect; where there are grounds to suspect child abuse or neglect, teachers shall urgently initiate a procedure to protect the rights of the child in accordance with the competent authorities and institutions.
• However, professionals lack relevant knowledge, skills and competences to identify relevant indicators of abuse, and the knowledge on how to deal with children victims of abuse.

<< Objectives >>

General objectives of the project were:
- Strengthening the profile of the teaching professions
- Improving professional and general competencies of teachers, headmasters and counsellors in primary schools and kindergartens
- Contribute to diminishing secondary victimisation of abused children

Specific objectives of the projects were:
- To develop and validate training programme and learning materials for primary school teachers
- To develop and validate training programme and learning materials for kindergarten teachers
- To develop and validate training programme and learning materials for kindergarten and primary school headmasters
- To develop and validate training programme and learning materials for counsellors in kindergartens and primary schools
in the field of understanding child abuse and neglect; and adequate reaction of teaching and support professionals.

<< Implementation >>

Main activities of the project were:
-	Intellectual outputs development
-	Evaluation of the intellectual outputs and their impacts
-	Dissemination of the developed intellectual outputs
-	Project management

<< Results >>

-	Detailed educational needs analysis 
-	Training programmes and learning materials for primary school teachers
-	Training programmes and learning materials for kindergarten teachers
-	Training programmes and learning materials for headmasters in kindergartens and primary schools
-	Training programmes and learning materials for counsellors in kindergartens and primary schools
-	Plan for inclusion of the learning materials into verified study programme of the Faculty of Education 
-	Evaluation of intellectual results
-	Dissemination of developed IOS (presentations for different dissemination target groups and publications in different media)

2020-1-UK01-KA201-079027.title: Science Teaching Educational Packs for Schools across Europe
2020-1-UK01-KA201-079027.summary:
<< Background >>

PISA reports show that the performance of European pupils in science has declined steadily since 2006. An increasing disaffection for scientific studies has been noted at a time when the number of jobs in the sector is on the rise. It has been stated that "teacher experience has the greatest effect on student achievement yet there is no requirement for primary teachers in Scotland to have any level of formal Science qualification". A survey of 52 primary teachers carried out by the partner schools in 2020 found that almost all of them would like to run more practical lessons with their pupils if provided with the resources and the training to use them. 
In the context of our project, it was felt that the plan to work with  our senior pupils to develop resources and use these resources to teach primary teachers and pupils would benefit all of the groups involved, increasing the levels of engagement and enjoyment, promoting their acquiral of key scientific and other skills and competences and meeting the skills gap in primary teaching. This would help to attract pupils to studying Science subjects, which is an ongoing battle across Europe. Interpersonal skills development and development of a European identity were also aims.

<< Objectives >>

The concrete outcome of our project is a resource pack for use by primary teachers, enabling them to run practical science lessons with their pupils. A main objective was the involvement of senior pupils in the production of this pack  and the training of  primary teachers in the use of the materials ( available on loan from each partner school) so that they became a sustainable resource. 
We hoped to further the internationalisation of our pupils as a result of their working as an international team to design, trial and teach using the resources and of socialising both remotely and at  LTT meetings. The project aimed to engage in interdisciplinary teaching and learning with Business studies, Science, Languages and Design as the core areas involved at various stages of the project. The aims were to improve pupils' scientific skills  and foreign language competences in a stimulating and creative way, to facilitate their engagement in voluntary work and to potentially increase their employability prospects.  The development of ongoing partnerships between primary and secondary teachers and schools was also planned. We hoped to increase the enjoyment of and engagement in Science of primary staff and pupils in a sustainable manner.

<< Implementation >>

In addition to the production of the resource pack and the activities carried out at meetings the following activities were carried out:
Staff and pupils were carefully selected to be involved in the project, ensuring that only people who were  genuinely interested would participate.
We shared our primary curricula and a set of activities was designed that related to one or more topics relevant to all of the curricula (Spain:' Gravity and Friction' and 'Magic Science' ; Belgium: 'Magnetism', 'Gravity' and 'Floating and Sinking'. Croatia: 'Fossils' and 'Time capsules'; Scotland: Vision and the Eye' and 'Fizzy Fun'). 
Our own pupils were taught the basic scientific principles involved, then we worked with them to develop relevant practical activities. These were trialled and, based on feedback, 4 lessons were selected for inclusion in the pack . All 4 lessons were translated.
We contacted and ran lessons for over 660 pupils at 20 primary schools . Other dissemination was via social media, radio, television, printed materials, websites and at meetings.
The resource packs were made available to primary teachers directly, by word of mouth, school websites, the project website, various teacher training organisations, which is ongoing.

<< Results >>

The main concrete output is the resource pack which consists of all of the materials required to run 4 practicals. This includes consumable resources such as balloons, cardboard, string, plaster of Paris and Playdoh and non-consumable resources such as safety goggles, beakers, containers, balls, magnets and a variety of magnetic items fossils, shells, periscopes, and more. Paperwork including colourful posters, lesson plans, worksheets and answer sheets are also included. Finally links to several videos and PowerPoint slide shows on the project website are also included.
Each partner school has retained a resource pack which is available to local primary schools on an ongoing  'borrow box' basis. The project website has a link on which primary teachers can order the borrow box, which will be restocked between uses as necessary. Some of the partner schools will also be involved in training on an ongoing basis.
The project website has been created on which teachers can access all of the written resources, videos, PowerPoints, some additional experiments, a contact page etc.
Over 750 primary teachers and pupils were taught as part of the trialling and dissemination processes.
All of the objectives set were achieved, in our opinion.

2020-1-UK01-KA201-079065.title: Finds Stories: Addressing mobility and language learning through object biographies.
2020-1-UK01-KA201-079065.summary:
<< Background >>

As we move, and we are becoming mobile, whether to go to the market or to immigrate to a foreign country, we also move our bodies through space and time. During this movement, we interact with countless objects that have different values for us. These movements and interactions leave traces on the objects, but also on our bones, which we can explore through various scientific approaches. The Finds Stories project explores the marks that mobilities leave and tells the narratives of movement and the impact it has on societies and people, with the greater aim to foster language learning and social inclusion through these. 

We applied for Finds Stories so as to recorded these movements and use the movement narratives so as to alleviate the impact that it is created to both the groups that are moving but also to the societies that are experience the movement.  By collecting and analysing biographical data, we uncover the diverse experiences of mobile groups and their material culture, shedding light on the diverse ways in which mobility shapes our world. Using creative arts, we enhancing these biographies and we create metanaratives that explore mobility's impact though a new research paradigm.

<< Objectives >>

We aimed to created a methodology around object biographies, their creative interpretations, and how these can be part of a Heritage Education teaching schedule. We aimed to showcase that as objects move through time and scape create stories, they have non-human agencies, that influences and interacts with humans. Putting objects, and their creative interpretations in the centre of a learning projects, you create a medium that is equally abstract but tangible and the students can connect with them. Equally and through an object biography approach we aimed to explore further how modern day Europe have been shaped as outcome of large or smaller scale migratory events. Finally we could see the educational and interpretative value of creative arts for object based studies. Finally we wanted to achieve broad engagement from students and other professionals with the project, during the time period that the project was active.

<< Implementation >>

Further to the training events for the participant organisations' staff, we undertook a large object biography recording campaign in collaboration with local communities and schools in six areas. At Kythera Island Greece, where migration movements towards Australia and from the Balkans took place. At the YMCA Basketball Museum Thessaloniki to explore objects associated with sports mobilities and the local to Thessaloniki Romani and newly arrived migrant groups. In North Western Greece, to record object associated with contemporary transhumance groups. In South Wales and the West of England to record objects associated with contemporary migration and refugee streams, and then at the Archaeological Museum in Zagreb to record objects related to historical mobilities in Europe. 480 objects have been recorded at the end of the project. Then, creative professionals and school students built creative interpretations of the object biographies, and the project educators developed educational resources. We run workshops, in Cardiff, Belgrade, and Thessaloniki where school students engaged with the project's resources and learned a language through them. We have also undertook a policy day and organise an end of project conference.

<< Results >>

Finds Stories produced four research papers that have been submitted in international peer-reviewed journals. One physical exhibition with more than 100 artefacts displayed, and a digital exhibition annotated with Finds Stories creative biographies. We produced an edited volume that is available in physical and digital format. The project created 40 creative biographies that offer a third paradigm in the interpretation of European mobilities, 100 educational resources, and numerous lesson plans, the majority of them available through the project's published handbook, also available in both digital and physical formats.  A database with 50 objects from the project's six case studies, their biographies, and associated educational resources have also been created alongside with a Massive Open Online Course that explains to educators the Finds Stories methods and how to use the project's resources. Finally we have submitted three policy papers, two in English and one in Greek.

2020-1-UK01-KA201-079120.title: Dyslexia Compass
2020-1-UK01-KA201-079120.summary:
<< Background >>

The Dyslexia Compass aimed to combat the negative implications of undiagnosed dyslexia on children’s and older students’ cognitive development, and consequent unnecessary strains on national education systems. It has done this by creating a pan-European consensus on diagnostic tools and thresholds to measure literacy and phonological fluency across languages and national perspectives of dyslexia, including differentiation for different orthographies (in the case of non-alphabetic languages where migrants and refugees are at risk of being ignored). In doing so, it has equipped teachers with diagnostic tools and guidance on operating to measure reading and literacy levels in a unified and aligned way across European countries. In this way, more accurate numbers of dyslexic students will be available, opening more doors to funding, intervention, remediation, and preventive measures. As such, the Dyslexia Compass project has taken significant steps towards reducing the impacts of the ‘Matthews Effect’ on development, mental health and inclusion of dyslexic children, especially those from migrant or disadvantaged backgrounds.

<< Objectives >>

Our methodology was to firstly understand in greater detail exactly what measurements are prevalent current in the EU, taking into account national and regional understandings of what dyslexia is.. This resulted in a comprehensive European report describing and classifying current tools used to measure dyslexia. The report was used as a departure point for the next stage of the project, which looked to establish clarity on the more effective tools to measure dyslexia. The result of this stage of the project was a training guide on various tools, how to properly implement them, and the recommended threshold for proper / improper literacy to establish someone as dyslexic. The final step of this stage of the project was to introduce a translation guide to the manual to facilitate the translation of one measurement from a tool in one European language to another. This final step marked a significant point in the project’s development and has helped to move the European understanding of dyslexia into previously unknown territory, with the creation of a singular tool to measure dyslexia across regions, nations, ethnicities and languages.

<< Implementation >>

Across 5 project partners coming from 5 different European countries, three Intellectual Outputs were created:
1. LITERACY TESTING ACROSS LANGUAGES which aimed to understand what measurements are prevalent in the EU, and resulted in a report describing current tools used to measure dyslexia contributing to greater pan-European knowledge of practices for measuring literacy
2. STANDARD TOOLS is a guide on the various tools available to measure dyslexia, including how to implement them, the recommended threshold to establish someone as dyslexic, and a translation for each in comparison to other measurements across Europe
3. STANDARD TOOLS (PITCHING THEIR TOOL) focussed on designing and creating a singular tool for measuring rates of dyslexia, complete with operating procedures and thresholds

When it came to the project as a whole, we implemented the following activities:
1. Planning. Activities such as workshops and meetings were carried out to decide what was needed by key stakeholders and intended beneficiaries
2. Execution. Partners shared tasks to create a pan-European report and a guide on tools to measure dyslexia
3. Application. Dissemination and multiplier events were held to spread the message of the Dyslexia Compass

<< Results >>

During the DYSLEXIA COMPASS project, we have produced a number of concrete outputs, including:
- extensive field and desk research into the tools currently in use across Europe to measure dyslexia;
- a report on the current state of tools in use and their respective measurements across the EU; 
- a set of specific tools to measure literacy that taken into account linguistic, national and regional variances;
- a collection of effective tools per language with standardised measurements;
- a companion to the tools to facilitate translation across tools
- a pan-European tool for measuring dyslexia, usage guide and translation guide across languages
- a guide for teachers and other stakeholders in the use of tools; and
- a project website and set of dissemination tools to reach target groups of primary school mainstream classroom teachers, classroom assistants, education authorities and dyslexia associations; and 

Ultimately, this project led to better professional outcomes; indeed, all partners involved reported increased awareness of dyslexia issues in their contexts, and began gearing their professional practices towards better provision for dyslexia.

2020-1-UK01-KA201-079226.title: Schools Programme for Ethical Enterprise Development
2020-1-UK01-KA201-079226.summary:
<< Background >>

The Consortium decided to apply for this project because it aligned with their shared passion for promoting youth entrepreneurship and sustainability. 
The project's objectives of providing students with lifelong skills and competencies through cross-curricular collaborations and non-formal learning in their local communities were considered essential to their personal and professional growth. 
The project addressed the need for reinforcing the development of key competencies, common values, civic engagement, participation, and environmental and climate goals in school education.
The SPEED project provided a set of tools and experiences to develop social and sustainable school enterprises, which aimed to change the lives of young people and improve their community by introducing them to new learning. 
As a result of this project, students in 4 European countries have had access to the SPEED Methodology, the SPEED Academy, the SPEED Tool Box, and the SPEED school enterprises. The project's innovative approach was changing the role of young people in school to become economic leaders for their community in a way that prioritises fairness and care for the environment.

<< Objectives >>

The consortium wanted to achieve the correct combination of new approaches of social innovation, social entrepreneurship and social inclusion with the development of key competences for pupils in the 4 European countries, by providing them with a set of tools for them to become leaders and changemakers in their community through the implementation of SPEED school enterprises. 
Addressing the needs for social inclusion and the challenges of the climate crisis along with its implications on the economy, the welfare system and the job market, were also part of the needs. 
The core goals were to identify, empower and train students and teachers along with additional stakeholders around their local community, with new resources in the field of social entrepreneurship and social innovation. 
It was a way to try to improve how enterprise is taught and experienced in schools, so that it is more aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals and addresses the needs of their own community. Young people experience the responsibility of taking the lead in dealing with environmental, social and economic problems, where they can learn and grow from their involvement and contribute to society and the economy in a fair way now and in the future.

<< Implementation >>

IO1 Methodology
A new methodology was developed by combining 3 existing ones: LocoSoco, FairShares-Shared Wealth, and NEMESIS-Social Innovation Education, to provide schools and communities in Europe with a framework to implement and run a SPEED school enterprise.
IO2 Academy
A training course available in 4 languages was developed for teachers, trainers and students. The Learning Course provided objectives, structures and requirements with constructivism and experiential learning. 
IO3 Toolbox
Development of a platform for communication and collaboration, individual user registration, a planner, a canvas for joint development, and a marketing platform.
IO4 School Enterprises 
The pilot phase of the project, providing tools for the implementation of SPEED social enterprises in schools. These enterprises were run by students with the support of teachers, staff, and the local community, and were part of the school's learning environment. 
IO5 Marketing and Road Show
The plan included creating products/services, defining target groups, marketing strategies, and promotional and action plans. The SPEED RoadShow was organised to showcase SPEED school enterprises and connect students and teachers from different countries.

<< Results >>

Concretely, the project produced tangible and intangible results: 
Tangible results included the methodology approach and the framework, the practical set of tools such as the e-learning tools available on the SPEED Platform, these will be available for all users for at least 5 years after completion of the project. And finally, the network of SPEED school enterprises, which allows for schools to connect to one another and exchange learnings and experiences. All outputs are in English, Greek, German and Croatian and are available on the SPEED website.
Additionally, intangible results from the project included the knowledge and experience gained by the participant organisations with regards to social innovation, social entrepreneurship and social inclusion; the increased skills and achievements developed by the interaction with the schools and pupils; the improved cultural awareness by working across the different European countries and the communication and language skills that were practised and developed during the duration of the project.
